item.title: [SCMP] Beyblade battles drive up sales at Hong Kong malls, but how long will the trend last?
item.description:
The sharp clatter of spinning metal tops, cheers, sighs of frustration and shouts of “Three, two, one … Go shoot!” echo across a shopping centre in Hong Kong’s New Territories on a weekday.

Dish-shaped plastic battle arenas known as “Beystadiums” have been set up not only in Tuen Mun Town Plaza, but also across the mall in different shops, where some players challenge shop staff to collect stamps for shopping vouchers.

The spinning toy popularised by Japanese anime in the early 2000s made a comeback in Hong Kong and across Asia early this year, with local fans flocking to public arenas to battle against other players and scrambling to buy hot models and rare parts.
item.content:encoded:
The sharp clatter of spinning metal tops, cheers, sighs of frustration and shouts of “Three, two, one … Go shoot!” echo across a shopping centre in Hong Kong’s New Territories on a weekday.

Dish-shaped plastic battle arenas known as “Beystadiums” have been set up not only in Tuen Mun Town Plaza, but also across the mall in different shops, where some players challenge shop staff to collect stamps for shopping vouchers.

The spinning toy popularised by Japanese anime in the early 2000s made a comeback in Hong Kong and across Asia early this year, with local fans flocking to public arenas to battle against other players and scrambling to buy hot models and rare parts.

Spotting the economic potential behind the hobby, local shopping centre operators across Hong Kong are converting public spaces into free battle zones to drive up foot traffic and sales and retain visitors.

The Tuen Mun Town Plaza even went a step further by scaling up the concept into a mall-wide strategy ahead of a major Beyblade tournament in August, encouraging shop operators to take part in the game and offer discounts to shoppers who present their tops.

“The strategy is about how a tenant can engage with customers through a shared interest, instead of directly selling to them,” said Bella Chhoa Peck-lim, chief commercial officer of Sino Group, which owns the shopping centre.

“It’s a soft-selling approach that allows staff and shoppers to start a conversation, drawing people into the store before making a sales pitch.”

What appeared to be a desperate measure by Hong Kong’s retail and catering sectors – still struggling with the trend of residents heading to mainland China for cheaper shopping and dining options – turned into an initial success.

Chhoa said the shopping centre had witnessed a “noticeable” 20 per cent surge in holiday foot traffic at the shopping centre after the promotion, as well as a 10 to 15 per cent rise in weekday attendance.

All in the game

At Hanamaruken, a ramen shop inside the Tuen Mun complex, co-founder Jelly Tong said her team upgraded the basic Beyblade provided by the landlord to a high-performance model to better compete with visiting players as they recognised the game’s potential to drive up business.

“Words then spread in their Beyblade chat groups that our store had an exceptionally strong set-up, and some kids ended up bringing six or seven friends over to challenge us,” Tong said. “Afterwards, they stayed here to eat and discuss our custom gear.”

The commercial benefits have extended beyond restaurants and toy retailers to high-end luxury tenants such as Luk Fook Jewellery. A regional manager said that setting up an in-store battle station helped break down traditional stereotypes surrounding luxury retail.

“We saw many new faces coming in after matching with our staff to browse our products and some actually made transactions,” said Patrick Ng Pui-kuen, the brand’s New Territories West district manager, who oversees the branches in Tuen Mun.

Among dozens of enthusiasts gathered at the shopping complex were 24-year-old warehouse worker Liu Chun-yin and his friend.

“Sometimes I show my spinning top at the nearby ice cream shop here to get special offers, or battle against the staff at the tea shop to win a discount,” Liu said.

His friend, a recent Beyblade fan, recalled a visit where he stayed at the venue from 2pm until 9pm, spending seven hours straight battling fellow players and purchasing food and drinks in between matches.

Over in D-Park in Tsuen Wan, dedicated free-play zones equipped with rows of desks have also drawn parents with young children alongside seasoned adult hobbyists.

Andy Yip, a 34-year-old civil servant from Kowloon East, made a dedicated trip to Tsuen Wan with his 11-year-old son and other family members, knowing there would be players at the venue.

“Before my son picked up the hobby, we spent most of our weekends in mainland China, but now we stay more in Hong Kong to accompany him, as he wants to play Beyblade with others,” he said.

Yip added that these outings were typically paired with dining and retail shopping, noting that he typically spent HK$1,000 (US$128) on dinner after his son played at D-Park, while their family members browsed at nearby shops during matches.

At Pioneer Centre in Prince Edward, a similar trend has recently unfolded, with management introducing a few Beyblade stadiums to attract a steady stream of parents and children, and launching a spend-to-draw promotion that offered exclusive models of the tops as prizes.

Eric Cheng, senior leasing manager at the mall, said the set-up and promotion in August had driven a 5 to 10 per cent increase in foot traffic compared with the same period last year, while sales at electronic goods and food and beverage outlets had jumped by 15 and 20 per cent, respectively.

“Compared with other intellectual property photo spots or traditional pop-ups, Beyblade’s interactive nature brings us much higher foot traffic,” Cheng said.

“Visitors at photo spots often leave after taking pictures, while playing Beyblade at the mall gets them to stay longer.”

Cheng said that longer stays could translate to higher spending as shoppers sought food and beverage options in between battles.

Only a short-term cure?

For all its resurgent popularity, the Beyblade trend offered only short-term benefits and was a temporary solution rather than a cure-all for the city’s broader retail sector challenges, according to one economist.

Professor Terence Chong Tai-leung, executive director of the Chinese University of Hong Kong’s Lau Chor Tak Institute of Global Economics and Finance, said shopping centres were ideal venues for Beyblade matches, which required space, and operators could set up play zones at a low cost.

“On a micro level, it drives temporary F&B spending as visitors have a reason to come,” Chong said, noting that overall retail has still failed to show significant growth over the past year.

But he stressed that such initiatives were insufficient to counter broader macroeconomic headwinds or the trend of residents spending across the border, pointing out that price remained the most significant factor driving consumer behaviour.

To stay relevant in the long run, Chong suggested that local shopping centres rethink their structural function, shifting from traditional sales hubs towards specialised themed venues or physical showrooms.

“Most successful malls in Hong Kong have distinct themes, and if you want to attract people, you have to concentrate,” he said. “For example, becoming the definitive hub for sneakers so that people will visit whenever they want to buy sneakers.”

Chong also suggested shopping centres evolve into showrooms where customers preview products before purchasing them online, rather than relying solely on traditional storefront sales.

“Due to structural shifts in shopping habits, consumer needs that used to require a mall visit can now be easily met through various online platforms.”

item.title: [SCMP] Israel-Turkey tensions rise after Netanyahu orders strikes on Syrian airbase
item.description:
Fears of a military confrontation between Israel and Turkey are growing after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu sought to assert dominance over Syria by ordering air strikes on a military airfield near the Turkish border.

The eight strikes on the Abu Al-Duhur airbase in northwest Idlib province on Tuesday were characterised by Netanyahu as a warning to Turkey against expanding its military presence in Syria or helping rebuild the Syrian armed forces.

Netanyahu’s office claimed Israel and Syria had agreed to “a status quo in security matters”, which Damascus was “on the verge of breaching” by permitting Turkish troops to deploy at the airbase near Aleppo.
item.content:encoded:
Fears of a military confrontation between Israel and Turkey are growing after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu sought to assert dominance over Syria by ordering air strikes on a military airfield near the Turkish border.

The eight strikes on the Abu Al-Duhur airbase in northwest Idlib province on Tuesday were characterised by Netanyahu as a warning to Turkey against expanding its military presence in Syria or helping rebuild the Syrian armed forces.

Netanyahu’s office claimed Israel and Syria had agreed to “a status quo in security matters”, which Damascus was “on the verge of breaching” by permitting Turkish troops to deploy at the airbase near Aleppo.

“Israel repeatedly warned Syria that such a deployment would pose a threat to Israel’s security. Syria chose to ignore these warnings,” Netanyahu’s office said in a statement issued on Tuesday evening.

The following day, the Israeli leader reframed the strikes as a “message” that he would not tolerate a Turkish military entrenchment in Syria that “advances southward, because it threatens us”.

“We conveyed that message: don’t,” Netanyahu told Israeli Army Radio. “But apparently they didn’t hear it, so we made sure they understood it better”.

His comments followed a rare expression of “deep concern” from Washington at Israel’s “unnecessary escalation”.

Because Israel gave no advance notice, the sudden appearance of its fighter jets on Turkish air-defence radars near the border could easily have triggered a clash.

Tom Barrack, the US special envoy for Syria and Iraq and ambassador to Turkey, said the Turkish military – the second-largest in Nato – “observed the aircraft heading north towards its territory and therefore could have reasonably prepared its own response.”

In 2015, Turkey shot down a Russian fighter jet under similar circumstances after it appeared to threaten an intrusion from Syrian airspace.

Observers echoed Barrack’s assessment in reactions posted on social media.

Turkey and Israel “may have no intention to get into a kinetic confrontation, but they could easily slide into one. Accidentally. Suddenly,” said Asli Aydintasbas, a Middle East fellow at the Brookings Institution. “This is why [Tuesday’s] incident was dangerous.”

Barrack, along with Turkish and Syrian officials, also disputed Israel’s initial claim of a build-up of “Turkish proxies” around Aleppo.

“The [Syrian] government has neither adopted a predatory posture nor maintained proxy forces,” Barrack said in an earlier social media post. “It has, in fact, repeatedly indicated a preference for de-escalation with Israel”.

Spheres of influence

Turkey has operated scores of military facilities across northwest Syria since intervening in the country’s civil war in October 2017.

But after rebels led by current President Ahmed al-Sharaa toppled the Assad government in December 2024, Turkish forces have not expanded their geographical footprint, according to observers.

Ankara briefly explored deploying forces to an airbase in central Syria soon after the takeover, but backed down after Israeli strikes hit the facility in March and April 2025, following visits by Turkish military delegations.

This incident established an informal status quo: Israel, which occupied part of southwest Syria soon after Assad’s fall, retained “freedom of action” over the southern half of the country, while the north became Turkey’s sphere of influence.

By striking Abu Al-Duhur on Tuesday, Netanyahu was now “asserting an Israeli security zone that stretches to the Turkish-Syrian border”, said Rich Outzen, a non-resident senior fellow with the Atlantic Council’s Turkey programme, who called the move “not wise”.

Analysts who spoke to This Week In Asia viewed the strikes as an ominous sign of things to come between Israel and Turkey.

Nir T. Boms, a counterterrorism expert and research fellow at Tel Aviv University’s Moshe Dayan Centre, said the incident had raised the risk of confrontation, though he thought “there is a long way to go” before one erupted.

“This is signalling to Damascus which, of course, is related to the growing Turkish role in shaping Syria’s military,” Boms said, adding that Israel was “concerned about this direction”, especially given the “track record of Turkish support for groups that have taken a very brazen line against Israel”.

Shaiel Ben-Ephraim, an Israeli-American geopolitical analyst and outspoken critic of the Netanyahu administration, expressed a similar view – saying that while Tuesday’s air strikes had increased the odds of an inadvertent confrontation with Turkey, “I don’t think that Israel wants a full-out war right now”.

He saw Netanyahu’s decision to escalate tensions partly as a political manoeuvre meant to rally right-wing support ahead of October’s general election.

“The typical use of security is to frighten voters into voting for the right,” said Ben-Ephraim, who is a senior analyst with strategic advisory firm Atlas Global Strategies.

Still, he warned of a “genuine risk” that miscalculation could trigger a wider confrontation, because “there are no clear borders for Turkish or Israeli influence in Syria and for Turkey this seems to be a primary interest”.

Giorgio Cafiero, CEO of the Washington-based risk consultancy Gulf State Analytics, said tensions between Turkey and Israel had been rising for years, “particularly since Ankara began filling a major vacuum in Syria” after Assad’s ousting in late 2024.

The latest strikes, within 45 miles (72km) of the Turkish border, “constitute a troubling development” because they showed that Israel “does not want to see Syria, under any leadership, rebuild itself militarily”, he said.

Such a scenario risked undermining Israel’s “vision for total dominance over the region”, Cafiero added, pushing the Netanyahu government to do “anything within its means to prevent any actor in the neighbourhood from challenging Israeli hegemony”.

So far, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has responded with relative restraint, rejecting Netanyahu’s claims of a military build-up as “untenable” on Wednesday, saying they “stem from Netanyahu’s intent to pursue expansionist and destabilising policies in the region ahead of the elections in Israel”.

But with Netanyahu’s leading rivals sharing his concerns about Turkey, analysts doubt a change of Israeli leadership would soften Israel’s approach towards Ankara.

“Most importantly”, the Israeli Defence Forces (IDF) were “hard-wired to solve every problem with military force and there is no counter, no diplomatic approach, to rein them in”, Ben-Ephraim said.

The Israeli foreign ministry had long ceased to counterbalance the IDF in any meaningful way and the concept of deterrence had “completely given way to pre-emption”, he said.

Ben-Ephraim expects “a long, tense confrontation between Turkey and Israel as Turkish ambitions increase while US power wanes” in the Middle East, Israel “grows more isolated” and Iran rebuilds.

Boms, by contrast hopes “a real change” in the Israeli government could “open a new slate” for different relationships across the region, Turkey included.

“But it takes two to tango and it does not seem that Erdogan is in a dancing mood,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Has Philippines’ Marcos missed his chance to stop the Dutertes?
item.description:
Less than two years before the Philippines chooses its next president, Ferdinand Marcos Jnr still has no candidate to carry his banner.

Sara Duterte-Carpio, his estranged vice-president and fiercest political rival, has already declared her intention to run and remains the early front runner, despite an impeachment trial that could bar her from politics.

Marcos said on August 14 that he would “certainly endorse a candidate” in 2028 but added: “Who that is I cannot tell you because even I don’t know.”
item.content:encoded:
Less than two years before the Philippines chooses its next president, Ferdinand Marcos Jnr still has no candidate to carry his banner.

Sara Duterte-Carpio, his estranged vice-president and fiercest political rival, has already declared her intention to run and remains the early front runner, despite an impeachment trial that could bar her from politics.

Marcos said on August 14 that he would “certainly endorse a candidate” in 2028 but added: “Who that is I cannot tell you because even I don’t know.”

The one candidate he almost certainly will not support is Duterte-Carpio, daughter of former president Rodrigo Duterte. Their 2022 alliance helped unite two of the Philippines’ most powerful political dynasties before collapsing into open war.

By launching her 2028 presidential bid earlier this year, the vice-president set up a succession battle that could decide not only who controls the Malacanang presidential palace after Marcos’ single, constitutionally limited six-year term, but also whether the country swings back towards Duterte-style strongman politics and a more China-friendly foreign policy.

On paper, Marcos’ former allies have rarely looked more vulnerable.

Rodrigo Duterte is in The Hague awaiting trial at the International Criminal Court on charges of crimes against humanity, while key allies of the family have been arrested on plunder charges.

At home, the Marcos administration has also allowed the machinery of government to move against Duterte-Carpio, who faces impeachment on allegations of corruption and betrayal of public trust.

A conviction on just one charge would be enough to remove her from office and bar her from future elections.

Yet Duterte-Carpio is still standing, and gaining ground. A June poll by WR Numero Uno showed her satisfaction rating rising to 55 per cent, from 33 per cent in March, while Marcos stood at 36 per cent.

Recent surveys by Pulse Asia Research Organisation, OCTA Research, WR Numero Research and Momentum Research have also shown her leading the early 2028 presidential field.

Analysts are now questioning whether Marcos moved too late to prevent the Dutertes from regrouping before the next election.

Ronnie Holmes, Pulse Asia president and a professor of political science and development studies at De La Salle University in Manila, called it “the central political puzzle” of Philippine politics.

Marcos had opportunities to contain the Dutertes earlier, Holmes said – including during the first impeachment initiative against Duterte-Carpio last year – but “chose accommodation over confrontation”.

“That decision may have allowed the Duterte camp time to regroup and rebuild its political base,” Holmes told This Week in Asia.

The rivalry is all the more combustible because Marcos and Duterte-Carpio rode to power together in 2022, uniting two dynasties with deep emotional claims on Philippine politics.

Marcos, the son and namesake of the late dictator ousted in the 1986 People Power Revolution, returned his family to Malacanang.

Duterte-Carpio brought with her the political machine her father built first in Davao City and then nationally as president, a machine powered by Mindanao’s resentment towards Manila, anti-elite politics and the strongman image Duterte cultivated through his deadly war on drugs.

Their alliance collapsed into a fight neither side has yet been able to finish.

The Marcos administration’s main weapon is the ongoing Senate impeachment trial, in which prosecutors are seeking to prove allegations of corruption, unexplained wealth and betrayal of public trust.

Senior officials in the executive branch have testified in support of the case, including allegations that Duterte-Carpio plotted to assassinate the president.

On August 11, the justice department filed a “grave threats” charge against the vice-president over a 2024 video in which she claimed to have hired an assassin to kill Marcos, his wife and his cousin.

Duterte-Carpio has denied any wrongdoing and says the cases against her are politically motivated.

The Duterte camp’s counter-attacks have produced weaker results. Supporters tried to evoke the spirit of 1986 by gathering at the EDSA Shrine in Quezon City in November 2024 and calling for Marcos’ resignation, but the protests failed to draw either mass public support or backing from the military.

Duterte endurance

The failed protests did not end the feud, they merely brought home the stalemate. Marcos has wounded the Dutertes but not yet neutralised them, lending weight to their supporters’ taunts that the president is “weak”.

Dr Jean Franco, a political-science professor at the University of the Philippines, said Marcos’ strategy had produced “hits and misses”, which had made that perception seem “warranted”.

Holmes said Marcos was “only recently” doing enough to prevent a Duterte comeback – “and arguably too late”.

Part of the problem, analysts say, is that the Duterte brand has proved sturdier than the legal cases against the family.

“Their enduring strength lies in the image projected by the former president, a brand that is purportedly anti-elite and decisive,” Holmes said.

Vic Rodriguez, a Duterte ally, put it down to “the Duterte charisma”. He credited Duterte-Carpio with an ability to “effortlessly connects especially with the masses. Without a doubt her father’s daughter”.

“Marcos relies on brute force, Dutertes [rely] on near-cultic popularity”, Rodriguez said.

Rodrigo Duterte was the first Philippine president to come from Mindanao, a southern region long resentful of what many there see as the dominance of “imperial Manila”.

The family’s pride in being Mindanaoan “makes many people in Luzon uncomfortable”, Rodriguez said.

Holmes agreed, saying: “Their brand as political actors from the periphery resonates, particularly in Central Visayas [Region] and Mindanao, which together account for roughly a third of the electorate.”

Franco said the Dutertes had tapped into the “imperialist Manila discourse” while also reviving the appeal of strongman rule.

“The father was able to surface the strongman appeal that Filipinos think is the answer to the perception that Filipinos need to be disciplined to improve law and order,” she said.

The family still has a large core of self-styled “Duterte Diehard Supporters”, or DDS, a badge of loyalty that has survived years of criticism over the drug war.

For many supporters, the Dutertes’ coarse language and threats are not liabilities but proof of toughness.

Dr Nuelle Duterte, a cousin of Duterte-Carpio and niece of Rodrigo, put it plainly: “Their brutality appeals to people. Matapang sila [they’re fierce], vs Marcos, who is weak.”

Racing towards 2028

That contrast could matter even more as the 2028 race approaches. Analysts say a victory for Duterte-Carpio could alter both the Philippines’ foreign policy and its style of governance.

Her father sought closer ties with Beijing during his presidency, playing down the South China Sea dispute and cooling security ties with Washington – an approach Marcos has largely reversed.

A Duterte-Carpio win could therefore trigger “a significant foreign-policy recalibration towards China” and raise concerns about “institutional accountability” and democratic governance, Holmes said.

Rodriguez rejected this view, however. “Nothing is farther from the truth. It is classic Marcos disinformation that is unfounded,” he said. “A Sara Duterte [presidency] will be similar to her Davao legacy of professionalism, efficiency and the Duterte brand of peace and order.”

For now, the race is still up for grabs. A survey released last week by Momentum Research showed Duterte-Carpio leading the list of possible presidential candidates, picked by 44.2 per cent of respondents.

Naga City Mayor Leni Robredo, who ran for president in 2022 and has said she is not interested in running again, came second with 23.8 per cent.

One option Marcos may still consider is persuading Robredo to run after all, paired with Senator Raffy Tulfo as her running mate.

Two surveys, by Octa Research in July and Tangere in May, suggested that hypothetical ticket could beat a Duterte-Carpio pairing with Senator Imee Marcos.

Val Villanueva, a former election strategist and now a finance columnist and analyst for Rappler, said current research data pointed to the Robredo-Tulfo tandem as “probably the most electorally competitive pairing against Sara Duterte”.

item.title: [SCMP] Why China’s reusable rocket breakthrough matters for the PLA’s ‘kill chain’
item.description:
A pair of landmark rocket recoveries in recent weeks has brought China a step closer to mastering reusable launch technology – a breakthrough analysts said could give the People’s Liberation Army an advantage in combat by increasing the resilience of its satellite-supported “kill chain”, the process of identifying, tracking and engaging a target.

In a first for China, commercial rocket company LandSpace recovered a stainless-steel booster using deployable legs after an orbital flight earlier this week. This followed a successful launch last month by state-owned China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation (CASC), which achieved the world’s first recovery of an orbital-class booster at sea using a net-capture system.

Defence experts said the technology would dramatically lower the cost of putting satellites into space and increase the frequency of launches. Mastering reusability will improve the PLA’s space capabilities – including communication, navigation and surveillance – much like how SpaceX supports the US military.
item.content:encoded:
A pair of landmark rocket recoveries in recent weeks has brought China a step closer to mastering reusable launch technology – a breakthrough analysts said could give the People’s Liberation Army an advantage in combat by increasing the resilience of its satellite-supported “kill chain”, the process of identifying, tracking and engaging a target.

In a first for China, commercial rocket company LandSpace recovered a stainless-steel booster using deployable legs after an orbital flight earlier this week. This followed a successful launch last month by state-owned China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation (CASC), which achieved the world’s first recovery of an orbital-class booster at sea using a net-capture system.

Defence experts said the technology would dramatically lower the cost of putting satellites into space and increase the frequency of launches. Mastering reusability will improve the PLA’s space capabilities – including communication, navigation and surveillance – much like how SpaceX supports the US military.

Malcolm Davis, a senior analyst with the Canberra-based Australian Strategic Policy Institute’s defence strategy programme, said space was the most crucial operational domain in modern warfare.

He said modern militaries relied heavily on space for everything from communications and battlespace awareness to positioning, navigation and timing using systems such as GPS.

Without those abilities, militaries could be left “effectively deaf, dumb and blind”, severely degrading their ability to communicate, understand what is happening on the battlefield and conduct operations, Davis added.

SpaceX has become a core enabler of US military space power. It provides rockets and relatively low-cost access to orbit to deploy and replenish large military satellite constellations through US Space Force projects, such as the Proliferated Warfighter Space Architecture.

LandSpace and CASC have yet to demonstrate the ability to reuse the recovered first-stage booster, but experts said reusability itself was the bottleneck.

Timothy Heath, director of the Virginia-based research firm Perceptum, said the principal advantage for the People’s Liberation Army would be the ability to replace or increase space capabilities during a conflict.

“In a conflict, the reusable rocket launch capability would allow the PLA to quickly recover from losses of space platforms or to expand space capabilities quickly,” he said.

“This could enable the PLA to maintain situational awareness, navigation and communications even as it loses satellites to adversary attacks.”

Namrata Goswami, a professor at Johns Hopkins University’s School of Advanced International Studies, said these reusable launch systems would become part of an integrated national infrastructure supporting commercial mega-constellations, military satellites, logistics and ultimately greater freedom of action in space.

She said reusable rockets, combined with replacement satellites and rapid launch operations, would be particularly important in a Taiwan contingency because the PLA increasingly relied on satellites for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR) as well as communications, BeiDou navigation and targeting across the Indo-Pacific.

“China is moving towards near-real time situational awareness that can support the tracking and targeting of mobile US and allied forces,” Goswami said.

“If damaged ISR or communications nodes can be replenished rapidly by China, disrupting the space layer may produce only temporary degradation rather than breaking the kill chain.”

Lieutenant General Douglas Schiess, the incoming US chief of space operations, said during his July nomination hearing that “the threat China poses is real”. He urged the US Space Force to strengthen its ability in the region to counter threats such as the PLA’s rapidly expanding space operations, particularly in the Indo-Pacific.

“They are using their intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance efforts to target our forces much farther than they ever have in the past. They’ve built a kill chain to be able to see our carrier strike groups, our bombers at much farther pace, speed and distances,” Schiess said.

In July 2023, China deployed swarms of satellites to monitor the Talisman Sabre joint military exercise between the US, Australia and other partners, ABC News reported at the time.

According to the Australian news service, 300 Chinese satellites conducted more than 3,000 overflights to survey ground-based activities.

China in 2024 established the PLA Aerospace Force, placing it directly under the Central Military Commission.

“I think the US will probably recognise that they have to live with the fact that the Chinese will be able to put satellites into orbit very quickly in the same way the Americans can,” Davis said.

“And I think that where the contest happens is not so much on Earth in terms of the US destroying Chinese launch systems or China destroying US launch systems. The contest happens in space where you have to fight in space on orbit.”

Space has become a key area of US-China competition. While China is still a few years behind the US, which has now moved to tackle full reusability with the Starship programme, experts said LandSpace’s achievements would help narrow the gap and erode the American advantage in space.

“Dropping the cost to launch will open up China’s space sector and encourage a lot of innovation and new space technologies that could have benefits for its national security,” said Victoria Samson, chief director of the space security and stability programme at the Washington-based Secure World Foundation.

“This might allow China to catch up to the United States in terms of space launch.”

Analysts said that the ability to produce satellites was also critical. Goswami said reusable rockets could become consequential when combined with China’s development of mass-produced satellites and large constellations.

As of April, China had 55 satellite manufacturing facilities with a combined annual production capacity expected to reach 7,360 satellites by 2030, according to Beijing-based research firm Hello Space.

SpaceX said in a regulatory filing earlier this year that it was able to produce an average of about 70 Starlink satellites per week between December and April, equivalent to roughly 3,640 satellites a year.

“We have seen Ukraine’s ability to use SpaceX’s Starlink satellites to fight Russia has become an important source of advantage. If China can launch many military satellites quickly and cheaply, this could provide a critical edge in battle,” Heath said.

item.title: [SCMP] SpaceX’s Starlink blackout punishes Myanmar civilians, not just cybercriminals
item.description:
SpaceX discontinued its Global Roam service for existing customers as of Monday. The US company offered no specific reason beyond regulatory compliance, but few would question the move, given the need to clamp down on the increasing number of cybercrime networks that tap into its Starlink services globally.

Yet in Myanmar, the Starlink move is a double-edged sword.

The country’s civil conflict has cut many people off from conventional digital communications. For conflict-affected communities, SpaceX’s decision could mean being disconnected from the internet.
item.content:encoded:
SpaceX discontinued its Global Roam service for existing customers as of Monday. The US company offered no specific reason beyond regulatory compliance, but few would question the move, given the need to clamp down on the increasing number of cybercrime networks that tap into its Starlink services globally.

Yet in Myanmar, the Starlink move is a double-edged sword.

The country’s civil conflict has cut many people off from conventional digital communications. For conflict-affected communities, SpaceX’s decision could mean being disconnected from the internet.

The move thus risks reinforcing the long-standing strategy of Myanmar’s military – and the current military-backed regime – governing through information control and the disruption of humanitarian services. The regime’s head recently noted that Starlink connections were being used by the online scam industry.

What he failed to mention was that many parts of Myanmar, including those held by anti-government forces, rely on Starlink to access the internet. Nearly 40 per cent of Myanmar’s townships now experience intermittent or total internet shutdowns every month.

Since the 2021 coup, the military has weaponised internet access, imposing mobile-network shutdowns and internet blackouts in conflict-ridden areas across the country. As the ensuing civil war has damaged telecommunications infrastructure, communities have been further isolated.

An estimated 13 million people – nearly a quarter of Myanmar’s population – rely on Starlink for digital access because no viable alternative exists in conflict zones.

Across much of Sagaing, Kachin, Karenni, Chin and other contested regions, healthcare providers, community-based organisations, schools and local administrative bodies depend on Starlink terminals to coordinate emergency medical referrals, organise humanitarian relief, deliver remote education and issue security warnings.

At least 6,000 schools run by local authorities and communities mostly operate online due to the ongoing civil conflict. Thousands of healthcare facilities in mixed-control and conflict areas also rely heavily on Starlink technology for daily coordination and operations.

For the relatively low price of around US$120 per month, one terminal can accommodate about 100 users. Most are humanitarian or community-based organisations and residents in conflict zones.

Myanmar is not officially licensed for Starlink operations. Formal regulatory approval would be required from the Myanmar authorities – something the military is not inclined to do, given Starlink’s use by both scam centres and opposition groups. Many terminals have reportedly been registered through other countries. All of which means the end of Global Roam has huge implications for the millions who depend on the roaming satellite service for emergency healthcare support, education and essential digital connectivity.

When the internet goes dark in a conflict zone, fear spreads faster than facts. Violence and human rights abuses become harder to document, verify, investigate and hold to account. In locations such as Saw township, where communities have faced military air strikes and bombing in recent months, the absence of reliable information has allowed rumours to spread rapidly. Villagers have fled in panic, sometimes towards danger. Satellite internet access enabled emergency medical teams and humanitarian workers to reach victims and provide immediate first-line support.

With Global Roam’s discontinuation and stricter guidelines for international use across other Roam tiers, local communities and humanitarian organisations in Myanmar are looking for alternatives.

A community worker in Myanmar’s dry zone said locally built mesh or radio networks could offer a temporary means of communication, but no alternative could match Global Roam’s affordability, portability, ease of deployment or scale.

Other options exist, in theory, such as geostationary-orbit satellites or an upgrade to Starlink’s Global Priority tier. But in practice, they are not realistic. High prices and limits on data usage put them out of reach for financially struggling local community organisations and people living in conflict zones.

There is another dimension here. Since 2025, Starlink has reportedly been under investigation by the US Congress for providing internet access to scam centres in Myanmar. This led to the shutdown of more than 2,500 terminals seemingly associated with scam compounds. Even before the recent policy change, users in Karenni (Kayah), Rakhine and parts of Sagaing had experienced Starlink access blockages as a result of crackdowns on scam operations.

Over the past five years, cybercrime syndicates along the Thai-Myanmar border have proliferated, using satellite internet to evade law enforcement and sustain billion-dollar scam networks targeting victims worldwide, despite crackdowns. SpaceX’s recent policy change shows that the company and US lawmakers are stepping up their response to criminal enterprises exploiting satellite technology.

But scam syndicates are not ordinary users. Local insiders anticipate that groups with the financial resources have already shifted to higher-priced connectivity options, including Starlink’s more expensive global plans, or switched to in-country internet services after relocating from the border areas to the inland Myanmar.

This is not the first time they have survived crackdowns. In 2025, China teamed up with the Thai and Lao authorities to launch a massive multinational operation against cross-border scam networks in the Thai-Myanmar border area.

Thailand has also cut off scam centres from landline internet, fuel and electricity. Last year, Starlink shut down devices used by the scam compounds. Yet the criminals adapted, shifting from industrial-scale operations to smaller ones, moving inland and changing their targets from Chinese nationals to Americans. These centres grew exponentially in 2025 and 2026.

More than 300 civil society organisations operating in Myanmar have urged the US government, SpaceX and the international community to consider establishing a “targeted restrictive mechanism” that denies scam centres access to the internet while preserving civilian connectivity.

Myanmar’s tech dependency dilemma represents a stark reality: the scam economy and humanitarian services both require internet access, but cutting off one could impose a far heavier burden on the other.

The question, therefore, is not whether governments and technology companies should combat cyber-enabled crime. They should. Rather, the question is whether they can do so without unintentionally undermining humanitarian operations and cutting off civilians from the internet.

Su Mon Thazin Aung is a Fellow with the Myanmar Studies Programme at ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute. She is also an Adjunct Assistant Professor at the Department of Southeast Asian Studies, National University of Singapore. This article was first published by the institute’s commentary website fulcrum.sg

item.title: [SCMP] India joins China and South Korea in push for Arctic shipping routes
item.description:
Climate change and conflict are conspiring to open up the Arctic to Asian commercial shipping, with China, South Korea and India all eyeing the icy short cut to Europe.

Last Saturday, Chinese shipping company Sea Legend launched the first scheduled weekly container service across the top of the world, marking the realisation of Beijing’s long-held ambition to build a “Polar Silk Road”.

It will not sail alone for long, however. This Sunday, South Korea’s PanStar Group plans to send its own pilot vessel from Busan through Russia’s Northern Sea Route (NSR) towards ports in the UK, the Netherlands and Poland.
item.content:encoded:
Climate change and conflict are conspiring to open up the Arctic to Asian commercial shipping, with China, South Korea and India all eyeing the icy short cut to Europe.

Last Saturday, Chinese shipping company Sea Legend launched the first scheduled weekly container service across the top of the world, marking the realisation of Beijing’s long-held ambition to build a “Polar Silk Road”.

It will not sail alone for long, however. This Sunday, South Korea’s PanStar Group plans to send its own pilot vessel from Busan through Russia’s Northern Sea Route (NSR) towards ports in the UK, the Netherlands and Poland.

India is also preparing to dispatch its first cargo ship along the same corridor next year.

“In 2027, we are planning to have the first pilot vessel running through the Northern Sea Route. We are seeing huge possibilities,” S. Venkatesapathy, a joint secretary in India’s shipping ministry, reportedly told the Arctic-Regions Forum in Arkhangelsk, Russia, on August 13.

Two crises are pushing Asian shippers north. The first is climate change: warming sea temperatures mean that the Arctic ice pack is no longer impassable in summer, opening a navigable window running roughly from July to October.

The second is geopolitics. Threats to shipping in the Red Sea, layered atop the near-total closure of the Strait of Hormuz amid the Iran war, have forced many shippers to divert around southern Africa, adding mounting costs and up to two weeks to journeys that once ran through the Suez Canal without incident.

The NSR promises to slash transit times between Asia and northern Europe by roughly two weeks compared to the Suez run, shortening shipping distances by up to 40 per cent.

Sea Legend says it can make the journey from Ningbo, China, to Felixstowe in the UK in around 20 days vs about 40 days via Suez.

“The NSR and the related Northeast Passage have great potential to connect Asia and Europe faster and more easily, and this potential is gradually starting to be realised,” said Ivan Lidarev, an Asian security expert at the Institute of South Asian Studies in Singapore.

“Significantly, it will also help transit more Russian energy resources to Asia.”

A route European explorers searched for and failed to conquer from the 1500s onwards is now the subject of serious commercial planning.

More than a short cut

For China, whose two-way goods trade with Europe reached €759 billion (US$887 billion) last year, according to European Union statistics, the advantages are obvious.

“China will be the main beneficiary,” Lidarev said. “The route will greatly facilitate its trade with Europe, a crucial trading partner amid tensions with Washington, and avoid US-controlled sea lanes and chokepoints.”

India’s interest in the NSR was as much about signalling as logistics, according to Cedomir Nestorovic, a geopolitics professor at ESSEC Business School who said using the route would advertise New Delhi’s “strategic autonomy” to Washington while also opening up a new channel to access Russian oil, gas and minerals.

Not only could the route shave weeks off India’s shipping times to Europe, Lidarev said it also offered Delhi leverage in talks on a long-awaited free-trade agreement with the United States.

Equally important was the enhanced connectivity to Russia’s far east that using the NSR could offer, said Uday Chandra, a political-science professor at India’s Ashoka University, pointing to Delhi’s parallel push to increase links between Vladivostok and Indian port cities such as Chennai, Visakhapatnam and Paradip.

China’s head start dated back to 2013, Chandra noted, when the first commercial transit of an Arctic shipping route by a Chinese merchant ship took place, five years before Beijing formalised its Polar Silk Road ambitions in a 2018 policy paper.

South Korea, meanwhile, plans to use Sunday’s trial voyage to test the commercial viability of the NSR, with its vice-minister of oceans and fisheries Nam Jae-hon recently proclaiming that the Arctic passage was “bound to become an alternative to Middle Eastern routes”.

The government-funded Korea Institute for Economic Policy think tank has estimated that travelling through the Arctic could cut journey times to Europe by about 10 days, shaving some 7,000km off the distance travelled.

In addition to South Korea, Lidarev said Japan had also shown an interest in the route, with Southeast Asian states such as Singapore set to follow, should the geopolitics align.

“Over the long term, if climate trends further extend the navigable window, East Asian economies will inevitably utilise the corridor to optimise seasonal trade,” Nestorovic said.

No Hormuz replacement

Despite the growing interest, traffic through the NSR remains modest. Last year, Norwegian non-profit research foundation the Centre for High North Logistics tracked 88 vessels making 103 transits, up from 97 in 2024 and just 43 in 2022.

Tanker shipments carrying Russian crude oil and petroleum products accounted for the bulk of the traffic last year, according to an analysis by the Eurasian Rail Alliance Index, alongside dry bulk carriers likely transporting coal eastward.

The route has its limits, however, offering no relief for energy flows restricted by chokepoints in the Middle East, which historically accounts for roughly half of China and India’s oil imports.

“The NSR cannot replace the Strait of Hormuz or the Strait of Malacca for Asia’s energy security,” Nestorovic said.

“The Arctic route connects northern Europe and Russian energy fields to East Asia, but it is geographically irrelevant for Middle Eastern energy flows.”

The NSR cannot replace the Strait of Hormuz or the Strait of Malacca for Asia’s energy security

Cedomir Nestorovic, geopolitics professor

Then there are the practical challenges. Navigable without icebreaker support for only three to four months a year, the NSR is also unpredictable due to the shifting Arctic ice floes and shallow waters that prevent the passage of mega-ships, according to Nestorovic.

Add to that sparse search-and-rescue coverage, steep insurance costs and environmental rules limiting commercial scale, and he said the route should be considered a supplementary seasonal corridor rather than a wholesale replacement for existing maritime arteries.

Environmental groups see other trade-offs. The non-profit Clean Arctic Alliance and Norwegian Bellona Foundation NGO have warned that the soot emitted by ships’ exhausts settles on Arctic snow and ice, increasing heat absorption and speeding up the melting of polar ice caps that opened up the route in the first place, exacerbating the effects of climate change.

Those trade-offs do not appear to be slowing Asia down, however, and a sea passage explorers gave up on centuries ago is now, for a brief window each summer, open for business.

Additional reporting by Agence France-Presse

item.title: [SCMP] China banned ivory, but Vietnamese gangs keep the trade alive
item.description:
Three months after leaving an inland port far up the Congo River, a consignment of timber arrived in Vietnam this summer concealing a secret it would take customs officials three weeks to uncover: nearly 1.2 tonnes of elephant ivory, smuggled halfway across the world.

Tracking data reviewed by This Week in Asia shows the shipment travelled some 9,000 nautical miles (16,700km) – with stops in Sri Lanka and Singapore – before reaching Quy Nhon, a port on Vietnam’s central coast.

Custom officers were tipped off to the contraband, sealed inside hidden compartments with wax, by port scanners that flagged hollow cavities in the timber.
item.content:encoded:
Three months after leaving an inland port far up the Congo River, a consignment of timber arrived in Vietnam this summer concealing a secret it would take customs officials three weeks to uncover: nearly 1.2 tonnes of elephant ivory, smuggled halfway across the world.

Tracking data reviewed by This Week in Asia shows the shipment travelled some 9,000 nautical miles (16,700km) – with stops in Sri Lanka and Singapore – before reaching Quy Nhon, a port on Vietnam’s central coast.

Custom officers were tipped off to the contraband, sealed inside hidden compartments with wax, by port scanners that flagged hollow cavities in the timber.

On August 6, they drilled into the hollowed-out logs and found 221 pieces of sawn tusk, most likely destined for China and potentially worth millions of US dollars.

Port authorities called it the largest seizure on record for Quy Nhon, yet it was far from the first time smuggled ivory was uncovered at a Vietnamese port.

Between 2009 and 2018 alone, some 56 tonnes of ivory were seized in Vietnam, according to international NGO the Environmental Investigation Agency (EIA), with a further 20 tonnes linked to the country seized elsewhere.

CITES, the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora, bans the trade in elephant ivory, requiring permits for the sale and transport of old artefacts.

After decades of being decimated by poaching, some of Africa’s elephant populations are now stabilising, largely thanks to China’s ban on elephant ivory sales. Imposed at the end of 2017, the ban slashed demand in what was the world’s largest market.

China’s domestic ivory ban, which leaves a loophole for people to keep possession of registered tusks highly prized in ornate carvings, followed its ban on the domestic rhino horn trade in 1993.

Prices for both ivory and rhino horn have tumbled since, and Africa’s elephants, decimated by poaching that cut numbers from around 1.3 million in 1979 to roughly 415,000 by 2015, have begun a tentative recovery, with conservationists now putting the total population at 450,000-490,000.

Compared to a decade ago, when “we had industrial-scale poaching and smuggling, we have made significant inroads”, said John Scanlon, CEO of the Elephant Protection Initiative, a pan-African alliance aimed at ending the ivory trade.

He credits a coordinated push by source, transit and destination countries, and praises China for crushing ivory stockpiles rather than merely banning their sale. But he is careful not to declare victory yet.

“That doesn’t mean to say [poaching] has stopped, or it cannot, in some unpredictable way increase again,” he told This Week in Asia. “You can’t rest on your laurels.”

The Hydra network

Demand for ivory has fallen in China since the ban, but black-market smugglers still carry out their illegal trade through Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia, where the newly wealthy prize elephant tusks as a marker of status.

Vietnamese syndicates now sit among the main players in a trade estimated to be worth hundreds of millions of US dollars a year.

In 2023, Nigerian courts jailed three Vietnamese nationals – Phan Viet Chi, Phan Hong Quan and Duong Van Thang – for six years apiece after convicting them of running the African end of a smuggling network nicknamed “Hydra”.

Hydra was not new to law enforcement. Five years earlier, Thai police had already moved against the Bach brothers, dual Vietnamese-Thai nationals linked to the network, arresting a suspected kingpin and even a wildlife-crime inspector at a Bangkok airport.

One of the brothers, Boonchai Bach, was detained in 2018 for allegedly smuggling 14 rhino horns worth around US$1 million from Africa to Thailand, but the case against him collapsed after a witness recanted.

An NGO later lamented that “one of the biggest wildlife crooks ever caught in history” had been let go. The Thai Supreme Court did sentence Bach to five years in prison in 2022, but he remains a fugitive.

At the market’s peak, a kilogram of rhino horn fetched around US$60,000 to US$65,000 – more than the price of cocaine and roughly on par with gold.

Impunity, still

This month’s seizure in Quy Nhon showed that “many of the other faces behind it [the ivory trade] still operate with impunity”, said Linh Nguyen, a senior wildlife campaigner with the EIA.

“Vietnamese and Chinese-led networks are still working across Africa and there is a sense that they are moving between southern Africa to Kenya, Tanzania and west,” she said, following the herds – and gaps in enforcement – wherever they lead.

Vietnam has made strides to shake off its unwanted reputation as a smuggling hub. Sentences for wildlife crime now run as high as 15 years behind bars and the EIA reports that both arrest and imprisonment rates have climbed.

“Vietnam has made a lot of efforts, but it can’t solve this problem alone,” Linh said, citing the circuitous route smugglers take as evidence of a global supply chain. “The government needs to engage with countries throughout the chain.”

The pressure has not let up elsewhere in the region, either. On August 16, authorities in Laos’ Bolikhamsai province, bordering Vietnam, seized 1.75 tonnes of tusks tied to a trafficking network and arrested 11 foreign nationals, the Laotian Times reported. Their nationalities were not disclosed.

CSI Savannah

Scientific advances have made it harder for wildlife traffickers to prosper. Forensic testing and DNA analysis can now trace a seized tusk back to the region that it came from, while intelligence sharing between customs agencies helps investigators zero-in on the syndicates working specific ports or smuggling corridors.

Interpol, the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime and a clutch of investigative NGOs now stand ready to assist almost any customs post in the world.

The Elephant Trade Information System, a global seizure database maintained by the WWF’s animal-trade monitoring arm Traffic, shows that more than 12 tonnes of ivory were seized in Vietnam at the trade’s peak in 2018.

“We can now find out very easily from forensic samples whether seized ivory comes from recent poaching, long-standing stockpiles or natural mortality of an elephant,’’ Scanlon said.

But conservationists know they face a formidable adversary, with deep pockets.

“A lot of this larger-scale smuggling is facilitated by corruption … transnational and organised by corrupting officials across boundaries,” Scanlon said.

In the illicit ivory trade, money still opens borders just as effortlessly as it unlocks commercial markets.

“Vigilance is key,” Scanlon added. “We don’t want to see this illegal market explode again.’’

item.title: [SCMP] Malaysia’s Anwar traded reform for power. Now Umno wants it all
item.description:
The roar from thousands of People’s Justice Party (PKR) delegates gathered at a grand convention centre in Melaka last weekend exuded all the confidence expected of a party leading Malaysia’s government.

The past three years have been the culmination of more than two decades of struggle for PKR, with it finally achieving its long-held goal of installing leader Anwar Ibrahim as prime minister and wielding the power to push through reforms.

Yet beneath the confident facade lurks a ruling party now scrambling to find its way.
item.content:encoded:
The roar from thousands of People’s Justice Party (PKR) delegates gathered at a grand convention centre in Melaka last weekend exuded all the confidence expected of a party leading Malaysia’s government.

The past three years have been the culmination of more than two decades of struggle for PKR, with it finally achieving its long-held goal of installing leader Anwar Ibrahim as prime minister and wielding the power to push through reforms.

Yet beneath the confident facade lurks a ruling party now scrambling to find its way.

PKR’s victory in the 2022 general election came at the cost of the very reforms it had promised to deliver, as Anwar had little choice but to negotiate compromises with erstwhile rivals, including former ruling party Umno, to steady his administration. Those trade-offs did not go unnoticed.

Anwar’s ruling Pakatan Harapan (PH) coalition, of which PKR is a founding and principal member, has suffered a series of bruising defeats across three state elections since November – and whatever platform the prime minister gave a once-deflated Umno has turned the party into the greatest threat to his rule.

Staring down the possibility of being turfed out of Putrajaya after just one term, PKR members are left wondering how to reverse the trend, especially as surging Malay nationalist sentiment carries a resurgent Umno forward.

“The delegates are all confused. They need clear direction,” a senior party leader told This Week in Asia, speaking anonymously due to the sensitivity of the matter.

“Before, it was about coming to power and raising Anwar as prime minister. Now what?”

Senior members who attended last weekend’s congress pointed to a disconnect between Anwar, his party’s top leadership and the rank and file, who have been left without a common purpose to rally around.

That gulf became apparent during Anwar’s opening speech at the congress last Saturday.

Delegates gave only a lukewarm response as their party president and prime minister listed out, at length, his administration’s successes in bolstering growth and investment numbers.

It was only when Anwar touched on the multibillion-ringgit scandal at the Tabung Haji pilgrim fund – made public last month – that the crowd roared to life, with some delegates passionately demanding retribution against Umno, the party in power when the alleged offences occurred.

That reaction offered the clearest indication yet that the prime minister and PH need to coalesce around a clear message if they hope to slow Umno’s momentum, and that of its nascent partnership with the opposition Pan-Malaysian Islamic Party (PAS).

“You see Umno and PAS talking about uniting the ummah [Muslim faithful], and claims that [PKR coalition partner] DAP is out to wrest power from the Malays. It’s simple messaging that people can easily understand,” the senior PKR leader said.

When comparing investments and other economic indicators, Anwar scored higher than past leaders, he said. “But the people here don’t understand all that. You need to present things using simple language.”

House of cards

The problems trace back to November 2022, when Anwar was named prime minister by former king Sultan Abdullah Ahmad Shah on condition that he form a unity government that included allies and rivals alike, to avoid a hung parliament.

The arrangement threw a lifeline to Umno, which had just suffered its worst electoral outing, winning fewer than 30 of parliament’s 222 seats.

From there, Anwar has been accused of setting aside his reform agenda and steering his government rightward, mirroring the previous Umno administration’s penchant for cracking down on sexual minorities and free speech in a bid to win over a Malay-Muslim majority suspicious of his motives.

Despite growing outrage from long-time supporters, the prime minister enjoyed a period of relative political stability over the first half of his five-year term, as economic growth and foreign investment hit record highs.

But that proved to be merely the calm before the storm.

The first salvo was fired in the Sabah state election last November, when Anwar’s PH coalition was all but wiped out. Hardest hit was the Democratic Action Party (DAP), the largest party in Anwar’s federal coalition, which lost every seat it contested.

Over the past two months, PH’s tenuous grip on power has truly sunk in, as it suffered back-to-back defeats at the hand of fellow federal partner, Umno.

Umno cruised to an extended supermajority in the southern state of Johor in July, then struck an informal alliance with Islamist rivals PAS to wrest control of Negeri Sembilan state from PH earlier this month.

The losses in the three state elections were the first tangible signs that Anwar and PH were in real trouble, after years of complaints from civil society groups and PH’s own support base about the lack of reforms following decades of promises.

Wong Chen, a three-term MP who quit PKR this month after being unceremoniously removed from a government post and cut off from his constituency fund, said the current trend pointed to PH losing the next national poll, which must be held by February 2028 at the latest.

If they don’t quickly reform in the last few months that they have, then they won’t even be able to win enough support

PKR defector Wong Chen on his former party

Wong, who later joined fellow former PKR leader Rafizi Ramli’s Bersama party, said the recent string of electoral losses proved that Anwar’s personal popularity was not enough to guarantee PH’s survival against Umno and PAS.

“They have to start accepting the fact that if they don’t quickly reform in the last few months that they have, then they won’t even be able to win enough support to be a strong opposition,” Wong said.

The losses did trigger a response from Anwar. Last weekend, he pledged that the government would proceed to repeal the controversial University and University Colleges Act 1971 – which student activists have long said stifles freedom of speech and expression – and fulfil promises to impose a two-term limit on the prime minister and separate the powers of the attorney general and public prosecutor.

But those pledges may amount to little if they only translate into legislative change, according to Timothy Wong, a senior analyst with government affairs consultancy BowerGroupAsia.

“There needs to be real action behind institutional reforms rather than relying solely on legislation to convince the majority,” he said.

“They will need to do more to convince a politically fatigued electorate, especially urban and middle-class voters who are feeling increasingly disenfranchised by the country’s politics.”

Complicating matters further is Anwar’s continued reliance on Umno, which long-time Malaysia watcher James Chin says has every reason to sabotage the prime minister’s reform push, leveraging its cabinet positions – and the budgets that come with them – to bolster its own electoral chances.

“If you want to do real deep reforms, you have to inform the cabinet. And of course Umno, which has a lot of ministers in cabinet, will try to sabotage it or not agree to it, so you’re stuck,” said Chin, a professor of Asian studies at the University of Tasmania.

“He [Anwar] knows deep down inside that Umno is plotting to win the next election and replace him as prime minister.”

Cracks in PH

Anwar caught a break, of sorts, last weekend, when delegates at DAP’s own convention voted decisively to remain within the governing coalition, after months of speculation the party might walk away.

But that lopsided vote belied the seething dissent within DAP’s ranks over how Anwar has managed the ruling coalition – especially his perceived favouring of Umno.

“Instead of bringing the coalition partners together, what has he done? He has divided us, pitted one against the other and empowered Umno. We cannot afford to ignore that,” DAP leader Sangeet Kaur Deo told her party’s convention.

“We cannot run away from the fact that today, under our government, Malaysia is more divided on racial lines than ever before. We cannot deny that there are scandals relating to corruption that have escalated during the time that we have been in power.”

Within PKR itself, the complaints are just as pointed. Some argue Anwar’s political instincts have curdled into self preservation.

His decision, in closing the party congress last Sunday, to announce an extra 222 million ringgit (US$54.6 million) in annual constituency allocations for MPs – money used for everything from pothole repairs to cash handouts for the needy – struck many grass-roots members as besides the point.

It did nothing to address the growing anger over stalled reform, critics say – with no explanation offered either for why three PKR MPs seen as loyal to Rafizi had their own allocations slashed.

Rafizi quit PKR after losing the deputy presidency to Anwar’s daughter, Nurul Izzah, in a contest he claimed was rife with nepotism.

Nurul Izzah has since stepped back too, beginning what the party has called a “leave of absence” to pursue her studies after serving her final days as her father’s deputy at the congress.

The extra funding fits a pattern: over the past two years, Anwar has pushed to increase cash handouts and maintain costly fuel subsidies despite the strain on public coffers, in a bid to win broader support.

One grass-roots leader offered a warning from history. “You can’t keep giving people freebies and expect them to love you. Look at what happened during BN’s time,” he said, invoking the Umno-led Barisan Nasional coalition that lost power in 2018 at the height of the 1MDB corruption scandal despite its own cash-handout scheme. “They still lost. We are doing exactly the same thing now.”

These internal rifts may not trigger an outright collapse of PH, but analysts warn that pressure from DAP and PKR supporters will keep mounting as long as Anwar prioritises political stability and his relationship with Umno over the reform agenda.

“The bigger danger is not PH formally breaking apart, but becoming increasingly hollowed out as an electoral alliance,” said public policy adviser Kamles Kumar, associate director for Malaysia at strategic advisory group Asia Group Advisors.

“If electoral losses continue, the question will increasingly shift from whether PH can stay together to whether staying together still benefits each component party.”

And the next test for PH is not far off. The Melaka state election, which must be called by February next year, is already looming and the Umno-led BN – which holds 21 of the state assembly’s 28 seats – has signalled its terms for any future deal: PH can have a shot at the seven seats BN does not currently control, but nothing more.

The bigger danger is not PH formally breaking apart, but becoming increasingly hollowed out

Kamles Kumar, public policy adviser

According to one Melaka-based PKR grass-roots leader, the party leadership is seriously considering the offer, even if it means accepting a subordinate role to Umno.

Yet this appears badly out of step with sentiments on the ground. “The top are talking about negotiating with BN, but we’ve already seen what happened in the two past state elections. On the ground, people are already sharpening their knives,” the insider said.

“As far as the grass roots are concerned, we have two choices. Fight and lose, or not do anything and die [politically].”

Anwar has promised party delegates he will listen: to their opinions, their suggestions and even their criticism.

For a party that spent 20 years fighting to put him in power – and is now watching that power slip through its fingers – the question is no longer whether he hears them.

It is whether, after everything, just listening will be enough.

Additional reporting by Iman Muttaqin Yusof

item.title: [SCMP] As natural disasters rage, does China’s ‘top-down’ climate model provide a way forward?
item.description:
A punishing drought is draining Europe’s great rivers, pushing the Loire, the Danube and the Rhine towards record lows.

At the Kaub gauging station, the reference point for shipping on the Rhine – Germany’s economic artery – the water level fell to 17cm (6.7 inches) this month, a low unseen since measurements began in 1880.

Meanwhile, wildfires are burning across southern Europe, forcing the evacuation of hundreds of thousands and producing the defining image of a European summer in which disaster has come to feel as seasonal as the holidays.
item.content:encoded:
A punishing drought is draining Europe’s great rivers, pushing the Loire, the Danube and the Rhine towards record lows.

At the Kaub gauging station, the reference point for shipping on the Rhine – Germany’s economic artery – the water level fell to 17cm (6.7 inches) this month, a low unseen since measurements began in 1880.

Meanwhile, wildfires are burning across southern Europe, forcing the evacuation of hundreds of thousands and producing the defining image of a European summer in which disaster has come to feel as seasonal as the holidays.

But this is not a story unique to any one continent or hemisphere. In recent weeks, smoke from intensified Canadian wildfires drifted down the American east coast, leaving New Yorkers struggling to breathe, while China has battled a prolonged heatwave and persistent floods while bracing for what could be the strongest El Nino cycle in the past 150 years.

The cascade of crises has revived an old question: how should societies adapt to a rapidly changing climate? It is one the world’s three leading economies are answering very differently.

The green transition is no longer something [China] needs external pressure to pursue. It’s a basic national development strategy

Jiangwen Guo, Chatham House

The results, analysts warn, are just as disparate. China’s government can set long-term plans and back them with public money and strong execution.

The United States leans heavily on its private sector, with little public effort to match. Europe sits uneasily between the two: its public institutions short of long-term vision and money, its private sector short of awareness.

“Compared with the Western system, China’s greatest advantage in these areas is its very strong capacity for top-down implementation,” said Jiangwen Guo, a senior research fellow in the Environment and Society Centre at Chatham House.

“That is the root of all of this.”

Governments everywhere face the same three challenges on climate adaptation, according to Guo.

The first is that adaptation is hard to quantify. Cutting emissions produces a number, so investors can see what their money bought; protecting a city against future heat does not, and public attention fades with the weather.

Each heatwave, wildfire or flood in Europe makes the threat feel real, she said, and once it passes, the scar is easily forgotten.

The second is that risk is intensely local, which makes region-by-region risk assessment an indispensable first step. China’s 2035 adaptation strategy, published in 2022, devotes a full chapter to it, an advance on its predecessors.

The third is that adaptation cuts across regions, industries and government departments, making coordination extremely difficult, especially when it is already a lower priority for many.

China faces all three, Guo said, but was likely to implement solutions better than most, with the central government recognising the need for climate adaptation and willing to invest in it.

“Across China, the green transition is no longer something the country needs external pressure to pursue. It’s a basic national development strategy,” she said.

That strategy carries benefits as well as drawbacks. China’s rapid production of solar panels, for instance, brought prices down and encouraged widespread adoption – but the abundant supply has proven difficult to stem, with fierce intra-industry competition driving down prices and leading the country’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology to deem the phenomenon an issue that must be “comprehensively addressed”.

European analysts said crucial elements were missing from the continent’s efforts to adapt to the rapidly changing climate.

“The economic and political mindset of our current leaders tends towards letting the market decide rather than planning for the long term,” said Clement Caudron, a project lead at The Shift Project, a Paris-based climate think tank.

France was not putting enough resources into its climate efforts, while the absence of a long-term vision and sufficient, stable public funding made it hard for businesses and ordinary people to plan ahead, according to Caudron.

Budget constraints were also limiting the government’s ability to launch major public investment programmes in strategic sectors, Caudron explained. Climate, he said, was often among the first items to be sacrificed in budget negotiations.

The Fonds Vert (Green Fund), a French government fund created in August 2022 after a summer of heatwaves to help local authorities pay for environmental infrastructure – including climate adaptation – has seen the money available for new projects fall from €2.5 billion (US$2.9 billion) in 2024 to €1.15 billion in 2025, and €837 million in this year’s budget.

“Exceptions do get made in major crises – during Covid, we allowed ourselves to spend public money to support the economy and stave off a collapse – which proves we can do it when we want to,” Caudron said.

“But for the climate, the emergency is evidently not deemed sufficient to justify the same.”

Similar challenges were present at the EU level, according to Antoine Oger, executive director of the Institute for European Environmental Policy think tank.

He said climate adaptation required systematic efforts and significant investment in near-term budgets, but the effects might only be felt in the long term, which are not in sync with politicians’ short-term mandates.

“For them it’s not particularly enticing to make some decisions that will have impact in 20 years from now, from a purely political perspective,” he said.

The EU also struggles with its complex governance system that makes the massive, coordinated effort necessary for harmonised climate adaptation policies difficult, according to Oger.

Where Brussels is hemmed in by electoral cycles and shared competences, Beijing can plan in decades, Oger said, crediting this area as one where China’s system had the edge.

“There are, of course, different governance layers in China, but this is a much more integrated system to deal with this sort of long-term change … The five-year planning is much better than an electoral cycle, from a governance perspective,” he said.

Oger said he was not arguing for the EU to adopt China’s model, which had problems of its own. But, he added, a system built around a stable, coherent and long-term outlook was better equipped for a slow-moving, systemic challenge like climate change. “That is just a fact.”

The EU also lags on private-sector awareness, an area where the United States offers a model, according to Thibault Laconde, founder of Callendar, a French firm that helps companies adapt to climate change.

Since the Los Angeles fires and a run of severe droughts, many American companies have moved to protect themselves against future extreme weather, he said. Corporate awareness, in his view, may matter more for adaptation than public awareness did.

“If you’re a company, you do not need an incentive to do it. It’s in your own interest to make sure your factory or your infrastructure can keep operating reliably,” Laconde said.

But the private sector-driven model in the US also had its own limitations – in particular, a lack of “patient capital” provided by the government – to help companies overcome their short-term impulses in their long-term investments, according to Todd Tucker, director of industrial policy and trade at the Roosevelt Institute.

The United States still did not have a national plan for climate adaptation, and most states lacked one too, wrote Madison Condon, a professor at Boston University School of Law, in a report published by the institute in July. Both China and the EU have adopted blueprints.

And there are some gaps in this realm the private sector cannot fill. When Washington moved to dismantle the National Centre for Atmospheric Research, American insurance actuaries formally objected, Condon noted, arguing the centre’s continuity was “not only a scientific necessity, but an economic one” for an industry that depended on its data to price climate risk.

Even in those areas where commercial providers present alternatives, opting for the private-sector option carries risks.

The US state of Connecticut licensed climate-risk scores from a private firm, an approach Condon warned left the government endorsing black-box models whose inputs and methodology it did not control, adding that publicly maintained models could serve as a check on private-sector data.

Regardless of the system, the increasing urgency of the need for climate adaptation is clear, and the costs of inaction are climbing, according to the UN Environment Programme.

Climate-related extreme events cost the world an estimated US$140 billion a year between 2000 and 2019, per the programme’s latest Adaptation Gap Report, an annual figure projected to reach between US$1.7 trillion and US$3.1 trillion by 2050, depending on how much the planet warms.

“Budgets may be tight. There may be many competing priorities. But the smart choice is to invest in adaptation now,” wrote the programme’s executive director Inger Andersen in the report, “to minimise loss of life, to soften damage to infrastructure and, ultimately, to protect economies from the stronger climate impacts that are approaching over the horizon”.

item.title: [SCMP] Philippine flood-control scandal resurfaces after latest monsoon deluge
item.description:
The latest floods to hit Metro Manila and parts of the Philippines’ main island of Luzon have turned a familiar seasonal disaster into a renewed test of political accountability for President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr, as anger over allegedly corrupt flood-control projects returns to the centre of public debate.

Analysts said the deluge had sharpened scrutiny of the slow-moving investigation into allegedly substandard and non-existent flood-control works, exposing the gap between Marcos’ anti-corruption message and the lack of visible results in communities that continue to bear the brunt of extreme weather.

Metro Manila was inundated on Monday with 201.7mm of rain in just five hours, leaving residents wading through floodwaters, vehicles stranded and some areas not usually considered flood-prone submerged.
item.content:encoded:
The latest floods to hit Metro Manila and parts of the Philippines’ main island of Luzon have turned a familiar seasonal disaster into a renewed test of political accountability for President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr, as anger over allegedly corrupt flood-control projects returns to the centre of public debate.

Analysts said the deluge had sharpened scrutiny of the slow-moving investigation into allegedly substandard and non-existent flood-control works, exposing the gap between Marcos’ anti-corruption message and the lack of visible results in communities that continue to bear the brunt of extreme weather.

Metro Manila was inundated on Monday with 201.7mm of rain in just five hours, leaving residents wading through floodwaters, vehicles stranded and some areas not usually considered flood-prone submerged.
