Outside the capital, villages across parts of Luzon were also swamped after weeks of southwest monsoon rains, forcing thousands of families from their homes and reviving a familiar question: why does the country keep flooding despite huge sums spent to prevent it?

That frustration was reflected by Senator Panfilo Lacson, who questioned why communities continued to be submerged year after year, despite nearly 2 trillion pesos (US$32.4 billion) being poured into flood-control projects since 2011.

“1.939 trillion pesos funded the DPWH [Department of Public Works and Highways] flood control management programme under three presidents from 2011 to 2025, and the result is uncontrolled floods,” he said in a statement on Tuesday.

In the town of Macabebe in Pampanga, a store owner barricaded the front of his shop with sacks of rice to stop water from seeping in, an image some local media outlets and content creators portrayed as a sign of creativity and resilience.

But other Filipinos pushed back online, with several posts rejecting the familiar celebration of resilience gaining traction.

“Can we pressure our government to come up with better solutions instead of romanticising Filipino resilience?” one widely shared post said. “Our fellowmen shouldn’t be suffering through this in the first place … as if we don’t pay taxes and we don’t have billions of funds for flood control projects.”

Another post, which drew more than 7,000 reactions, captured the frustration more bluntly: “Rain is natural. Heavy flooding isn’t. Until now, no one has been held accountable for the billions’ worth of corruption in flood control projects. Until now, the government remains reliant on aid.”

Scandal back in focus

The latest floods have returned attention to the country’s investigation into allegedly corrupt flood-control projects, while intensifying criticism of the government’s failure to protect communities from a disaster that returns with each rainy season.

During his state of the nation address in late July, Marcos announced that errant high-ranking officials of the DPWH, contractors and lawmakers had been detained and charged over their involvement in the scheme, a year after investigations began.

In his address the previous year, Marcos said 545 billion pesos had been spent on flood-control works since 2022 across nearly 10,000 projects, but most had been found to be substandard or “ghost” projects, implicating a number of lawmakers, government officials and contractors who allegedly colluded in the scheme.

Last month, the Department of Justice said 841 million pesos had been recovered from those implicated in the scandal and deposited in the national treasury.

As of late July, 45 individuals and two contracting firms had been charged in 26 flood control-related cases in court.

But observers echoed a public sentiment that has grown louder with each flood: progress in holding people accountable and getting answers from the scandal has been too slow relative to its scale.

“More than a year since the issue was raised, there were only a few people who were charged in courts. At this stage, most of the alleged perpetrators should have been facing the judicial process,” said Nathaniel Candelaria, an assistant professor of political science at the University of the Philippines Diliman.

Arjan Aguirre, an assistant professor in Ateneo de Manila University’s political science department, said the investigations had moved too slowly given the scale of the allegations and the amount of public money involved.

“At this point, we should already be seeing clearer findings, stronger accountability and concrete action against those responsible,” he said.

Aguirre said the slow pace of the investigations raised concerns they might not be fully independent or could become politicised, especially if people felt they were being used to target political opponents or pressure lawmakers.

“Ultimately, the credibility of the probe will depend on whether it can demonstrate that accountability is being pursued consistently, regardless of political affiliation,” he added.

Political risk

Observers said the sluggish pace of inquiry would only sow further distrust in the Marcos administration, as the president grappled with modest ratings.

Marcos’ trust rating dropped to 34 per cent in June from 35 per cent in March, while his rival, Vice-President Sara Duterte-Carpio, polled at 57 per cent, according to local pollster Social Weather Stations.

“This year’s flooding could further deepen public anger and distrust towards the government,” Aguirre said.

Every time communities were submerged, Aguirre said people were reminded not only of the billions supposedly spent on flood control, but also that the same vulnerabilities persisted.

Despite the Marcos administration touting its accomplishments in the anti-corruption investigation and Marcos himself promoting a stronger anti-corruption message, analysts said actual shortcomings would continue to overshadow any progress.

“While some people were already facing cases, I do not think the administration is successful in this issue … the people need to know the truth about the flood control scandal and those who were involved, regardless of political affiliations, must face justice,” Candelaria said.

Aguirre said the Marcos administration appeared to be putting considerable effort into improving its image and promoting an anti-corruption message, but this had not been matched by the same urgency in addressing the flood-control scandal and institutionalising reforms.

Marcos risked having his anti-corruption agenda viewed as “political messaging rather than meaningful reform” if people continued to experience flooding while seeing little concrete progress in the scandal, Aguirre said.

With flooding still a constant threat for many Filipinos, the issue looks set to haunt the administration right up to the 2028 national elections, when Duterte-Carpio has indicated she will run for the presidency.

“The Duterte camp has been using the flood control scandal against Marcos from the beginning and I expect them to continue doing so in the 2028 campaign. They have been effective in framing the issue as evidence that Marcos is politicising the investigation and protecting his allies,” Aguirre said.

“The delays we are seeing now only give greater credence to that narrative. If the government fails to produce clear findings, prosecutions, and reforms, the Duterte camp can easily turn the scandal into a broader argument that the Marcos administration talks about anti-corruption but is unwilling to hold its own allies accountable.”

item.title: [SCMP] ‘No bandwidth left for the family’: why many Singaporeans want to be child-free
item.description:
As Singapore’s Prime Minister Lawrence Wong prepares to unveil plans to ease the strain on families during his National Day Rally speech on Sunday, a new survey points to a difficult question behind the city state’s record-low fertility rate: what if a substantial share of residents no longer want children at all?

Nearly one in four Singaporeans aged 18 to 44 surveyed by YouGov in July said they had no children and did not intend to have them in the future.

Zahir Latif and his fiancée are among them.
item.content:encoded:
As Singapore’s Prime Minister Lawrence Wong prepares to unveil plans to ease the strain on families during his National Day Rally speech on Sunday, a new survey points to a difficult question behind the city state’s record-low fertility rate: what if a substantial share of residents no longer want children at all?

Nearly one in four Singaporeans aged 18 to 44 surveyed by YouGov in July said they had no children and did not intend to have them in the future.

Zahir Latif and his fiancée are among them.

For eight years, the couple have returned to the same question: should they have children? Each time, the conversation has ended in the same place.

They worry about money, time and the fear of losing themselves, Zahir, 42, said. The unstable income that comes with freelance work – he is a content creator and his fiancée is a writer – has also made parenthood feel incompatible with the life they have built.

Taking on a stable 9-to-5 job could mean giving up any semblance of work-life balance, he added.

“Besides money, time is something Singapore struggles to give back to its citizens,” he said. “If you want to get enough sleep, your day is pretty much over in a few hours after work.”

The couple’s decision reflects one of the most striking findings of the survey, based on responses from 496 Singaporean adults aged 18 to 44 collected in July: 23 per cent said they did not currently have children and did not plan to have them in the future. A 2023 YouGov poll found the proportion was 25 per cent among 1,023 respondents aged 18 to 55.

The limits of policy were also evident, with 30 per cent of Singaporeans aged 18 to 44 saying there was nothing the government could do to make them more willing to have children.

Lower-cost preschool and childcare was the policy most likely to encourage parenthood, cited by 35 per cent of respondents in that age group, while improved work-life balance through national initiatives and increased cash incentives were each mentioned by 31 per cent.

The findings showed that giving Singaporeans their time and lives back was as critical as providing financial support, said Vincent Chua, an associate professor of sociology and anthropology at the National University of Singapore.

Singapore’s economic system had made work and raising a family “mutually exclusive” activities, Chua said.

“Modern capitalism demands maximum extraction of labour – not just in terms of hours, but in cognitive focus and emotional energy, and raising a family is an intensive, non-market activity requiring immense emotional and physical bandwidth,” he said.

“In a highly competitive society, there is simply no bandwidth left for the family.”

Zahir said that any scenario they had considered involving children usually meant moving abroad, where cost and time pressures were less intense. “Unless Singapore changes its work culture, no amount of money can change our minds.”

Singapore’s resident total fertility rate fell to a record low of 0.87 in 2025, even after years of state support aimed at making parenthood more affordable and manageable.

Those measures include baby bonus cash gifts, grants and co-matching for children’s savings accounts, healthcare support for newborns, preschool subsidies and lower fee caps at government-supported childcare centres.

In April, Singapore also expanded its shared parental leave scheme from six to 10 weeks, increasing the total government-paid parental leave to 30 weeks for eligible parents.

Officials have repeatedly said the challenge goes beyond money.

In April, a work group chaired by Minister in the Prime Minister’s Office Indranee Rajah was formed to tackle the declining birth rate, with a mandate to review support across marriage and parenthood.

Last Saturday, Indranee told local media that the team had been receiving feedback from Singaporeans, with a full report expected early next year.

“What is clear is that many do aspire to get married and have children,” she said. “But at the same time, they do encounter challenges including the cost of raising children, the need for time with family, caregiving arrangements and housing.”

Prime Minister Wong earlier this month acknowledged the growing barriers faced by those navigating parenthood.

“Across the world, family life is coming under greater strain. Expectations have risen, and parents feel pressured to give their children the best possible start in life. At the same time, many are caring for ageing parents while balancing the demands of work,” he said during his National Day message on August 8.

The government was taking a fresh look at issues such as the cost of raising children, access to affordable childcare and other ways to lighten the load on families, he added.

Wong is expected to speak about the plans in more detail during his National Day Rally speech on Sunday.

Focus on family well-being

Even so, analysts say Singapore’s fertility challenge should not be read as beyond repair, but as one that may require a broader definition of success: making family life more sustainable for those who already have or still want children, rather than relying only on incentives to lift birth numbers.

“I would not call it hopeless,” said Tan Poh Lin, a senior research fellow at the Institute of Policy Studies, of efforts to raise Singapore’s birth rate. “However, I do view that the demographic transition has now entered a new phase where more simply do not want children regardless of circumstances.”

Singapore was likely to shift its focus to improving family well-being throughout parenthood and expected measures would include enhancements to cash gifts and childcare leave to benefit families with older children, Tan added.

“Apart from more financial and workplace support, what is needed by families is a greater sense of economic security, including access to upskilling opportunities and employment support,” she said. “What is needed is the right environment, crucially a sense of stability and security.”

To have generous family-friendly policies like those in Nordic countries, Chua said society must accept a high-tax social model.

While the Nordic model was enticing, he added that it might not be replicated easily in Singapore due to its work culture.

“Workers who actually utilise such generous leave would likely face career discrimination and employers might simply self-censor and avoid hiring married couples with young children altogether,” he said.

Tax manager Debbie Lin has been wrestling with whether to have a second child. While her heart is set on giving her daughter a sibling, she vividly remembers the sacrifices she had to make for motherhood.

Lin rejoined the workforce in February after putting her decade-long career on pause for two years to focus on raising her daughter. “When I look at peers who are continuously employed, I estimate that I am now around 30 to 40 per cent behind some of them in terms of salary and career progression,” she said.

Companies needed to be encouraged to adopt family-friendly policies, Lin said, to dispel fears prospective parents might have about opportunity costs to their careers.

“A family-friendly policy that employees are afraid to use is not really a family-friendly policy,” she added.

item.title: [SCMP] Hong Kong Tiananmen vigil organiser, former leaders guilty of inciting subversion
item.description:
The now-disbanded alliance behind Hong Kong’s annual Tiananmen Square vigil and two of its former leaders have been found guilty of inciting subversion under the national security law by advocating an end to “one-party dictatorship” in mainland China.

In a 216-page judgment delivered at West Kowloon Court on Friday, three High Court judges ruled that any attempt to overthrow or undermine the Communist Party of China’s leadership could constitute a subversion offence because the country’s constitution did not permit Western-style democracy.

They found the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China, its former chairman Lee Cheuk-yan and former vice-chairwoman Chow Hang-tung had incited public hatred towards the party by likening Beijing’s crackdown on protesters in 1989 to local authorities’ suppression of the 2019 anti-government demonstrations.
item.content:encoded:
The now-disbanded alliance behind Hong Kong’s annual Tiananmen Square vigil and two of its former leaders have been found guilty of inciting subversion under the national security law by advocating an end to “one-party dictatorship” in mainland China.

In a 216-page judgment delivered at West Kowloon Court on Friday, three High Court judges ruled that any attempt to overthrow or undermine the Communist Party of China’s leadership could constitute a subversion offence because the country’s constitution did not permit Western-style democracy.

They found the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China, its former chairman Lee Cheuk-yan and former vice-chairwoman Chow Hang-tung had incited public hatred towards the party by likening Beijing’s crackdown on protesters in 1989 to local authorities’ suppression of the 2019 anti-government demonstrations.

While stressing it was not unlawful for the alliance to organise vigils to mark the crackdown, the panel said the defendants had used the annual event to attract new supporters and instigate them to take action to oust the ruling party.

“[The defendants] did not genuinely and honestly believe that their words and deeds were not in breach of the national security law. They just refused to pull back from the brink and were bent on embracing the alliance’s resistance line to the very end.”

Justices Alex Lee Wan-tang, Johnny Chan Jong-herng and Anna Lai Yuen-kee will hear oral mitigation arguments on August 28 before delivering the sentences.

Beijing’s national security office in Hong Kong said the defendants should be harshly punished for severely undermining the city’s fundamental interests and endangering the state’s constitutional order.

A government spokesman praised the verdict as a reasoned judgment, while accusing “external forces” of making “blatant and persistent” attempts to vilify local authorities through political manoeuvres and misleading statements.

Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said that anyone who tried to “shift the goalposts” or cover up their crimes with “clever words and flattery” would not escape justice.

Security minister Chris Tang Ping-keung said the verdict highlighted the importance of the Chinese constitution in the city’s constitutional order and offered clearer guidelines for law enforcement.

Police Chief Superintendent Steve Li Kwai-wah, of the force’s national security department, declined to say whether future discussions of the 1989 crackdown would constitute an offence. He said event organisers had to comply with relevant laws.

Former lawmaker Lee and Chow, a barrister, have been remanded in custody for nearly five years. A fourth defendant, former vice-chairman Albert Ho Chun-yan, has also been detained for more than four years and is awaiting sentencing after pleading guilty to the offence in January.

Lee’s wife, Elizabeth Tang Yin-ngor, said she was “very angry” over the ruling because she felt the judges did not give sufficient consideration to the defence’s arguments and evidence.

Chow’s mother said she hoped that “flowers of all colours can blossom”.

The court heard that putting an end to “one-party dictatorship” was among the alliance’s five operational objectives, which also included vindicating the 1989 protest movement and building a democratic China.

The trial centred on Article 1 of the Chinese constitution, which was amended in 2018 to describe the party’s leadership as the “defining feature of socialism with Chinese characteristics”.

The judges noted that the article effectively required the country to be run solely by the party as a socialist state. The role of other “democratic” parties, they said, was restricted to taking part in the “patriotic united front” under the party’s leadership.

The defence contended that all the alliance’s objectives were a legitimate exercise of fundamental human rights.

Lee testified that the one-party system was incompatible with the constitution’s preamble, which provides for “multiparty cooperation and political consultation” under the party’s leadership.

Chow argued that pursuing democratic change in society should not be considered illegal in the first place.

The judges rejected their assertions, saying the defendants did not simply seek more diverse political participation on the mainland but hoped to overthrow and undermine the party.

They said Lee, Ho and Chow had all along been hostile towards the regime and refused to make any compromise.

The defendants never saw any opportunity for a peaceful dialogue with central authorities or any chance that Beijing would agree to amend the constitution again, the judges added.

Set up after the 1989 crackdown, the alliance organised annual candlelight vigils in Hong Kong’s Victoria Park to mark the event and call for accountability and democratic reforms across the border. The event had been the only large-scale public gathering on Chinese soil to remember the 1989 crackdown.

Police prohibited the vigil for the first time in 2020 on public health grounds related to the Covid-19 pandemic. The 2021 event was banned for similar reasons before the alliance disbanded in September that year.

Inciting subversion in Hong Kong carries a maximum sentence of 10 years’ imprisonment under the national security law. Any company or organisation that commits an offence under the law can be handed a fine of an indefinite sum.

In a statement, UK Foreign Office Indo-Pacific minister Rosie Winterton said the verdict was “further demonstration that acts of remembrance in Hong Kong are now treated by the authorities as threats to national security”.

An EU spokesperson said: “The conviction … confirms the continuing deterioration of the freedoms of expression and assembly and a further shrinking of the space for independent civil society in Hong Kong.”

The foreign ministries of France and Germany also issued a joint statement saying the countries “deeply regret” the guilty verdict and called for the immediate release of Chow, who was awarded the Franco-German Prize for Human Rights and the Rule of Law in 2023.

The Australian government said it was “deeply concerned” by the verdict, while calling on Beijing to “cease suppression of freedoms of expression, assembly, media and civil society” and to repeal the national security law.

US Assistant Secretary of State Riley Barnes called for the defendants’ immediate release, arguing that the vigils sought only to remember the past and honour the lives lost in the Tiananmen crackdown.

Additional reporting by Leopold Chen and Connor Mycroft

item.title: [SCMP] The Mistral paradox: Europe’s push for tech sovereignty relies on China’s Z.ai
item.description:
On August 11, a tiny line buried in a lengthy press release from French company Mistral AI spoke volumes about the strategic and technological dilemmas facing the European Union, as the bloc prepares to navigate an autumn period full of geopolitical and trade upheaval.

In a bid to roll out “European infrastructure for sovereign AI”, Mistral – Europe’s great hope in the global artificial intelligence race – said it would begin offering other companies’ models, while keeping the service itself under European control.

Mistral’s model of choice is GLM-5.2, an open-weight large language model developed by Zhipu, also known as Z.ai, one of China’s six “AI tiger” companies, included since 2025 on the US’ entity list because of national security concerns regarding military modernisation.
item.content:encoded:
On August 11, a tiny line buried in a lengthy press release from French company Mistral AI spoke volumes about the strategic and technological dilemmas facing the European Union, as the bloc prepares to navigate an autumn period full of geopolitical and trade upheaval.

In a bid to roll out “European infrastructure for sovereign AI”, Mistral – Europe’s great hope in the global artificial intelligence race – said it would begin offering other companies’ models, while keeping the service itself under European control.

Mistral’s model of choice is GLM-5.2, an open-weight large language model developed by Zhipu, also known as Z.ai, one of China’s six “AI tiger” companies, included since 2025 on the US’ entity list because of national security concerns regarding military modernisation.

The decision to plug a Chinese AI brain into what would effectively be a European shell has raised eyebrows given the shoddy state of EU-China relations, but on practical terms it makes some sense.

Despite a deluge of political chatter about creating a sovereign European AI offering, the bloc has lagged both the US and China in investment and innovation.

Geoeconomics expert Shahin Vallee from the German Council on Foreign Relations said that a pivot to “AI adoption rather than innovation” therefore represented “the right strategy for Mistral and for Europe”.

Europe “cannot compete or win on frontier models and raw computing power” and with US companies generally favouring closed models, “GLM-5.2 was simply the strongest option on the table”, he wrote in a note.

However, Mistral’s choice was also a demonstration of how Europe’s political and commercial incentives frequently pull the company in different directions.

While the EU is engaged in a bitter trade dispute with China and desperately trying to wind down its reliance on Beijing, European companies are finding themselves enticed by cheap and advanced Chinese technological offerings.

As well as Mistral, a series of European carmakers including Volkswagen, Mercedes-Benz, BMW and Stellantis, have partnered with Chinese outfits to tap what is seen as their superior electric vehicle technology.

Mistral’s was “a geopolitical move with profound ramifications that the US demanding more ideological alignment from its allies is unlikely to reverse and might in fact accelerate”, Vallee wrote.

It is a dynamic that places Brussels more firmly in the crossfire of a US-China tech rivalry that has already taken some unexpected twists.

While Europe’s governments have shown willingness to follow American tech initiatives – the European Commission and several member states signed up for the US-led Pax Silica initiative in June – there is some suggestion that US policies are pushing its companies into Beijing’s arms.

“When I was in Brussels in June, I was surprised that the mood towards America was more negative than towards China,” said Joerg Wuttke, a Washington-based partner at consultancy Albright Stone Group.

“Because the Chinese are predictable, practical, and you can do stuff with them, and they stick to it normally,” said Wuttke, who spent decades as the top European business lobbyist in China.

“Turnberry and all that happened afterwards has basically eroded any trust in the US administration, it’s just never ending.”

On August 14, three days after Mistral’s announcement, Reuters reported that the US planned to force Pax Silica signatories towards exclusive technological alignment – a move that could eventually make European use of Chinese models politically difficult or incompatible with the initiative’s direction.

On the same day, Bloomberg reported that Washington had sent letters to Nato allies suggesting the deployment of US military assets would be predicated on how supportive they were of Trump’s foreign policies, including his war on Iran.

A day earlier, a White House report named the EU among a “tier 1” group of trading partners facilitating the “illegal transshipment” of Chinese goods to dodge US tariffs.

The week before, the European Central Bank was said to have been “blindsided” by Washington’s dramatic sale of euros to prop up the ailing Japanese yen.

“There’s a squeeze on Europe from various fronts to extract more wealth out of it,” said Davide Oneglia, a London-based macroeconomist at research firm TS Lombard. “Europe is seen as still rich enough to pay for stuff, while not strong enough to defend itself industrially, technologically or militarily.”

At the same time, Beijing has been aggressively pushing an alternative to the US model of closed, proprietary AI platforms, presenting its own models as open, global goods.

Kyle Chan, an expert in China’s industrial policy, wrote in his High Capacity newsletter that “China’s main message to the world is: ‘We’re Android, and the US is Apple’”.

“The US offers a closed system where power and profits flow back to Washington and American corporations. China offers an open system where everyone, including the Global South, can participate and benefit.”

The ultimate goal of China’s policies is to dilute American influence in frontier technologies globally, according to Chan.

“Beijing casts China as the open partner and the US as the hegemonic gatekeeper willing to restrict access to technology for its own national interest,” he said.

“That argument likely resonates because many countries already worry about over-dependence on American technology platforms, a concern sharpened by recent US restrictions.”

According to Vallee, the extra wrinkle of AI could have “profound ramifications” ahead of an autumn in which the EU-China trade dispute is expected to come to a head.

“To me the combination of US aggression and China’s openness is pushing Europe into tighter cooperation with China,” he said in an interview.

“My sense is that the opinion in Europe, rightly or wrongly, over the last few years has evolved towards considering that the risk with the US is a similar, if not greater to the risk from China.”

However, deepened corporate exposure on Chinese technology could undermine Brussels’ efforts to take Beijing to task on trade, Vallee said. “I find it hard to imagine that the EU actively engaged in the highest level of technology integration with China through AI will attempt a very hardball strategy on trade.”

Alicia Garcia-Herrero, an Asia-focused economist focused at the Brussels-based Bruegel think tank, warned that using Chinese models just because of US export controls could be a dangerous strategy for European firms. “The idea that they’re open weight doesn’t mean that they’re free.”

Eventually, companies will be commercially required to charge for these models if they are to survive, according to Garcia-Herrero. “This is an additional dependence,” she said. “We also shouldn’t go there because that would give China an additional leeway on us.”

item.title: [SCMP] US designates academic Min Zin as ‘wrongfully detained’ in China
item.description:
The US State Department said on Thursday that it had determined after a detailed investigation that Min Zin, an American political analyst of Chinese descent detained by Beijing last month, was being improperly held.

That formal designation shifts the case from a State Department consular issue to one handled by its presidential office dealing with hostage affairs.

Thursday’s terse statement, which said the decision was made by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, adds another irritant to the fraught bilateral relationship just weeks before Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump are scheduled to hold a summit in Washington.
item.content:encoded:
The US State Department said on Thursday that it had determined after a detailed investigation that Min Zin, an American political analyst of Chinese descent detained by Beijing last month, was being improperly held.

That formal designation shifts the case from a State Department consular issue to one handled by its presidential office dealing with hostage affairs.

Thursday’s terse statement, which said the decision was made by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, adds another irritant to the fraught bilateral relationship just weeks before Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump are scheduled to hold a summit in Washington.

“Secretary Rubio has determined that US citizen Min Zin is wrongfully detained in China,” the agency said in a release attributed to Assistant State Secretary Dylan Johnson. “This follows an extensive review of the circumstances surrounding his June 3 detention in Yunnan, China, where Mr Zin had travelled to attend an academic conference at the invitation of the Chinese government.”

The US agency further noted that this is the second wrongful detention designation involving China, following the case of Youlin Chen, a seismologist arrested in November 2024 at Beijing International Airport as he prepared to fly home to Boston.

“The safety and security of US citizens is the State Department’s top priority,” the State Department added. “We will continue to advocate for Mr Zin and call for the release of all US citizens who are arbitrarily detained or exit banned in China.”

The Chinese embassy in Washington said China is a country governed by the rule of law. “Its judicial authorities handle cases in accordance with the law, and there is no such thing as so-called wrongful detention,” said embassy spokesman Liu Chang.

In the past, however, Beijing has maintained that any imprisonment and travel restrictions imposed on Americans are legitimate and in keeping with Chinese law.

In June, a week after the arrest, Foreign Ministry spokesman Lin Jian announced at a regular press conference that Zin had been detained on suspicion of “engaging in espionage and endangering China’s national security” without elaborating.

Eric Lebson, chief strategy officer with Global Reach, a nonprofit group that works with families to return Americans wrongfully detained abroad, said in an interview on Thursday that he received assurances from the National Security Council [NSC] that the Trump administration will raise these cases with Xi next month if they are not resolved.

“President Trump has been really consistent since taking office in his second term that bringing home Americans is a personal priority for him,” Lebson said. “He hasn’t just told his people to do it. He has personally involved himself in the efforts.”

Global Reach has worked closely with the Chen family and advised Zin’s family informally, he said, adding that Trump’s efforts have seen some 110 Americans returned.

Zin, also known as U Min Zin, was a student activist during Myanmar’s 1988 pro-democracy uprising. After hiding for several years in Myanmar, he fled to Thailand before applying for and receiving asylum in the US.

He received a master’s degrees in Asian studies in 2010 and political science in 2011 from the University of California, Berkeley, and advanced to a doctoral degree program in political science at UC Berkeley. He is not currently enrolled.

In 2016, Zin founded the Institute for Strategy and Policy – Myanmar (ISP-Myanmar) and has written extensively in Foreign Policy and other journals about the Southeast Asian nation’s post-coup politics and economy. He has also written about Beijing’s influence in Myanmar’s border regions, including its ties to both the military government and ethnic armed groups.

The institute, originally based in Yangon, relocated to Thailand after the 2021 military coup that ousted Aung San Suu Kyi’s democratically elected government and plunged Myanmar into civil war.

In a statement on Thursday, ISP-Myanmar said it welcomed the State Department designation and urged the agency to make Zin’s release a top priority ahead of next month’s summit.

China is Myanmar’s largest trading partner and a key investor, particularly through Belt and Road Initiative projects such as the China-Myanmar Economic Corridor, oil and gas pipelines, ports and mining operations. China has publicly backed the junta and maintained engagement despite the ongoing conflict and criticism of the political transition.

Chen’s case, meanwhile, remained largely under the radar until last month when his relatives went public about his detention nearly two years after the arrest, also on espionage charges.

Their disclosure came shortly after Trump brought up Chen’s case with Xi during their May summit in Beijing, Lebson said, and Global Reach was hearing from NSC and State Department officials that there was little indication of movement from Beijing.

China formally charged Chen on May 1, 2025, with espionage, leading to his wrongful detention designation in March of this year. Chen’s speciality involves using public seismological data to measure underground nuclear tests, notably studying North Korea’s past test blasts.

The Biden administration secured the release of three Americans from China in November 2024. An equal number of Chinese were released at the same time. The rare exchange saw the US ease its travel warning on visiting China and drop a “D” designation indicating a nation that wrongly detains visitors.

Lebson said the two cases and Thursday’s statement could see tougher travel warnings reimposed, adding that there seemed to be a disconnect between Beijing’s desire for more people-to-people exchanges and the potential chill these cases may have on tourists, academics and corporate executives.

Under the 2020 Levinson Act, a wrongful detainment designation is determined based on a set of criteria that may include innocence, whether the detention is designed to increase leverage on the US, how it relates to human rights activity and whether the legal proceedings violate due process standards.

A wrongful detention label moves the case from the State Department’s Bureau of Consular Affairs – which handles routine traveller help – to the Office of the Special Presidential Envoy for Hostage Affairs, which has more tools and clout.

These may include drawing on dedicated negotiators who are authorised to work with high-ranking US and foreign officials, intelligence agencies and third parties to secure the detainees’ release; the use of public and political pressure, as seen with Trump’s May request; and the potential for financial sanctions, travel bans or diplomatic penalties.

Zack Cooper, an analyst with the conservative American Enterprise Institute and a former NSC official, said Thursday’s relatively short statement and its attribution to an assistant secretary may be an effort to balance their desire for a successful summit with a bid to gain the release of Americans.

In July, shortly after Trump made his appeal to Xi in May, China agreed to release Beijing Zion Church founder Pastor Ezra Jin Mingri after 266 days in detention.

“The administration might hope that they can use this moment ahead of the Xi visit to make progress on wrongfully detained American citizens, just as they did with Pastor Jin earlier this summer,” Cooper added.

These cases add to a long list of differences between the two nations involving strategic technology and rare earths restrictions, export bans, military chest thumping, tariffs and trade.

item.title: [SCMP] More Hong Kong consumers allege coercive beauty sales in wake of Opatra crackdown
item.description:
More consumers in Hong Kong have come forward to allege aggressive sales tactics across the beauty sector, including credit card abuse, unwanted physical contact and pressure to buy costly products, on the back of a crackdown on the local operations of a UK-based brand.

Legal experts warned that such practices could breach the Trade Descriptions Ordinance, which prohibits harassment, coercion and misleading conduct used to pressure consumers into making purchases they otherwise would not have made.

Non-consensual physical contact could also trigger additional criminal liability, they added.
item.content:encoded:
More consumers in Hong Kong have come forward to allege aggressive sales tactics across the beauty sector, including credit card abuse, unwanted physical contact and pressure to buy costly products, on the back of a crackdown on the local operations of a UK-based brand.

Legal experts warned that such practices could breach the Trade Descriptions Ordinance, which prohibits harassment, coercion and misleading conduct used to pressure consumers into making purchases they otherwise would not have made.

Non-consensual physical contact could also trigger additional criminal liability, they added.

Following the arrest of two managers at the Hong Kong operator of UK-based beauty chain Opatra London over coercive sales practices, its company secretary resigned, while customs officers continue investigating six customer complaints involving disputed sums between HK$1,800 (US$230) and HK$100,000.

Customs said that the number of complaints had risen to 25 as of Thursday and an investigation was under way.

Opatra’s headquarters in the United Kingdom said on Friday that it and the Hong Kong distributor had agreed to suspend operations.

The brand’s four Hong Kong branches – two in Sha Tin, one in Yuen Long and one in Causeway Bay – have suspended operations since the controversy flared up about a week ago.

Now, more victims have detailed alleged aggressive sales tactics they have encountered while shopping for beauty products.

For 22-year-old university student John*, it took just a few seconds to be dragged into what he described as a “beauty trap” on the busy Hankow Road in Tsim Sha Tsui in May.

Outside a Lionesse shop, John said he was approached by a saleswoman who handed him a “free sample”.

He said the woman told him he had “dark eye circles” before applying an unidentified skincare product directly to his face. Concerned about a possible skin reaction and caught off guard by the ambush, John said he agreed to enter the shop.

Once he was seated, John said staff applied another liquid, claiming it was a HK$1,560 deep cleanser. They then showed him the “dirt” removed from his skin in a mirror in an attempt to persuade him to buy the product, he said.

John said he was then hurried into signing an electronic form, with the signature box enlarged to the point that he could not read the contract terms, including a “no refunds” clause.

Instead of handing over the product, the saleswoman then directed him to a free facial and bombarded him with questions about his age and employment status, along with two other staff members, John said.

Under pressure, he agreed to purchase a HK$30,000 annual facial package, but explicitly requested an instalment plan capped at HK$2,500 a month due to his credit card limit, he said.

John alleged that one of the salesmen took his card and made multiple attempts to process transactions exceeding HK$2,500.

Bank records showed five unsuccessful attempts, he said, for HK$30,000, HK$8,440, HK$5,000, HK$7,500 and, finally, HK$2,500. He said the bank immediately blocked the card because of the suspicious activity.

He said he ultimately paid HK$2,500 via PayMe to a merchant named “Vertex Innovations Limited” so he could leave the shop.

When he sought a refund through the Consumer Council, Lionesse’s management denied allegations of high-pressure sales practices, arguing that the open shop environment meant he could have “left immediately”, John said.

The company said the failed transaction records reflected standard authorisation procedures between the bank system and the merchant terminal and did not constitute improper sales practices. It declined to provide a refund, instead offering to exchange products of the same value.

In response to queries from the South China Morning Post, Apex Retail, which manages Lionesse in Hong Kong, declined to comment on individual allegations or circumstances that did not involve identifiable customer matters.

Recalling the experience, John said: “I’m just a student. The incident put immense psychological pressure on me and forced me to waste a lot of time organising bank records, payment details and relevant documents to file a complaint.”

He added: “I never intended to get involved in beauty services, but this experience made me realise how dark and manipulative beauty sales could be.”

He is now seeking a chargeback of HK$4,060 from the bank.

Company registration records show the directors of Apex are Ozel Barnos, Eli Vaknin, Sagi Vardi, Yogev Itzhak Vardi and Yinon Avraham Vardi.

The company website, which has become inaccessible, said it started as an Israeli family business and now had about a dozen shops in the city, under the brands of Earth, Napara, Privilege Boutique, Avinichi, Dualsonic and more.

Another firm to come under scrutiny was The Mineral Boutique, a brand under Beauty Express Group that has at least five branches in major shopping centres.

A 42-year-old clerk surnamed Wong alleged that similar tactics were used when a saleswoman applied a product directly onto her skin without permission at the Log-on shop in Festival Walk, Kowloon Tong, in June.

Wong said the saleswoman claimed the product could only be removed using a specialised device inside the counter area.

Once inside, Wong alleged, staff repeatedly grabbed her hand when she tried to pull away and cornered her while attempting to sell her high-value products, alongside a store manager.

Wong said that when she tried to leave, the saleswoman replied: “What is there left to think about? You’ve already seen the results.”

Wong said the remark prompted her to leave immediately and then file a formal complaint with City’super, the parent company of Log-on.

In a response to Wong, City’super said it had investigated the incident, reiterated that aggressive sales tactics were strictly prohibited and offered her a gift box.

City’super told the SCMP that it had received two customer “comments” about the counter’s services in the past year, as well as “a limited number of comments or complaints” over the past five years.

It said all cases had been investigated and handled through established procedures.

Asked whether such complaints influenced lease renewals, City’super declined to comment on specific contractual arrangements.

“We evaluate business relationships and commercial arrangements based on a range of factors including compliance with applicable laws and regulations, operational requirements, customer feedback and other relevant considerations,” it said.

Beauty Express Group declined to comment on the complaint, citing a lack of sufficient information to identify the customers involved.

It told the SCMP that it did not tolerate aggressive sales practices, non-consensual physical contact or any conduct that compromised a customer’s ability to make a free and informed purchasing decision.

The group’s directors include Aviad Ben Ezra and Baruch Szerer. Other brands under the group include Telosin, Premier by Dead Sea, Gratiae and more.

Lawyer Eric Chan Pak-ho said the tactics used on the student could constitute an offence under the Trade Descriptions Ordinance. However, the key question was whether sales staff had used “harassment, coercion or undue influence” to persuade John to agree to each purchase.

Chan added that concealing no-refund policies could increase the company’s legal liability.

Under the law, practices that significantly impair a consumer’s freedom of choice or conduct and cause them to make a purchase they would not otherwise have made are considered an offence.

Commercial lawyer Kenix Yuen Pui-kwan said that applying beauty products to a consumer’s skin might not, in itself, breach the ordinance.

“However, if that conduct forms part of a broader sales strategy involving harassment, coercion or undue influence, it may be relevant,” Yuen said.

Depending on the nature of the physical contact, other criminal issues could also arise, she cautioned.

Dr Amos Cheung, a clinical psychologist registered with the Hong Kong Psychological Society, said falling victim to high-pressure sales tactics did not mean a person lacked intelligence.

Such tactics were carefully engineered to exploit human vulnerability and bypass rational reasoning, he said.

Offering free samples could make shoppers feel indebted and reluctant to refuse invitations to enter a store, while applying products to someone’s face without consent could also help identify customers who were more susceptible to manipulation, he said.

Sales representatives could exaggerate imperfections in shoppers’ appearance in ways linked to their self-esteem and sense of self-worth, pushing them towards “emotional reasoning”, Cheung said.

“Such feelings of fear, anxiety and restlessness could impact your rational reasoning process and push you into a state of emotional reasoning,” he said.

He added that compliments could also lower customers’ guard by making sales staff seem friendly and trustworthy.

“If you are unsure about a store’s sales tactics, do not visit it alone,” he said.

“It’s important to be alert to words intended to trigger unnecessary anxiety, shame and panic, and prepare your response, such as ‘I never purchase out of impulse. I will think about it.’ Then, leave immediately.”

*Name changed at interviewee’s request

item.title: [SCMP] Why North Korea is ‘keeping the door open for dialogue’ with Trump
item.description:
At first glance, Kim Yo-jong’s latest message to Washington looked like a rebuff to US President Donald Trump’s insistence that he would meet her brother Kim Jong-un later this year.

But analysts said the North Korean leader’s powerful sister stopped well short of shutting down Trump’s outreach, using a carefully worded statement to leave room for renewed summit diplomacy while making clear that Pyongyang intended to set the terms for any return to dialogue.

In her statement, released by North Korean state media late on Wednesday, Kim Yo-jong dismissed Trump’s decision to scale back joint US-South Korea military exercises as meaningless, demanded a complete halt to the drills and warned again against what Pyongyang calls Washington’s “hostile” policy.
item.content:encoded:
At first glance, Kim Yo-jong’s latest message to Washington looked like a rebuff to US President Donald Trump’s insistence that he would meet her brother Kim Jong-un later this year.

But analysts said the North Korean leader’s powerful sister stopped well short of shutting down Trump’s outreach, using a carefully worded statement to leave room for renewed summit diplomacy while making clear that Pyongyang intended to set the terms for any return to dialogue.

In her statement, released by North Korean state media late on Wednesday, Kim Yo-jong dismissed Trump’s decision to scale back joint US-South Korea military exercises as meaningless, demanded a complete halt to the drills and warned again against what Pyongyang calls Washington’s “hostile” policy.

Yet the statement also contained openings that appeared calibrated for Trump.

Kim Yo-jong neither confirmed nor denied Trump’s claim that the North Korean leader had responded positively to his latest overture, saying only that it was “perhaps” the one foreign policy matter involving the country’s “supreme leadership” about which she was not informed.

She also emphasised that Pyongyang had repeatedly said Kim Jong-un held “personally good memories and feelings” towards Trump.

The ambiguity allowed North Korea to avoid embarrassing Trump while reaffirming the “excellent” personal relationship between the two leaders, analysts said, suggesting Pyongyang aimed to keep the door open to talks, but only if Washington accepted a much higher entry price.

That could include US acceptance of North Korea as a nuclear-armed state, the exclusion of denuclearisation from the immediate agenda and a negotiating framework shaped by Pyongyang rather than Washington, they said.

Trump, meanwhile, appeared to hint that North Korea’s denuclearisation could be put on the back burner during the initial stage of any renewed negotiations.

Shortly after the statement was released, Trump said he would meet Kim Jong-un later this year, noting that North Korea had 57 “very powerful” nuclear weapons.

His remarks came amid reports that he was pushing for a meeting during his next trip to Asia, likely to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit scheduled to take place in Shenzhen, China, in November.

“Yeah, I will be,” Trump told reporters when asked whether he expected to meet Kim Jong-un later this year.

On whether he was exchanging written letters with Kim Jong-un, Trump said, “I can’t tell you that.”

Trump held three ultimately fruitless bilateral meetings with Kim Jong-un during his first term: in Singapore in June 2018, Hanoi in February 2019 and the inter-Korean border village of Panmunjom in June 2019.

Observers say Trump’s renewed attention on North Korea could reflect his eagerness to score a major foreign policy coup, potentially helping divert attention from the protracted war against Iran, which has tarnished his image as a peacemaker and contributed to inflation ahead of the US midterm elections in November.

But it remains to be seen whether Kim Jong-un will respond to Trump’s overtures, given North Korea’s growing ties with Russia and China, which have reduced Pyongyang’s need for help from the United States, analysts say.

“By publicly reaffirming the ‘excellent relationship’ between Kim and Trump, Pyongyang is keeping the door open to dialogue,” said Hong Min, a senior analyst at the Korea Institute for National Unification.

Even if Trump exaggerated Kim Jong-un’s alleged positive response to a meeting, Pyongyang’s statement showed how it was avoiding embarrassing the US leader, Hong added. “Taken more positively, the message could be interpreted as: ‘We have received no message, so if you are serious, then send a genuine one.’”

Professor Yang Moo-jin of the University of North Korean Studies said Pyongyang was raising all the security issues it considered relevant to its interests, thereby increasing the threshold for dialogue.

The statement also widened the security agenda beyond Washington, including Japan’s recent military moves and South Korea’s development of nuclear-powered submarines.

Kim Yo-jong on Wednesday issued a direct threat against Japan, warning that if it “attempts to make the wrong choice, it will now face an immediate and unsurvivable, annihilating strike”.

The key takeaway from her message, Yang noted, was not whether communication had taken place regarding a possible resumption of Trump-Kim summit diplomacy, but rather North Korea’s emphasis on the preconditions for restarting dialogue.

“Pyongyang is arguing that merely scaling back US-South Korea joint military exercises is not enough and that Washington must fundamentally abandon its hostile policy towards North Korea,” Yang said.

“By rejecting reports of additional North Korean troop deployments to Russia, while also raising concerns over Japan’s recent military moves and South Korea’s development of nuclear-powered submarines, North Korea appears to be seeking to raise the threshold for resuming US-North Korea dialogue.”

The timing of the statement, coinciding with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi’s visit to Seoul, also appeared intended to demonstrate Pyongyang’s determination to maintain the initiative on Korean peninsula issues and signal to both China and Russia that North Korea would not recklessly rush into dialogue with the US, Yang noted.

For Yu Ji-hoon, a research fellow at the Korea Institute for Defence Analyses, the statement suggests Pyongyang continues to see value in the personal rapport between Kim Jong-un and Trump even as it dismisses the significance of scaling back military exercises.

“This could be an attempt by Pyongyang to separate Trump from broader US policy towards North Korea, keeping open the possibility of resuming their summit diplomacy,” Yu said.

Professor Lim Eul-chul of the Institute for Far Eastern Studies at Kyungnam University said Pyongyang was well aware that Trump was in urgent need of a fresh diplomatic coup ahead of the November midterm elections.

“Kim Jong-un also understands that even if another summit with Trump does take place, the talks could be derailed at any time due to opposition in Washington or Trump’s own whims,” Lim said.

“Nevertheless, from North Korea’s perspective, the uncertainty created by Trump represents not only a threat but also a strategic opportunity.”

That could allow Kim to maximise his leverage until Trump came forward with sufficiently dramatic concessions, potentially including a permanent end to US-South Korea military exercises and explicit public recognition of North Korea as a nuclear-armed state, Lim said.

Leif-Eric Easley, professor of international studies at Ewha Womans University, agreed that Pyongyang was unlikely to agree to talks any time soon.

With North Korea benefiting financially from helping Russia in the Ukraine war and receiving Moscow’s blessing for its de facto nuclear status, Easley said all these gave Kim Jong-un “leverage to demand greater support from Beijing”.

While the North Korean leader might seek “further economic and reputational benefits” from Washington, Easley predicted this would occur after the US midterm elections when Trump “is expected to be in a weaker domestic political position and in search of headline-grabbing foreign policies”.

item.title: [SCMP] Despite US sanctions on Xinjiang cotton, China’s textile industry weathers the storm
item.description:
When the US government announced the addition of 43 Chinese companies to an import blacklist in late July over allegations of forced labour in the country’s western Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region – including several household food and apparel brands – the local reaction to the news was surprisingly calm.

“It felt like a sudden batch of companies was added out of nowhere … but it shouldn’t have much of an impact on the sector,” said the owner of a cotton-ginning mill in southern Xinjiang, who spoke on condition of anonymity.

This was a far cry from the panic triggered four years ago, when Xinjiang cotton became a geopolitical flashpoint between Washington and Beijing.
item.content:encoded:
When the US government announced the addition of 43 Chinese companies to an import blacklist in late July over allegations of forced labour in the country’s western Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region – including several household food and apparel brands – the local reaction to the news was surprisingly calm.

“It felt like a sudden batch of companies was added out of nowhere … but it shouldn’t have much of an impact on the sector,” said the owner of a cotton-ginning mill in southern Xinjiang, who spoke on condition of anonymity.

This was a far cry from the panic triggered four years ago, when Xinjiang cotton became a geopolitical flashpoint between Washington and Beijing.

Back in June 2022, the mill owner was sitting on a massive stockpile of unsold cotton, anxious about falling trading prices and losing his downstream buyers to the effects of the Uygur Forced Labour Prevention Act (UFLPA) – a US law that effectively bans American imports of all products with inputs from Xinjiang.

“At least for Xinjiang cotton, I feel the industry has weathered the storm,” he said. Now, the local processing rates of cotton products are “remarkably high” – around 30 to 40 per cent – and development across the entire cotton textile supply chain is booming, he added.

“From spinning and weaving to printing and dyeing, companies are steadily expanding their scale,” the mill owner said.

His change in attitude might also be a snapshot for a broader change in the global political landscape. After significant export diversification efforts and a shift in the balance of power between China and the US – especially since last year’s sweeping trade war – Chinese industries seem to be reacting to US sanctions with greater resilience and confidence.

However, analysts and industry insiders said this was no time to relax. Despite the goodwill generated by the summits held or planned between the two countries’ leaders this year, they said the risks for Chinese firms were only bound to increase amid lingering bilateral tensions.

Its most significant impact has been reshaping how US fashion companies manage sourcing, compliance, and supply chain transparency

Sheng Lu, University of Delaware

The US broadens its list

Passed by the US Congress and signed into law in 2021, the UFLPA establishes a “rebuttable presumption” that all goods from the region involve forced labour – a charge Beijing consistently denies – and specifically bars listed companies from exporting their goods to the US unless they can provide clear and convincing evidence to the contrary.

The latest additions to the list, which took effect on August 3, represent an expansion of 30 per cent – the largest single increase in the list’s history – bringing the total number of companies to 187. Sectors covered include gold, pharmaceuticals, aluminium, garments and food, according to the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

A few industry leaders in the cotton, textile and apparel sector in China were included on the list, including Henan Tongzhou Cotton and Fujian Septwolves.

Septwolves said the company was “shocked and saddened” by its inclusion on the list, and that the company’s core business was focused on the domestic market, so its operations would be unaffected. Tongzhou Cotton has not replied to requests for comment from the South China Morning Post.

In a statement, China’s Ministry of Commerce called the additions “completely lacking in factual basis” and described the move as an “act of economic coercion”, saying it “would do whatever was necessary to protect the rights and interests of Chinese firms.”

The country’s National Textile and Apparel Council also issued a statement saying that there was “no ‘forced labour’ of any kind” in Xinjiang’s cotton and textile sector, adding that cultivation and harvesting were largely automated, with over 90 per cent of the region’s cotton harvested by machine.

“The US action gravely damages the order and stable operation of global textile supply chains,” the council said. “Xinjiang produces approximately one-fifth of the world’s cotton, and China accounts for nearly one-third of global textile and apparel exports.”

According to figures from China’s National Bureau of Statistics, the region produced 6.17 million tonnes of cotton in 2024, up 20.2 per cent from the 5.13 million tonnes recorded in 2021, the year the UFLPA was approved.

In its statement, the textile council called upon international apparel brands to “respect the facts” regarding Xinjiang’s development, cautioning them to “keep commercial operations from being coerced by politics, and avoid becoming tools of anti-China forces in the US.”

Re-sourcing textile resources

Years after taking effect, the UFLPA had yet to cause an immediate or complete decoupling of the US-China textile and apparel trade, said Sheng Lu, a professor in the department of fashion and apparel studies at the University of Delaware. China is still regarded as indispensable for textile raw material sourcing among US importers, he added.

“The impact of the UFLPA has been more nuanced than many initially expected,” Lu said. “Instead, its most significant impact has been reshaping how US fashion companies manage sourcing, compliance, and supply chain transparency.”

According to US Department of Commerce data, in value terms only 6.4 per cent of US cotton apparel came from China during the first five months of 2026, down from 9.9 per cent a year earlier and 21.9 per cent in 2019, marking another record low, Lu said.

That said, Lu added he did not expect the latest expansion of the UFLPA entity list would trigger another mass relocation of apparel sourcing.

“Many leading US fashion companies reported sourcing only a single-digit share of their total apparel volume or value from China and appear to have already reached their desired level of exposure to China,” he said.

“Rather than continuing to accelerate their exit from China, these companies are increasingly focused on optimising their broader sourcing portfolios while maintaining limited sourcing from China, which continues to offer strong manufacturing advantages in areas such as small minimum order quantity, flexibility and agility, and vertical integration.”

China’s industry adapts

A general consensus among Chinese textile exporters is that a workaround for dealing with the UFLPA has been gradually established: use foreign cotton when traceability is required, and Xinjiang cotton otherwise.

Some industry insiders said most traceability only existed on paper, leaving an ample grey area in which to manoeuvre.

One sales manager at a major textile manufacturer in eastern China said the UFLPA had been like a hammer hanging over the company’s head, but there was never a clear timeline as to when strict enforcement of the policy would actually begin.

It was a big headache for the company, which exports sofa covers to the US, when the policy was first implemented in 2022, the manager said, adding that some downstream clients began to ask for traceability documents for the raw materials, having to prove that their products did not use Xinjiang cotton.

But all of the company’s products were made with cotton from the region, the manager said, attesting to the material’s quality. His American clients tended to steer clear of products containing cotton, because “they don’t want to get mixed up in politics,” he added.

“So, we try to avoid promoting cotton goods and focus on other fabrics instead.”

Fang Huiling, senior analyst at Shanghai-based Orient Futures, said field surveys across Xinjiang and other provinces showed that Chinese cotton growers had found ways to circumvent the US sanctions by diversifying export destinations and separating production lines for export and domestic markets.

“After years of sustained sanctions by the US, domestic companies have become accustomed to the situation and built greater resilience. That’s why I believe the impact [of the latest UFLPA sanctions] on China is limited,” Fang said.

I honestly feel like this is the toughest year of my 11-year career in the industry

Hua, textile factory owner

Instead, they might even inflict greater pain on US cotton growers than those in Xinjiang, Fang said. American agricultural products were easy targets for Beijing during trade tensions with Washington, she said, adding that as one of its countermeasures during last year’s trade war, China imposed an additional 15 per cent tariff on US cotton.

“China is the world’s largest textile producer and was once the top purchaser of US cotton,” Fang said. “Chinese buyers have gradually diverted their purchases away from the US towards countries like Brazil, weighing heavily on American cotton growers.”

However, not all industry insiders were so optimistic.

“Imported cotton is more expensive – sourcing from places like Brazil or Myanmar costs about 2,000 yuan (US$297) more per tonne once you factor in shipping, customs clearance, and other fees,” said Hua, who owns a textile factory in eastern China’s Zhejiang province that mainly serves overseas clients, adding this difference included the costs incurred from preparing and providing traceability information to the US.

“But it’s not just a matter of price; the main issue is quality,” said Hua, who preferred to go by a surname. “Imported cotton has higher defect rates than Xinjiang cotton.”

While costs have gone up, Hua’s American clients were not accepting price increases, he said, adding the appreciation of the yuan continued to squeeze his profit margins.

“I honestly feel like this is the toughest year of my 11-year career in the industry.”

In tall cotton – for now

But even with the ups and downs of the US-China relationship, which have affected the enforcement of certain trade measures more generally, making sure that UFLPA is being complied with has always been patchy, according to Nick Marro, global trade lead at the Economist Intelligence Unit.

“This could reflect a lack of expertise or personnel on the US Customs side, but also a lack of very strict guidance coming from the policymakers themselves,” Marro said.

But Hua said he would not dare test the leniency of US law enforcement, since getting caught would mean substantial fines and the seizure and eventual forfeiture of the entire shipment.

More than 24,300 shipments with a total value of almost US$1 billion had been blocked since the act came into force, according to DHS.

“Everyone fears that the ban on Xinjiang cotton is just the beginning – what we’re all really worried about is whether the US might eventually impose a complete ban on textile exports down the road,” Hua said.

For the sofa cover exporter in eastern China, orders from the US have been resilient this year – a relief after last year’s tit-for-tat tariff war that once brought bilateral trade to a near standstill.

“Unless some unforeseen policies come out, things generally look fairly optimistic for now,” the manager said.

But manufacturers in Xinjiang have long ceased pinning their hopes on the mercy of the US.

“The Chinese government should just move the headquarters for all those must-have goods the US relies on China for to Xinjiang,” the cotton mill owner said. “That way, if you want to buy them, you have to buy from Xinjiang.”

As an example, he cited rare earth elements – the valuable minerals crucial to hi-tech and defence supply chains.

item.title: [SCMP] China’s drone production capacity can only meet 60% of war demand: study
item.description:
Even when fully mobilised, China’s industrial system would only be able to meet 60 per cent of the country’s military demand for drones in a conflict, according to a rare study looking into the expected effects of a sudden war.

The estimates were produced by an artificial intelligence model that covered a multilevel supply chain linking drone assembly plants with subsystem and component suppliers. The study also accounted for inventories, production capacity, order backlogs, budgets and civilian factory conversion.

The paper was published online in the Journal of System Simulation on July 24. It was led by Professor Zhang Jihai, director of the National Defence Mobilisation Research Centre, and his team from the Beijing Institute of Technology.
item.content:encoded:
Even when fully mobilised, China’s industrial system would only be able to meet 60 per cent of the country’s military demand for drones in a conflict, according to a rare study looking into the expected effects of a sudden war.

The estimates were produced by an artificial intelligence model that covered a multilevel supply chain linking drone assembly plants with subsystem and component suppliers. The study also accounted for inventories, production capacity, order backlogs, budgets and civilian factory conversion.

The paper was published online in the Journal of System Simulation on July 24. It was led by Professor Zhang Jihai, director of the National Defence Mobilisation Research Centre, and his team from the Beijing Institute of Technology.

The university has a strong military research background and is among the few Chinese universities subject to US sanctions.

“Modern warfare competition is no longer merely about the performance of weapon systems, but more fundamentally about industrial capacity – especially the comprehensive capability of production mobilisation for military equipment,” the researchers wrote.

The study found that capacity expansion could not quickly close the gap because new production lines took time to build.

Recent conflicts have shown how quickly modern wars can consume precision weapons, with Reuters reporting on August 4 that the US Army had used “virtually all” of its army tactical missile systems and precision strike missiles during its five-month war with Iran.

The war in Ukraine gives an even clearer example for drones, with a Pentagon official saying on July 27 that Ukraine was expected to produce 6 million to 7 million small first-person view attack drones in 2026 – about 500,000 a month – while US production remained a fraction of that level.

“Under high-intensity demand shocks, the supply chain, although possessing certain mobilisation and recovery capabilities, still faces a significant supply-demand gap,” the researchers wrote.

But the simulation also raises a bigger question about the scale of mobilisation, as the result would look very different if a major war brought companies that did not normally produce military equipment into the defence supply chain.

“Modern warfare, like wars in the past, is ultimately about supply chains,” said a Chinese weapons and equipment expert, who declined to give his name because of the sensitive nature of his work.

He warned that the ability to rapidly expand production could matter as much as the weapons already available. The expert holds a doctorate in weapons and equipment engineering and works in a field involving classified facilities.

“The rapid production capability can fully meet the demand, but the supply of core components is not that simple,” he said.

What would happen in China during a period of war would likely be similar to what happened “during the Three Major Campaigns”, the weapons specialist said.

The rapid production capability can fully meet the demand, but the supply of core components is not that simple

Chinese weapons specialist

He was referring to the three decisive strategic battles between the People’s Liberation Army and Kuomintang forces during the Chinese civil war. “It is a classic example [when] ordinary people were all mobilised to supply materials,” he said.

Such mobilisation could produce a very different outcome from a model that counted only existing military and civilian weapons manufacturers, according to the expert.

During the Covid-19 pandemic, for example, Chinese companies outside the medical sector rapidly switched production to masks and other protective equipment when demand surged.

In a major war, manufacturers that do not normally produce weapons could similarly become part of the military supply chain. These could include companies producing electronics, batteries, vehicles, machinery and consumer technology.

The distinction matters because a factory that does not make drones today may still have machinery, electronics expertise, battery technology, supply networks or manufacturing capacity that could be adapted for military production.

Zhang’s simulation therefore describes only one version of wartime capacity. A nationwide industrial mobilisation involving large civilian manufacturers could produce a very different result.

China already dominates large parts of the global drone supply chain and holds a huge share of the consumer drone market. Chinese-made consumer drones account for roughly 90 per cent of the US consumer market.

But industrial dominance in peacetime does not necessarily mean that production can be rapidly converted into military output during a major war.

The study used an unmanned aerial vehicle supply chain to simulate a sudden wartime surge in demand. The model linked military demand with a multilevel supply chain covering equipment and component suppliers, subsystems and a final assembly plant.

It also included inventories, production capacity, order backlogs, budgets, production safety and the ability of civilian manufacturers to switch to military production.

Civilian factories could not be converted instantly because of limits on capacity, technical adaptation and conversion efficiency.

“Capacity expansion and conversion are not activated continuously, but rather exhibit phased triggering and discontinuous implementation,” the researchers wrote.

In one simulation, demand rose to three times its normal level after the war began.

The system responded by releasing inventories, increasing overtime production, building new production lines and converting civilian capacity. Yet cumulative wartime order fulfilment reached only 63.4 per cent.

The unnamed expert said the study should therefore be treated mainly as an “argumentative study” rather than a prediction of what would happen in an actual war.

Zhang’s team compared no mobilisation, rule-based mobilisation and an AI-based strategy across 30 simulations. Median wartime order fulfilment rates were about 34 per cent, 51 per cent and 58 per cent respectively.

The AI strategy’s average fulfilment rate was 8.4 per cent higher than the rule-based approach. It was also 24.3 per cent higher than no mobilisation.

“The large language model-based [AI] mobilisation strategy achieves superior delivery performance and a higher wartime order fulfilment rate compared with no-mobilisation and rule-based mobilisation strategies,” the researchers wrote.

The AI model assessed inventory, production capacity, order pressure and budgets before selecting suppliers for expansion and civilian firms for conversion.

The model also found that increasing available mobilisation funding from 60 per cent to 140 per cent of the baseline raised wartime order fulfilment from 54.9 per cent to 62.3 per cent. Further spending produced smaller gains.

Factory construction times, conversion capacity and other physical constraints limited how quickly additional funding could create usable production capacity.

“There is a clear trade-off constraint between equipment supply assurance and production safety,” the researchers wrote.

item.title: [SCMP] China is using Jiang Zemin centenary to signal political continuity
item.description:
The centenary of Jiang Zemin’s birth, marked on August 17 with a memorial in Beijing attended and addressed by President Xi Jinping, was more than an occasion to commemorate a former Chinese leader. It was also an exercise in political history: a moment to locate Jiang, the era he led and the reform legacy associated with him within the broader story of the Communist Party of China’s evolution and China’s modernisation.

That is what makes the event politically significant. The question is not simply why China is commemorating Jiang so prominently. It is why the leadership has chosen this particular historical moment to reaffirm his place in the country’s political narrative and what that says about how Beijing views the road from reform and opening up to Chinese modernisation today.

Xi’s speech placed Jiang squarely within the history of the party, describing him as the core of the party’s third-generation central leadership and as a principal founder of the important notion of the “Three Represents”. It also highlighted Jiang’s contributions to reform and opening up, socialist modernisation and China’s development.
item.content:encoded:
The centenary of Jiang Zemin’s birth, marked on August 17 with a memorial in Beijing attended and addressed by President Xi Jinping, was more than an occasion to commemorate a former Chinese leader. It was also an exercise in political history: a moment to locate Jiang, the era he led and the reform legacy associated with him within the broader story of the Communist Party of China’s evolution and China’s modernisation.

That is what makes the event politically significant. The question is not simply why China is commemorating Jiang so prominently. It is why the leadership has chosen this particular historical moment to reaffirm his place in the country’s political narrative and what that says about how Beijing views the road from reform and opening up to Chinese modernisation today.

Xi’s speech placed Jiang squarely within the history of the party, describing him as the core of the party’s third-generation central leadership and as a principal founder of the important notion of the “Three Represents”. It also highlighted Jiang’s contributions to reform and opening up, socialist modernisation and China’s development.

The formulation matters. It presents Jiang neither as an isolated political figure nor simply as the representative of a bygone era. Instead, it places him within a chain of political leadership and national development stretching across several decades.

For China’s leadership, historical continuity has considerable political importance. The reform era was not a single event but a succession of experiments, adjustments and institutional changes undertaken by different generations of leaders.
