Understanding the exam’s role as a critical ladder for social advancement allowed him to empathise with the intense pressure students faced from parents and teachers, helping them to navigate their anxieties with genuine insights.

Macfarlane’s anthropological and historical perspectives offer comfort to China’s young generation by framing their personal struggles within a broader historical and spatial context.

Many of his audience said they found relief in realising that their private worries were shared by peers across different times and cultures, allowing them to learn from how others navigated similar challenges.

Yang Zhongcheng, a 20-year-old student at Beijing University of Technology, has rarely missed an update since he started following Macfarlane on RedNote in 2025. “This helped me jump out of the well and view myself from a broader, more compassionate perspective,” he said.

Surrounded by peers locked in fierce academic competition and facing the rapid advance of AI, Yang felt disoriented by the overwhelming pace of society but had learned to let go of his perfectionism and focus on the present through Macfarlane’s content.

Yang added that he particularly appreciated Macfarlane’s non-patronising approach. “[He] makes me feel we are totally equal, and that he’s keeping us company rather than lecturing us.”

Echoing this sentiment, Macfarlane observed that a lot of Chinese education and family life was hierarchical. While young people were accustomed to being told what was right or wrong, they often harboured a quiet resistance to top-down lecturing, he said.

Macfarlane also attributed his appeal to his Cambridge background and distinct delivery characterised by a refined accent, clear language and a measured pace.

According to Macfarlane, the questions he receives cover themes spanning jobs to relationships and technology changes, yet nearly all boil down to how to cope with a rapidly shifting world.

“Is there really no future for humanities majors?” one user wrote in the comments section of Macfarlane’s RedNote channel. “How can an ordinary person lead a fulfilling life?” another asked, while a third wondered, “Why do humans never seem to learn from historical lessons?”

Macfarlane said the questions were not surprising “because China has gone through the biggest economic, social, political and ideological change of any civilisation in history in the fastest time”.

He noted that such a swift and dramatic transformation had a profound impact on people’s psychology, attitudes and feelings, with the younger generation of Chinese bearing the brunt.

Unable to draw on the experiences of their elders, who grew up in an entirely different era, young Chinese were left to question almost everything. Into this void stepped Macfarlane, offering an empathetic listening ear and a broader perspective.

Beyond personal solace, the channel has also fostered cross-cultural understanding. Instead of traditional top-down lectures, these digital interactions encourage young viewers to ask questions and discuss ideas openly in the comments.

Li Lin, a 19-year-old student whose desire to explore Western culture was sparked by the videos, said Macfarlane’s content “inspires young people to grasp the differences between East and West, while actively exploring diverse cultures and the depth of civilisations”.

Driven by the professor’s insights, fellow viewer Yang was even inspired to spend a few weeks visiting Cambridge.

While Macfarlane clearly knows China well, some of his audience feel that his advice occasionally misses the mark because of the inherent limits of viewing the country through a Western lens.

For Li, Macfarlane’s different viewpoint is a benefit. “Eastern and Western thoughts are neither right nor wrong; they are simply distinct perspectives shaped by different historical and social backgrounds,” she said.

“And this very difference is precisely the bridge for us to learn from and understand one another.”

Cultural exchange is largely one-way

Macfarlane acknowledged that the cultural exchange generated by his videos remained largely one-way, with Chinese audiences making far more effort to understand the West than vice versa.

Yet he noted that the reach of his videos extended beyond China, drawing in “TikTok refugees” who migrated to RedNote when a ban of the platform in the United States seemed imminent last January.

Against this backdrop, Macfarlane said he hoped his channel would serve as a bridge to the wider world, sparking curiosity about China among non-Chinese audiences and gradually dispelling deeply rooted mistrust.

He also aimed to foster a deeper realisation of China as one of the world’s “greatest, most ancient, and most sophisticated civilisations” – one with immense wisdom to share, especially after having made such great efforts to absorb the best of the West, he added.

However, Macfarlane stressed that such mutual dialogue remained hindered by prejudice in the West, even as language barriers had gradually faded with AI translation technologies.

Western perceptions of China were often decades out of date and compounded by geopolitical anxiety, he argued. China’s rise challenged long-held assumptions in the West about its superiority in political governance, free-market capitalism, innovation and religious faith.

“Our economies have stalled and inequality is growing hugely in the West. And then we look at China – China is still growing reasonably and it has, to a considerable extent, made that wealth available across [society],” Macfarlane said.

He also pointed to a subconscious Western fear of retaliation stemming from a history of imperialist aggression against China, which has fuelled political and media distrust.

Despite these geopolitical headwinds, Macfarlane remains convinced that the solution lies in sustained, grass roots engagement.

“The deep answer is more exchange – more Chinese coming here, more of our Western people going to China, working with and becoming friends with Chinese,” he said. “And then we might have a chance of living in a more peaceful world.”

item.title: [SCMP] The 11 key achievements of China’s ‘iron premier’ Zhu Rongji – in his own words
item.description:
Known for his sharp intellect, no-nonsense demeanour and relentless drive for reform, China’s former premier Zhu Rongji was the primary architect of the country’s transition from an isolated, rigidly planned economy to a market-driven titan connected to the rest of the world. During his tenure from 1998 to 2003, he engineered an economic “soft landing”, steered the nation through the Asian Financial Crisis and secured entry into the WTO, laying the groundwork for the country’s historic transformation.

Here is a look back at his key contributions, remembered through his most memorable and hard-hitting quotes.

1. Spearheading Shanghai’s revival
item.content:encoded:
Known for his sharp intellect, no-nonsense demeanour and relentless drive for reform, China’s former premier Zhu Rongji was the primary architect of the country’s transition from an isolated, rigidly planned economy to a market-driven titan connected to the rest of the world. During his tenure from 1998 to 2003, he engineered an economic “soft landing”, steered the nation through the Asian Financial Crisis and secured entry into the WTO, laying the groundwork for the country’s historic transformation.

Here is a look back at his key contributions, remembered through his most memorable and hard-hitting quotes.

1. Spearheading Shanghai’s revival

During his time as Shanghai’s mayor from 1988 to 1991, Zhu restructured the city’s industrial base, focused on exports and kick-started the construction of the Pudong New Area, an economic development zone. Early on, he recognised that foreign direct investment was key to the city’s future growth.

“If there’s one thing about me, my guiding principle, it’s independent thought. I feel that whatever’s on my mind is what I should say out loud. … What Shanghai needs most right now is grounded, practical follow-through.” – Giving a speech as a candidate for Shanghai mayor in 1987.

2. Defusing “triangular debt”

When Zhu was appointed governor of the People’s Bank of China in 1993, the country’s financial and payments system faced immense challenges with banks and state-owned enterprises (SOEs) hopelessly enmeshed in “triangular debt”.

Put simply, the phrase describes a chain of debts – Company A owing money to Company B, Company B owing money to Company C and Company C owing money to Company A – which can paralyse the economy.

Zhu tackled this issue by injecting targeted funds, establishing the responsibility of borrowers and allowing those unable to pay their debts to go bankrupt.

“The main source of triangular debt is that government departments, localities and enterprises blindly carry out construction projects in pursuit of rapid growth, resulting in a large fixed asset investment gap.” – Speaking at a national conference on clearing up triangular debt on September 3, 1991.

3. Engineering a “soft landing” for the Chinese economy

In the early 1990s, China’s breakneck economic expansion led to surging inflation and speculation, prompting fears that the boom would spin completely out of control. As head of the central bank, Zhu imposed strict macroeconomic tightening, controlled the money supply and clamped down on loose credit and speculative fixed-asset investments. Such tough measures successfully steered China towards a “soft landing” without triggering a devastating crash.

“Having worked in economics for over 50 years, I’ve felt the brunt of our country’s recurrent syndrome: the moment life gets even slightly better, then comes the grandstanding, the blind complacency, the pointless thrashing about and the totally ignorant decision-making.” – Giving a speech at the Ninth Plenary Meeting of the State Council, January 27, 2003.

4. Weathering the Asian Financial Crisis

As premier, Zhu had to face down the 1997-1998 Asian Financial Crisis, standing firm against pressure to devalue the Chinese currency, which helped stabilise regional markets and prevent a cascading competitive devaluation across Asia.

He also provided steadfast economic backing to Hong Kong as speculative attacks hit the local currency and stock market, leaving a legacy as a resolute crisis manager.

He also launched massive domestic infrastructure spending, aggressive restructuring of state-owned enterprises and financial sector reforms.

“No matter whether there is a minefield ahead of me or a deep abyss, I will charge forward, never looking back and dedicate myself wholeheartedly to the country until my last breath.” – Speaking at a press conference soon after his appointment as premier on March 19, 1998.

“The past year was extraordinarily tough for me – far tougher than I had anticipated. First, I did not expect the Asian financial crisis to hit with such severity. Second, the historic, devastating floods that struck our country also caught me off guard.” – Speaking at a 1999 press conference.

5. Backing Hong Kong’s future

Throughout his tenure as premier, Zhu was the face of Beijing’s support for Hong Kong in the wake of the 1997 handover, frequently reminding mainland and local officials alike of their historic duty to ensure the city’s success under the framework of “one country, two systems”.

“I just do not believe Hong Kong cannot be run well. If Hong Kong goes down the drain, it’s not just your responsibility – it’s ours, too. If Hong Kong, after returning to the motherland, gets ruined on our watch, wouldn’t that make us ‘sinners of the nation’? That will not happen.” – Remarks in Hong Kong on November 19, 2002.

6. Overhauling the tax system

Zhu presided over a landmark overhaul of China’s fiscal structure, introducing a tax-sharing system that divided powers and revenues between the central and local governments, cementing Beijing’s macroeconomic control.

By the early 1990s, China faced a severe fiscal crisis that threatened Beijing’s ability to govern effectively and could have undermined the country’s economic transition. Under the then fiscal contracting system, local governments collected revenues and negotiated fixed remittances to the central government, which often led to provinces hiding funds in off-budget channels to avoid sharing funds with Beijing. Deprived of money, the central government struggled to maintain macroeconomic control, manage regional disparities and fund national infrastructure projects.

Zhu Rongji spearheaded the landmark 1994 tax-sharing reform by intensively negotiating with reluctant provincial leaders to secure their compliance. The reform abolished discretionary negotiations in favour of a clear, rule-based tripartite tax scheme, with the newly created State Administration of Taxation collecting both central and shared taxes.

The results of the 1994 overhaul were immediate and transformative. In the first year, the central government’s share of total national tax revenues surged from 22 per cent to over 55 per cent, instantly revitalising Beijing’s fiscal capacity and cementing its authority over monetary and economic policy.

However, the reform left behind a persistent structural imbalance: while Beijing centralised revenue collection, local governments still had to pay for most public services. This mismatch eventually forced local authorities to rely heavily on off-budget financing, land sales and local government financing vehicles – creating fiscal challenges that China continues to navigate today.

“At present, the central government’s finances are in dire shape, nearly unsustainable. If the central government’s revenue is not properly concentrated and its financial resources are not strengthened, we will not be able to make our ends meet, and ultimately the whole country will suffer and everything will be stalled.” – Speaking to Guangdong province cadres during his tax reform research trip in September 1993.

7. Modernising the financial sector

Under Zhu’s watch, China launched sweeping reforms of its financial sector. He clarified the functions of the central bank, deepened reforms of commercial banks, foreign exchange systems and the securities and futures markets to create a unified and strictly managed financial system.

“If you are not diligent in your duties, nor honest in your work, indulging in wining and dining, issuing arbitrary approvals, practising nepotism, cultivating relationships everywhere, and treating state property as if it were yours, and you still sit on the podium giving a report, how can the people sitting down there not criticise you?” – Criticising financial officials’ misconduct at the 1993 National Financial Work Conference.

8. Persisting with painful SOE restructuring

Zhu placed SOE reform at the heart of China’s economic transition. Championing a modern enterprise system defined by “clear property rights and separated government and enterprise functions,” he drove a massive restructuring that controversially resulted in millions of lay-offs, while simultaneously pushing for a new social security net.

“State-owned enterprises only need a third of their current workforce … I refuse to believe that SOEs cannot perform just as well as foreign and private companies.” – Remarks made in 1999 during an interview with German newspaper Die Zeit.

9. Reshaping urban housing

In 1998, Zhu unveiled China’s housing blueprint, which aimed at replacing a system in which housing was mostly provided by the state with one in which private firms did the heavy lifting, laying the foundation for the urban housing market which later became a major driver of the Chinese economy.

“Right now, some cities are recklessly selling off land and carrying out mass demolitions without thinking through the consequences, completely ignoring the displaced residents. If this continues, it’s going to threaten social stability. The proceeds from land sales must first go towards rehousing evicted residents – the central government simply cannot afford to shoulder this burden.” – His handwritten comments on June 4, 1994, regarding the Ministry of Construction.

10. Championing WTO entry and Sino-US diplomacy

Zhu was perhaps the most important official behind China’s gruelling 13-year marathon to join the World Trade Organization (WTO), securing the country’s integration into the global economy. During his historic US visits, he deployed charm, wit and firmness to manage the nations’ complex ties.

“There will be differences of opinion between us. Yet only friends who hold differing views can be the best of friends; only honest critics make true friends.” – Speaking in the United States in April 1999

“When President Lincoln fought to preserve America and opposed secession, he did not hesitate to use force. We ought to learn from President Lincoln.” – Responding to a question from the press on Taiwan in Washington on April 8, 1999.

11. Crusading against corruption

Perhaps what endeared him most to the public was his fiery disdain for corrupt officials. He demanded integrity and famously staked his own life on the fight against corruption, during both his time in Shanghai and Beijing. He was also a strong advocate for simplified protocols, clean government and high efficiency.

“I have prepared 100 coffins here; 99 are for corrupt officials, and one is for myself. It’s a matter of mutual destruction, but it will bring long-term stability and development to the country and restore the people’s confidence in our cause.” – Giving a speech at a central anti-corruption conference in 1998.

“All I hope is that after I step down, the people will say, ‘He was an honest official, not a corrupt one,’ and I will be fully satisfied. If they can be a bit more generous and add, ‘Zhu Rongji actually got a few real things done,’ I’ll be very thankful.” – Conducting a press conference at the annual sessions of China’s top legislature and political advisory body, known as the two sessions, in March 2000.

item.title: [SCMP] Sado Island’s cultural renaissance: a Japanese journey from exile to artistic haven
item.description:
Dawn is still several hours away when we arrive at Ogi Port, on Sado Island’s southeast corner. The town is dark and silent as we cast our lines ashore and secure the boat.

As soon as the lines are made, we fall into our bunks, exhausted after a three-day voyage north through the Sea of Japan, or East Sea.

We plan to rest for 24 hours and then carry on towards Hokkaido, Japan’s main northern island, to escape the summer heat and typhoons of the country’s southern waters.
item.content:encoded:
Dawn is still several hours away when we arrive at Ogi Port, on Sado Island’s southeast corner. The town is dark and silent as we cast our lines ashore and secure the boat.

As soon as the lines are made, we fall into our bunks, exhausted after a three-day voyage north through the Sea of Japan, or East Sea.

We plan to rest for 24 hours and then carry on towards Hokkaido, Japan’s main northern island, to escape the summer heat and typhoons of the country’s southern waters.

After several hours of sleep, we walk into the town of Ogi in search of a late breakfast, stopping at Origine, a tiny six-seat restaurant where all is quiet, with no chef or customers in sight.

“These are the croissants I read about in the online reviews,” my partner says, pointing to a tray of flaky pastries. Fresh croissants after days of stodgy on-board meals are too much to pass up, so we sit down and wait, given hope by the fact that the kitchen counter shows signs of recent activity: used mixing bowls and cutting boards, ingredients chopped and ready for the stove.

Fifteen minutes later, just as we are about to leave, the chef steps inside from the street, surprised to see he has customers. Soon, we are drinking fresh coffee and enjoying a French-inspired brunch.

While we eat, we chat with Kaoru Ito, the chef, via translation apps. Sado, he tells us, is going through a renaissance, with tired professionals from Japan’s big cities coming to the island in search of a quieter life.

“It’s a beautiful island with a lot of nature,” he types, describing the mountains, ancient shrines and history of art and culture that drew him to Sado from a previous life in Tokyo and other mainland cities.

“I need to visit my baker to pay for those croissants. He speaks English. Do you want to come along and meet him,” he asks.

We have nowhere else to be, so we pile into Ito’s car and drive to the nearby village of Hamochihongo. There, we meet Marcus Soto, a baker from New York who moved to Japan decades ago. After chatting for a few minutes in his shop, T&M Bread Delivery, Soto asks us what our plans are for the coming days.

“Well, we were planning to leave tomorrow, but …”

“I’m hosting a dinner party in a few days,” says Soto. “You should join.”

And that is how our love affair with Sado begins.

The S-shaped, 855 sq km island (330 square miles), which also resembles the kanji character for “work” (工), if you look at it sideways, holds a complicated and dark place in Japanese history. Although it is only about 30km (19 miles) from the main island of Honshu, it long served as a place of exile for dissidents and political losers. Emperor Juntoku (1197-1242) and Zeami Motokiyo (1363-1443), a master of Noh, the classic form of Japanese masked dance theatre, were both banished from Kyoto and sent into exile on Sado.

Another chapter in Sado’s life began in 1601, when gold was discovered in its mountains, which soon became home to Japan’s largest gold mine. The mine closed in 1989 – its tunnels and ivy-covered concrete structures have since become popular tourist sights – but was recently back in the news, when South Korea protested its designation as a Unesco World Heritage site because about 1,500 Koreans were conscripted and forced to work in the mine during World War II.

The story of forced labour has largely been brushed aside in Japan’s telling of the mine’s history, but the stain remains.

Sado has also suffered from the depopulation that has afflicted so much of rural Japan. The island’s population has fallen from 113,000 in 1960 to below 50,000, leaving it littered with abandoned farms and homes, known as akiya (“empty house”).

Despite those challenges, the intellectuals and artists who were exiled to Sado helped it develop a strong cultural identity, which endures. Sado has more Noh stages per capita than anywhere else in Japan, and it is home to a vibrant taiko drumming community, which includes Kodo, a group that tours the world.

Warm and cold ocean currents meet at the island, creating an ecosystem rich in plants from both Hokkaido, in the north, and Okinawa, far to the south. As well as seeds, those currents bring a bounty of marine life, from bonito and yellowtail tuna to squid, creating rich fishing grounds.

On Sado, mountain ridges hem in the Kuninaka Plain, which, during the summer months, is bright green with some of Japan’s highest-quality rice.

Ito and his wife, Sayuri, take a day off from their restaurant to lead us on a tour of the island. They show us the Seisui-ji temple, founded in AD808 and now gently rotting away in a forest of swaying cedar trees. We sip sake at Gakkogura, an unneeded school that has been refurbished into a brewery and cafe that hosts a sake-making course popular with participants from around the world.

That night, Ito invites us to join a summer solstice party at the shrine in Ogi, where we meet more of their friends: writers, actors and entrepreneurs who have brought an urban sense of style and ambition to the rural island.

After months of cruising Japan’s coastlines, from port to port, where we rarely meet the same people twice, we are glad of the social interaction. Few of our new friends speak enough English to carry a conversation, so we again rely on translation apps, our stilted conversations lubricated by sake and laughter.

Soto’s dinner party takes place in a grand old house in Aikawa, a seaside area that was once the administrative centre for the nearby gold and silver mines. Grand old homes here are interspersed with museums and relics of the mines: the decaying, ivy-clad processing plant, alongside a bell tower and a replica of the magistrate’s office, where gold was graded and stored.

Many guests at the party share a similar story – tired of high-stress, career-driven lifestyles in Japan’s big cities, they have come to Sado to become sommeliers, restaurateurs or farmers. Each one, in their own way, is contributing to the magic we feel on the island.

One morning, a week after arriving in Sado for our “24-hour rest stop”, we prepare to cast off our lines to return to sea. Just as we are pushing our boat off the dock, Ito and another friend appear with a giant drum and cymbals. They bang out a traditional taiko farewell and shout goodbyes as we steer our boat out past the sea wall.

“We’ll be back!” we shout across the water.

We spend the summer in Hokkaido, but everything we see and do is held up in comparison with the warmth we felt on the S-shaped island.

Four months later, with Japan’s summer heat having dissipated, we make the return voyage south, our boat seeming to steer itself towards Ogi Port.

This time, we stay with Tsuyoshi Ito (no relation to Kaoru), in an akiya that he bought, together with a large parcel of land, for the equivalent of about HK$300,000 (US$38,256).

Like many rice farmers on the island, Ito uses sustainable farming practices, with fewer pesticides and fertilisers, while relying on a labour-intensive method of hanging the rice on racks in the field to dry under the sun, which enhances its flavour. We pitch in, labouring in terraced fields surrounded by steep green hillsides and hanging the rice stalks up to dry.

We recognise familiar faces at the supermarket and see the same friends at social events. At a noodle-making party hosted by an enthusiastic collector of vintage Japanese noodle machines, we meet more people who are adding to Sado’s creative spirit, including a music composer and a kimchi maker.

Just down the coast from Ogi Port, on a tiny island in a protected bay and accessible only by walking bridge, stands Teijiro Yamamoto’s former villa. Built from driftwood and other timber scraps in 1911 by the first national-level government minister to come from Sado, it had been abandoned and fallen into disrepair until a few years ago. Refurbished by volunteers, it now hosts small cultural events and parties.

We visited the structure on our first visit, and met the people who were lovingly restoring it. On this trip, friends invite us to the villa for a moon-rising party, to celebrate October’s full harvest moon.

The simple house, with its twisted driftwood beams and raw-wood finish, has panels that open to sweeping views of the sea and surrounding forest. About a dozen of us sit on tatami mats, sipping tea, bathed in moonlight. Everyone speaks in whispers, an eye kept on the slow rise of the silvery orb.

The next morning, we once again untie our mooring lines and sail out of the harbour. This departure feels more final, as our travel plans will steadily take us further away from Sado in the coming months. We wonder if we’ll ever see our new friends again.

Ten months later, we are sailing through Setonaikai, the inland sea at the heart of Japan. We are far from Sado, but it is still on our minds. Our calendar reminds us that in a few weeks, the island will be flooded with visitors for the Earth Celebration, an annual three-day taiko drumming event.

We don’t have time to sail across for the festival so we moor our boat in a marina in Wakayama, rent a car, book ferry passage and go online to buy some of the last festival tickets available, then message our friends to tell them we are on our way.

It’s a 600km (373 miles) drive across Honshu and a three-hour ferry journey from Joetsu, but we make it back to Sado Island to find the normally quiet Ogi Port buzzing with festival energy and thudding to the beat of drums.

Sado’s guest houses are unable to cope with the influx, so visitors pitch tents in the lively festival camping area and we hop between friends’ homes, spending one night sleeping on the floor of a restaurant when a vacant room cannot be found.

A food and crafts market wraps around the harbour and small troupes of drummers and dancers, dressed in masks and colourful costumes, perform in the narrow streets during the day, cheered on by shoppers and fuelled by sake offered by business owners as they pass. Elsewhere, groups take to small stages erected around Ogi Port.

Each night, between 10 and 15 members of Kodo take to the main, harbourfront stage, accompanied by other percussionists from around the globe.

In between concerts, we see Sado from a different perspective, exploring the beaches and rocky shorelines by car, admiring weathered old farmhouses overlooking bright green rice fields.

Four days later, we awake to find the main stage being dismantled and a long queue of cars waiting to board the ferry back to the mainland. Despite the strong sense of island isolation, one could catch the first ferry of the day from Sado to Niigata city and then jump on the Shinkansen to be in Tokyo in time for an early lunch.

Once again, it is time for us to say goodbye to the island.

“You might as well just buy an akiya on Sado; you’re here often enough!” one of our friends jokes as they hug us another farewell.

It is just the kind of idea that will keep Sado alive in our dreams.

This year’s Earth Celebration takes place from August 21 to 23. Tickets cost between 17,000 yen (HK$850/US$108) and 21,000 yen, and are available here

item.title: [SCMP] Zhu Rongji: reformer who led China’s economic transformation through ‘minefield or abyss’
item.description:
“Regardless of what lies ahead – be it a minefield or a deep abyss – I will forge ahead unswervingly, dedicating my entire life and energy to the country until my dying day.”

Those words, spoken at the dawn of his premiership, came to define Zhu Rongji, China’s towering economic reformer who died in Beijing on Wednesday. He was 97.

His remarks at a press conference in 1998 came as China was undertaking sweeping state-owned enterprise (SOE) reforms that caused widespread job losses, even as it reeled from the 1997 Asian financial crisis.
item.content:encoded:
“Regardless of what lies ahead – be it a minefield or a deep abyss – I will forge ahead unswervingly, dedicating my entire life and energy to the country until my dying day.”

Those words, spoken at the dawn of his premiership, came to define Zhu Rongji, China’s towering economic reformer who died in Beijing on Wednesday. He was 97.

His remarks at a press conference in 1998 came as China was undertaking sweeping state-owned enterprise (SOE) reforms that caused widespread job losses, even as it reeled from the 1997 Asian financial crisis.

Zhu, dubbed China’s economic tsar by the media, was known for his determination to steer the country through the rough waters of reforms and external shocks during his tenure as vice-premier and premier between 1991 and 2003.

He shook up the centrally planned economy, overhauled the state-owned business sector, fought corruption, revamped the tax system and secured China’s entry to the World Trade Organization – changes that some economists say brought about a historic transformation in China’s economic system, ushering in a modern state and making it an integral part of the world economy.

His straight-talking, no-nonsense style earned him a host of nicknames – including “iron-face Zhu”, “no-nonsense leader”, “problem solver”, “fire-brigade captain”, “crisis manager” and “troubleshooter”.

He was also the global face for China’s economic reform and opening up to the world. In April 1999, Zhu became the first Chinese premier to visit the United States in 15 years, travelling to Washington with a clear mission: negotiate China’s entry into the World Trade Organization.

The going was tough. Despite major concessions offered by Zhu on market access, US president Bill Clinton declined to finalise the agreement during the visit and it was not until November that the bilateral agreement was finally signed.

Backed by then president Jiang Zemin, Zhu pressed on despite strong criticism from within China about the concessions made to the foreign companies.

Zhu said in 2001, when China formally joined the WTO, that the 15 years of negotiations had caused his “black hair to turn grey”.

Looking back, China’s accession to the WTO overhauled its economy and turned the country into the world’s leading manufacturing powerhouse – a shift that drove its rise to global power status today.

Zhang Zhiwei, president and chief economist at Pinpoint Asset Management, said China’s accession to the WTO was a game-changer.

“Many vested interest groups in China were strongly against the accession, but [Zhu] stood firmly to support it. I think it’s fair to say that the WTO accession wouldn’t have happened without his strong endorsement.”

“This reform turned out to be a game changer for China and the global economy. His contribution to China’s economic miracle cannot be underestimated.”

Zhu was also crucial in laying the groundwork of China’s market economy, according to China watchers.

“Zhu Rongji was the indispensable architect and driver of China’s transition from a largely improvised reform economy into a more disciplined, internationally integrated market-oriented system,” said Denis Simon, former vice-chancellor of Duke Kunshan University and teacher at Schwarzman College.

“He stabilised the macroeconomy, restructured state industry, repaired the banking system and drove China into the WTO.”

According to Wang Dan, China director at Eurasia Group: “Zhu was the real founder of China’s socialist market economy … He has carried out the most important reforms during [his tenure] in the 1990s, such as the tax-sharing reform, stripping off non-performing debts from banks, resolving the triangular debts, restructuring the state enterprises, and unifying the dual exchange rate system.”

“The new policies rolled out afterwards are mainly reinforcements of his reforms,” Wang noted.

When Zhu became vice-premier in 1991, the economy was plagued by runaway fixed-asset investment, excess money supply, soaring inflation and financial market chaos. He successfully used measured but persistent macroeconomic controls to steer China out of a period of inflation.

Zhu’s frequent contact with foreign politicians and entrepreneurs and the straight-talking image he projected also helped to boost confidence about China’s ability to manage its economy.

Paul Triolo, partner at DGA-Albright Stonebridge Group, said: “I met Zhu Rongji during my time working in the US Embassy in Beijing in 1995-1997 … He generated a lot of confidence in the ability of the Chinese government to tackle the complex issues raised by reform and opening, particularly the reform of SOEs.”

Triolo referred to what he called “Zhu’s patient, almost scholarly approach to explaining the issues”, saying they “went a long way with his role as explainer-in-chief of China’s evolving economic policy … that was creating openings for Western businesses in sectors previously closed to such investment and participation.”

Bert Hofman, former World Bank country director for China, said Zhu was also open-minded and willing to seek advice from overseas experts to solve China’s economic problems.

“I first met Zhu in 1993 in Zhongnanhai along with the participants of the Dalian conference,” Hofman said, referring to the leadership compound in the Chinese capital.

“That conference was originally intended to focus on establishing the ‘socialist market economy’ but Zhu asked the participants to focus on his immediate headache – resurging inflation.

“The conference discussed many of the elements that got into the ‘decisions’ on establishing the socialist market economy, but for Zhu it was even more important that we delivered ideas for what was to become the ‘16 point programme’ of summer 1993.”

“To illustrate his unorthodox thinking: he asked the World Bank to invite experts from Taiwan [with] experience in fighting inflation,” added Hofman, who was a World Bank economist in Beijing in 1993.

Apart from pushing for market reform, Zhu is also well known for his determination to fight corruption and to crush vested interest groups.

In the same press conference in 1998, he famously said: “I’ll have 100 coffins prepared. Ninety-nine are for corrupt officials and the last one is for myself.”

“Chinese Premier Zhu Rongji was one of the bravest and most forward-looking Chinese leaders of his generation,” said Denis Wilder, senior fellow of the Initiative for US-China Dialogue on Global Issues.

“Zhu was the first leader to recognise and spotlight the massive corruption within the [People’s Liberation Army] that was distorting the Chinese economy; he insisted that general secretary Jiang Zemin take action.

“Going up against the incredibly powerful military, sometimes dubbed PLA Incorporated, was politically dangerous but necessary to keep the Chinese economic reforms moving forward.”

Triolo said he was also impressed with Zhu’s courage to stand up to entrenched interests that pushed back on reform and opening.

“He stressed that each round of reform generated further interests which would then oppose further reform, particularly in the SOE sector, which was one of his main points of focus. Hence policy had to continuously adjust to ensure that reform did not stall as it generated resistance to further progress.”

According to Shi Yinhong, distinguished professor at Beijing’s Renmin University, the bold and profound reforms undertaken by Zhu were made possible because of the leeway granted by party secretary Jiang.

“Zhu and [former premier] Wen Jiabao after him were strong premiers just because the party top leaders allowed them to do so, and the party leaders benefited from the sufficient space given to them to conduct the reforms in the areas entrusted to them. It is something memorable.”

Zhu’s determination to defend Hong Kong’s US dollar-pegged exchange rate during the 1997 Asian financial crisis also helped the city weather that unprecedented storm.

At the 1998 press conference, Zhu had declared that Beijing would maintain Hong Kong’s pegged exchange rate system “at all costs”. He also made “three guarantees” – minimum gross domestic product growth of 8 per cent, keeping inflation under 3 per cent, and not devaluing the renminbi.

The strong stance helped to stabilise other Asian currencies that were then in free fall.

Zhu made four official visits to Hong Kong – in the capacity of Shanghai mayor, vice-premier and premier.

During his final visit to Hong Kong in 2002, Zhu reaffirmed Beijing’s backing at a time when the city was still reeling from the financial crisis and the local government under the first chief executive Tung Chee-hwa faced mounting political pressure.

“If Hong Kong is not managed well, not only do you bear responsibility, we also bear responsibility,” Zhu said at the time.

“Hong Kong has returned to the motherland; if it is ruined in our hands, wouldn’t we become the sinners of our nation? It will not happen.”

However, economists also point out that Zhu’s policies created many economic problems that took years to resolve, such as the widening rural-urban divide caused by the priority accorded to export-oriented industries starting in 1994 and the mass lay-offs in SOEs.

“Many of his policies also fomented or aggravated the imbalances and contradictions of the Chinese economy that underlined the current economic impasse,” said Ho-fung Hung, a professor at Johns Hopkins University.

“His reform of state enterprises led to the dismantling of social welfare and public goods, such as housing, that those enterprises had provided.

“All these policies led to the explosion of inequality and social insecurity and, hence, lagging domestic consumption, which is haunting the Chinese economy today.”

The tax-sharing system and the privatisation of home ownership introduced by Zhu also left local governments heavily reliant on the property market for revenue, a model that became a strong driver of the Chinese economy for years before a prolonged slump set in.

Born in 1928 in Changsha, capital of the central province of Hunan, not far from Mao Zedong’s hometown, Zhu joined the Communist Party in 1949, the same year Mao founded the People’s Republic.

After graduating from Beijing’s prestigious Tsinghua University with a degree in electrical engineering in 1951, Zhu began his career as a civil servant with a government agency.

He was branded a “rightist” in 1958 during Mao’s Anti-Rightist Movement after he criticised some of the projects in Mao’s Great Leap Forward as unrealistic. Zhu was expelled from the party and demoted.

During the Cultural Revolution, from 1966 to 1976, he worked in obscurity, either as a minor functionary or in labour camps. But his political career was slowly rehabilitated when Deng Xiaoping came to power in the late 1970s and he rejoined the party in 1978.

For most of the 1980s, Zhu worked at the State Economic Commission, a powerful central government agency in charge of managing the economy. He organised large-scale transfers of foreign technology, oversaw several big national projects and encouraged foreigners to invest in joint ventures.

Zhu’s ability won the appreciation of economic policy planners at the time and he may have been one of only a few senior officials backed by both Chen Yun, the late godfather of Chinese central planning, and reformist patriarch Deng.

As mayor of Shanghai – China’s most populous city and commercial hub – from 1988, Zhu cemented his reputation for efficiency and clean governance as he oversaw an ambitious programme to emulate the international standing of New York, London or Hong Kong, turning the city’s Pudong New Area, a Singapore-sized area across the Huangpu River from its famous Bund, into a Chinese Manhattan.

He served as vice-premier from 1991 to 1998, and premier from 1998 to 2003.

Zhu kept a low profile after retiring from premiership in March 2003, having declared that he would not write an autobiography or comment on government work after stepping down.

After an appearance in 2015, he was notably absent from military parades, events where retired state leaders traditionally appear. His rare public outings were mostly related to the Tsinghua University School of Economics and Management, where he served as the founding dean in 1984.

He also made rare recorded remarks in English. Once when a compilation of his replies to the press during his years as premier and vice-premier, Zhu Rongji Meets the Press, was published by Oxford University Press in 2011, and another time when the English version of the multi-volume Zhu Rongji on the Record: The Road to Reform 1991–1997 was published in 2013.

Former US secretary of state Dr Henry Kissinger and the former West German chancellor Helmut Schmidt wrote forewords for the latter.

Zhu is survived by his wife Lao An, daughter Zhu Yanlai and son Zhu Yunlai.

Additional reporting by Cary Huang, Frank Tang, Siqi Ji, Carol Yang and Holly Chik

item.title: [SCMP] Malaysia’s monarchy charts a new course amid political flux
item.description:
When Malaysian artist Darwisy Mustafani received a commission to paint the country’s king and queen, he did not reach for an ordinary canvas.

Instead, the 25-year-old from the northeastern city of Kota Bharu transformed songket – the lustrous handwoven fabric once reserved for Malay courts and ceremonial dress – into a portrait of the sultan and his wife before a golden-domed palace.

The portrait, commissioned in 2024 by Malaysia’s police force as a gift for Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar and Queen Raja Zarith Sofiah, opened a door Darwisy had never expected. Further royal commissions followed, including work linked to other Malaysian palaces and Brunei’s royal household.
item.content:encoded:
When Malaysian artist Darwisy Mustafani received a commission to paint the country’s king and queen, he did not reach for an ordinary canvas.

Instead, the 25-year-old from the northeastern city of Kota Bharu transformed songket – the lustrous handwoven fabric once reserved for Malay courts and ceremonial dress – into a portrait of the sultan and his wife before a golden-domed palace.

The portrait, commissioned in 2024 by Malaysia’s police force as a gift for Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar and Queen Raja Zarith Sofiah, opened a door Darwisy had never expected. Further royal commissions followed, including work linked to other Malaysian palaces and Brunei’s royal household.

“My focus has never been about painting royal figures simply because they are royal,” he told This Week in Asia. “I never planned for my work to become closely associated with royalty, but I’m grateful that it has opened the door for me to share Malaysian culture with a wider audience.”

On TikTok, viewers watch Darwisy layer paint over woven gold thread, gradually revealing royal faces against patterns that carry centuries of courtly history. Many of those following the process are young Malaysians encountering the monarchy not through a constitutional textbook or palace ceremony, but through an algorithm.

“They first discover my work because they enjoy watching the creative process,” he said. “Then they become curious about the story behind the artwork and the cultural meaning of the materials.”

That curiosity is growing at a moment when Malaysia’s royal institutions have become increasingly visible far beyond ceremonial life.

Since the country’s first transfer of federal power in 2018 shattered six decades of rule by one coalition, Malaysia has endured collapsing alliances, three prime ministers in less than three years, shifting parliamentary majorities and its first hung federal parliament.

Those ruptures repeatedly placed decisions about government formation before the king, drawing greater public attention to powers that had long existed in the constitution but were rarely exercised under the stable, dominant-party politics of an earlier era.

The result is not an absolute monarchy supplanting parliamentary democracy, constitutional experts say, but an old institution operating under new political conditions.

“The rulers tend always to have been influential players,” Anthony Crothers Milner, an Australian historian of Southeast Asia who has written extensively on Malay political culture, told This Week in Asia. “From time to time one reads that the rulers have suddenly gained power, but, in fact, they tend always to have been influential players.”

What has changed is the political landscape around them, according to Milner.

Broken majorities

Malaysia has one of the world’s most unusual constitutional arrangements. Nine of its 13 states are headed by hereditary Malay rulers, who elect one among themselves as the Yang di-Pertuan Agong, or king, for a five-year term through a secret ballot conducted by the Conference of Rulers.

The other four states, Penang, Melaka, Sabah and Sarawak, have appointed governors and do not take part in choosing the federal monarch.

Executive authority is exercised by the elected government, while the king generally acts on ministerial advice. The constitution nevertheless grants the monarch limited discretionary authority, most notably in appointing as prime minister the lawmaker whom he believes commands the confidence of parliament’s majority and in withholding consent to a request to dissolve parliament.

For decades, those reserve powers attracted little public attention because the governing coalition normally arrived at the palace with a clear majority.

That changed in February 2020, when Mahathir Mohamad’s resignation brought down the Pakatan Harapan (PH) government and sparked a sequence of royal consultations with lawmakers and party leaders to determine who commanded sufficient parliamentary support.

The constitutional machinery was tested again after the November 2022 general election produced no outright winner. Then king Sultan Abdullah Sultan Ahmad Shah interviewed political leaders and urged rival coalitions to consider a unity government before appointing Anwar Ibrahim as prime minister.

Azmi Hassan, a senior fellow at the Nusantara Academy for Strategic Research, said the monarchy’s role was not new, but had become more conspicuous. “Previously, much of it was done behind closed doors and in a very discreet manner,” he said.

Without a resolution, Malaysia might have returned to another election and produced another inconclusive result, Azmi said. “In that sense, the nation has looked to the monarchy as a stabilising institution.”

Constitutional lawyer Lim Wei Jiet said weaker parties and unstable coalitions had created greater room for royal institutions to influence the course of government formation.

“When political parties are not as strong as they used to be, the monarchs invariably fill that power vacuum and play a much more influential role in governance, at least compared to pre-2018,” he said.

The monarchy’s higher profile has continued under Sultan Ibrahim, the Johor ruler who began his five-year federal reign in January 2024.

In April, the king said he would determine the best candidate to lead the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission after the incumbent’s term ended, while warning that the appointment should not be politicised. Under the constitution, the commission’s chief is appointed by the king on the prime minister’s advice.

Such episodes have prompted renewed debate over how convention, written law and royal influence intersect, particularly when the constitution vests formal authority in the monarch but requires most decisions to follow government advice.

Wan Ahmad Fauzi Wan Husain, a Malaysian constitutional scholar specialising in the monarchy, said the institution should not be interpreted solely through the conventions of Britain’s Westminster system, which shaped Malaya’s colonial administration before independence in 1957.

“Our monarchy does not mirror Westminster,” he said. “It is rooted in the Great Malay Melaka Sultanate.”

He argued that the rulers retained constitutional prerogatives inherited from the pre-colonial Malay states and were obliged to safeguard Islam, constitutional supremacy, the rule of law and public peace.

“The growing presence of the monarchy in the political sphere is not unconstitutional, but rather consistent with the constitutional order,” he said.

Other constitutional lawyers take a narrower reading, emphasising that royal authority is largely exercised on advice and that personal discretion is confined to specified circumstances.

The Malaysian Bar, the professional body representing lawyers in Peninsular Malaysia, has described the monarch as possessing extensive formal authority but limited personal power, except during exceptional situations in which discretion comes into play.

The state vs the crown

The palace’s growing prominence has not come without friction.

“Dr [Mahathir] came quite close to abolishing the monarchies in 1983 and 1993,” Andrew Harding, a leading scholar in Malaysian constitutional law, told This Week in Asia.

In 1983, Mahathir confronted the Malay rulers, triggering a constitutional crisis when he introduced amendments aimed at limiting the king’s authority to withhold or remove the palace’s power of assent to legislation while shifting emergency powers away from the monarch.

Mahathir faced strong opposition as the rulers resisted, leading to a months-long constitutional stand-off before a compromise was reached.

The outcome was a subsequent constitutional amendment in 1984 – limiting royal assent: if the king does not assent to a bill within 30 days, it automatically becomes law. The king was also granted 30 to 60 days, depending on the approved bill, to return it to parliament for further debate if it was not assented to.

The palace’s constitutional role regarding emergency remained intact, as Mahathir backed down from his initial proposal to transfer that power to the prime minister, and state-level powers also remained intact.

This was the first modern-day battle between state-elected leaders and the monarchy in Malaysia’s history. But it was not the last.

Mahathir has had a sticky relationship with Johor’s royal family dating back to the early 1990s, when his government revoked immunities from the Malay rulers following alleged assaults by the Johorean royalty.

Between 2018 and 2020, when Mahathir returned to power as prime minister, he again opposed the Johor palace. He went as far as calling the Johor crown prince, Tunku Ismail Sultan Ibrahim, a “little boy” during a public argument over whether the federal government or the royal family had the ultimate right to administer the state government and appoint top officials.

The latest row in June involved the crown prince criticising Member of Parliament Syed Saddiq over his political stance and governance.

Syed responded that politics was “not a Hollywood movie”, sparking a heated public exchange between him and the Johor royal.

Harding said political fragmentation since 2018 had created greater room for the monarchy to exercise and extend its established constitutional functions, including in the appointment of governments and decisions over whether to dissolve legislatures.

“It is true that politics abhors a vacuum,” he said.

Nine crowns

The public clashes only showcase one dimension of Malaysia’s constitutional monarchy.

The debate is complicated by the fact that Malaysia does not have a single uniform monarchy.

Each royal state has its own constitution, succession rules and historical relationship between palace, government and traditional authorities. Johor’s royal house has long maintained a highly visible place in the state’s public life, while Negeri Sembilan follows a distinctive system drawn from Minangkabau custom.

There, the Yang di-Pertuan Besar is selected from eligible princes by four territorial chieftains known as the undang. The system amounts to an elective state monarchy nested within Malaysia’s elective federal monarchy.

Its complexity burst into national view this year when a succession dispute involving Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir, several chieftains and a rival claimant spilled into public declarations, court proceedings and competing interpretations of the state constitution.

The palace consolidated its position following the Negeri Sembilan polls on August 1, with Tuanku Muhriz dismissing the undang of Jelebu and revoking the royal titles of several figures linked to the succession dispute, clearing the way for the swearing-in of the new state government and Barisan Nasional’s Ismail Lasim as the new menteri besar the following day.

BN secured a win in the state polls, taking 18 of the 36 seats, defeating PH’s 11 and ultimately forming the state government with a supermajority of 25 through electoral cooperation with opposition Perikatan Nasional.

Tuanku Muhriz urged freshly elected assemblymen to ensure the interests of the state and its people are put above political or personal considerations.

“To the candidates who were unsuccessful in this election, I hope that all of you will continue to serve the people with dedication and contribute to the well-being of society and the progress of Negeri Sembilan,” the ruler said during the swearing-in ceremony at Istana Besar Seri Menanti.

His remarks followed months of political and royal uncertainty that strained Negeri Sembilan’s unique constitutional system, underscoring that the state constitution remains intertwined with state governance even as the broader royal dispute continues through the courts.

A rare postponement of the Conference of Rulers’ meeting set for June 23-25 had pushed the Negeri Sembilan succession dispute into politics. The next meeting is yet to be determined.

In June, Prime Minister Anwar said the federal government continued to recognise Tuanku Muhriz, after Tunku Nadzaruddin Tuanku Ja’afar was proclaimed as the new ruler at a hotel in neighbouring Melaka.

The dispute remained entangled in litigation and arguments over the authority of the undang and the state’s royal council.

Wan Ahmad Fauzi said the controversy exposed a widespread misunderstanding of Negeri Sembilan’s royal structure.

“The ruler of Negeri Sembilan is not the Yang di-Pertuan Besar alone,” he said, arguing that the constitutional duties of the ruling chieftains should not be dismissed as merely customary positions.

The episode differed sharply from the 2022 federal deadlock, but both forced Malaysians to confront the architecture beneath their monarchy, including powers and traditions that usually remain distant from everyday political debate.

Historian Milner said the central question was whether the monarchy could continue supplying stability when elected institutions faltered.

“Monarchy, on the face of it, is an outdated institution,” he said. “In recent times, however, it may be gaining new support, especially as people look at other types of constitution.”

Constitutionally, Malaysia’s political upheavals stemming from its democratic process have shown that the monarch has played a decisive role, exercising some level of discretion on who leads the nation based on parliamentary majority and support.

Lim, the constitutional lawyer, said decisions made by the palace had gone beyond what was widely deemed as a ceremonial role previously.

“So when political parties are not as strong as they used to be, the monarchs invariably fill that power vacuum and play a much more influential role in governance, at least compared to pre-2018,” he told This Week in Asia.

According to Lim, rulers’ constitutional powers are enumerated in the federal constitution and have the force of law which is not open to question while the constitutional convention acts as a long-standing practice derived from the UK which Malaysia’s system is largely based on.

From legal observations, Lim said monarchs were not overstepping their constitutional powers. “I think the constitution is working as intended for now.”

However, he said constitutional convention might evolve, stemming from any instability of political coalitions.

“For example, it may now be a constitutional convention for the king to be consulted on the annual budget or on major public policies before they are rolled out, which I definitely see happening unlike before,” Lim said. “The monarchs will no doubt be playing a larger role in governance due to the instability of political coalitions.”

New normal

Awang Azman Awang Pawi, a political analyst at the University of Malaya, said Malaysia appeared to be entering a form of conditional new normal as long as politics remained fragmented.

He said the monarchy was likely to remain more visible in matters involving government formation, legislation dissolution and determination of majority support.

“The healthiest constitutional model is one in which the monarchy remains influential but firmly bound by the constitution; respected but not politicised; and committed to safeguarding the democratic process rather than competing with the elected government.”

That prominence carries advantages and risks. Royal intervention can help break a deadlock when no political leader commands a majority, but sustained dependence on the palace may allow political parties to avoid the harder task of rebuilding durable coalitions and settling disputes through parliament.

The institution’s legitimacy also rests partly on remaining above partisan combat, even as political actors increasingly appeal to rulers, invoke palace relationships or portray royal approval as a source of authority.

For Darwisy, those arguments remain beyond the purpose of his portraits. His focus is the cultural language surrounding the institution and how it can reach a generation more familiar with short videos than royal archives.

“Not everyone reads history books, but today many people connect with art on social media,” he said. “My hope is that people don’t just see a royal portrait, but also discover and appreciate the beauty of Malaysian culture through the artwork.”

item.title: [SCMP] Vintage charm is blended with modern elegance in a timeless Hong Kong flat
item.description:
Needing a designer to renovate his newly purchased, 38-year-old apartment in Central, businessman Harry Sun found the perfect fit in an unexpected place. He and interior designer Dominic Cheung, co-founder of Crimson Company, were both regulars at the same tailor’s shop – and when their paths crossed, the introduction sparked an instant connection. The two shared sensibilities that extended beyond sartorial savoir faire to a mutual appreciation for classicism with a youthful touch.

Thus began a harmonious collaboration to make over the 620 sq ft mid-rise apartment in quintessentially “old” Hong Kong, with its views of historic St Paul’s Church ringed by mature trees.

Sating his penchant for vintage and antique European designs, Sun already had an assemblage of finds he’d been collecting from markets since his university days in Britain. These would inform the interiors, as Cheung revised the floor plan from two bedrooms to one, enabling a bigger dining room and a slightly enlarged bathroom.
item.content:encoded:
Needing a designer to renovate his newly purchased, 38-year-old apartment in Central, businessman Harry Sun found the perfect fit in an unexpected place. He and interior designer Dominic Cheung, co-founder of Crimson Company, were both regulars at the same tailor’s shop – and when their paths crossed, the introduction sparked an instant connection. The two shared sensibilities that extended beyond sartorial savoir faire to a mutual appreciation for classicism with a youthful touch.

Thus began a harmonious collaboration to make over the 620 sq ft mid-rise apartment in quintessentially “old” Hong Kong, with its views of historic St Paul’s Church ringed by mature trees.

Sating his penchant for vintage and antique European designs, Sun already had an assemblage of finds he’d been collecting from markets since his university days in Britain. These would inform the interiors, as Cheung revised the floor plan from two bedrooms to one, enabling a bigger dining room and a slightly enlarged bathroom.

“Our goal was to create a space with a strong, yet quiet, architectural identity that feels both intentional and deeply personal,” says Cheung. “By integrating classic European details within a modern, clean envelope, we created a backdrop designed not to dominate, but to age gracefully over the years.”

His client’s brief for “cosiness” – a space that could tastefully house his furniture and objets d’art – excited Cheung, himself a lover of things vintage.

“Vintage pieces big and small can introduce a storytelling element, adding more depth to the space. Our shared vision was to juxtapose old and new, without making it look like an antique shop.”

An 18th century Louis XVI commode and a 19th century Louis Philippe gilded mirror set the tone for the dining room, where, additionally, mid-century modern Wishbone chairs are paired with a custom-made Calacatta marble table. Resisting the temptation to install ornate chandeliers, lighting designer and Crimson Company co-founder Rosana Asencios opted instead for two simple brass pendants. “Their patina will change with age,” she says, “responding very well to the antique pieces and the history in the room. It’s about having a sleek accent, without being too overwhelming.”

French-inspired wall mouldings and herringbone oak flooring lend subtle sophistication.

In the separate living room, twin bay windows frame neighbourhood views, and a mahogany library wall houses Sun’s collections of books – history and literature among his favourites – and vinyl records.

A green velvet sofa adds a youthful, mid-century modernist touch beside a vintage handmade rug. Sun’s prized analogue turntable sits atop a minimalist, Scandinavian-inspired coffee table; all other audiovisual equipment is concealed behind slatted joinery inlaid within the wall panelling.

With his client needing to work from home only occasionally, Cheng tucked a study nook into a walkway, behind two pocket doors inlaid with antique glass panels.

Cheung’s intent to “frame different moments in the home” is evident in the simply furnished bedroom, where two elegant oak and glass pendants, a custom bed and an oak-finish wardrobe take centre stage. The only hung artwork is a small framed print picked up on a trip to Italy during his school days.

Proving that even a compact kitchen can have style as well as substance, handmade Moroccan splashback tiles pair gracefully with natural stone benchtops, brass knobs and pulls punctuating the light-grey, powder-finished cabinetry.

The same quiet refinement carries through to the bathroom. Neither space is merely entered – one arrives from the dining room via a dramatic Nero Marquina marble arched portal and floor threshold.

Every corner and every wall holds a focal point, yet nothing feels forced or crowded.

“In this not-so-big apartment, a lot is happening, but you don’t feel like a lot is happening. The flow is easy,” Cheung says.

The result is a harmonious dialogue between modernism and classicism, where all details are intentional but never laboured.

A delighted Sun says the refurbishment, completed in December 2024, never ceases to amaze him. “It’s one of those places that’s well built, well designed and feels very comfortable when you live there.”

Living room

Mahogany bookcase, designed by Crimson Company and built by Design for Life. Sofa, from B&B Italia. Coffee table, from Norr11. Record turntable, from Cambridge Audio. Side table, from Mater. Wall lamp, from Santa & Cole. Vintage handmade rug, from Blanc Marine Boutique. Artwork is a Liu Peng landscape, from Asian Art Platform Singapore

Dining room

Calacatta Viola dining marble, designed by Crimson Company and built by Design for Life. Wishbone chairs, from Carl Hansen & Søn. Candela di Vals pendant lamps in natural brass, from Viabizzuno. Sun found the small oil painting of a fig years ago. In the alcove, a Louis XVI mahogany commode with Carrara marble top, from Inessa Stewart’s Antiques. Above it, a Louis Philippe gilt mirror with crown, from 1stDibs. Behind the mirror, Ianthe Mono wallpaper in Lapis from Liberty Fabrics

Dining room detail

Nero Marquina marble arched portal defines the threshold leading to the bathroom and kitchen. Wall mouldings and wall finish, in St Leo plaster paint (stleointeriors.com). Polished brass dimmer switches and sockets, from Varilight (varilight.co.uk). Wall-hung printed abstract, from The Poster Club (theposterclub.com)

Study nook

Pocket doors in the study nook feature antique glass inlay panels. Vintage brass handles from Etsy. Desk joinery in burl wood veneer, designed by Crimson Company and built by Design for Life, who also installed the herringbone-pattern engineered timber floor

Bathroom

Brass-framed mirror and cabinetry with custom Calacatta Viola marble vanity top, designed by Crimson Company and built by Design for Life. Basin and French gold-finish tapware, from Kohler. Small lamp, from Audo Copenhagen. Overhead light, from Visual Comfort

Bedroom

Bed with upholstered headboard, custom-designed by Crimson Company and built by Sankon Interiors. Pair of hanging lamps, from Santa & Cole. Bedside tables, from Ikea. Wardrobe in oak timber finish, designed by Crimson Company and built by Design for Life

Kitchen

Kitchen cabinetry with natural quartz stone tops, by Crimson Company and Design for Life. Handmade Zellige tiles, from Zia Tile. Brass knobs and pulls, from Willow & Stone. Artwork on benchtop, by Molly Supplee

item.title: [SCMP] Ready player 3: India offers Asean a US-China alternative
item.description:
At a food fair in New Delhi, a vegetable exporter from the Philippines set out its wares: bags of dried moringa and lemongrass, bundles of taro leaves and a bowl of laing, the creamy coconut-milk stew made from them.

The question Dry Tech Manufacturing wanted to answer was simple: could the simple Filipino food it sells under its Sheentaro brand tantalise the taste buds of the world’s most populous country?

India has hundreds of millions of vegetarians, more than any other country on Earth, making it the ideal market for Sheentaro’s plant-based and ready-to-cook products, Dry Tech vice-president Corinne Anne Cordero told This Week in Asia.
item.content:encoded:
At a food fair in New Delhi, a vegetable exporter from the Philippines set out its wares: bags of dried moringa and lemongrass, bundles of taro leaves and a bowl of laing, the creamy coconut-milk stew made from them.

The question Dry Tech Manufacturing wanted to answer was simple: could the simple Filipino food it sells under its Sheentaro brand tantalise the taste buds of the world’s most populous country?

India has hundreds of millions of vegetarians, more than any other country on Earth, making it the ideal market for Sheentaro’s plant-based and ready-to-cook products, Dry Tech vice-president Corinne Anne Cordero told This Week in Asia.

“That’s the main reason why we decided to sign up on short notice,” she said of the Indusfood expo, held in Greater Noida at the start of this year.

“With India having a bigger population than China … and a lot of them are vegetarian, we thought they’d be more open to those types of food ingredients.”

Sheentaro’s products were previously showcased at the China-Asean Expo in Nanning and Cordero said the reception was so positive that “when this opportunity in India came about, we said ‘let’s try it again’”.

Southeast Asian nations are increasingly looking to India as an alternative market, arms supplier and technology partner as China and the US vie for regional influence.

India is more than happy to oblige, observers say – though it also knows its limits. It cannot out-trade China, nor can it supplant America’s security umbrella. What is offers instead is room to manoeuvre, free of the demand to choose sides.

That message travelled to Manila last month, where India’s foreign minister, S. Jaishankar, used Asean-led meetings to press the case for deeper cooperation, calling it the only way to “de-risk and diversify”.

He spoke of energy security and food security, and how precarious both had become. Neither these nor public health could be taken for granted in this new “era of volatility and disruption”, Jaishankar said, identifying maritime trade as a further source of anxiety.

A more stable and secure future was in reach, he said, but only by working together: an animating theme of India’s Act East Policy, launched 12 years ago to forge stronger economic, strategic, and cultural ties with Southeast Asia and the broader region.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi were also in the Philippine capital last month for talks with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations on the South China Sea, supply chains and security – a reminder of how much great-power rivalry still shapes regional diplomacy.

The economic dimension of India’s engagement push was on full display earlier in July, when Delhi hosted talks on upgrading the Asean-India Trade in Goods Agreement, a decade-old free-trade pact that officials say no longer reflects current realities.

Two-way trade came in at US$128 billion in the 2025-26 financial year, according to India’s Commerce and Industry Ministry – respectable, but only a fraction of the US$1 trillion and change that China did with the bloc.

Analysts say India’s strategy appears to be centred around pairing diplomacy with trade, defence exports and maritime cooperation, offering Southeast Asia a third option beyond the US-China binary.

It is best described as “a search for mutual wins”, according to Arvind Raj, a geopolitical analyst and associate research fellow at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies’ Centre for Multilateralism Studies in Singapore.

A more multipolar neighbourhood would give Southeast Asian nations more choices and more room to hedge, he said – as India, in turn, secured a larger foothold in a region that it had long courted from the margins.

Summitry to substance

For years, India’s Asean diplomacy has been heavy on the ceremony, but light on the delivery.

“Asean sits at the centre of India’s Act East Policy on paper, but for most of the past decade the relationship ran on summitry rather than substance,” said Oorja Tapan, a doctoral researcher of international politics at Jawaharlal Nehru University in Delhi.

Analysts say the clearest evidence of how that dynamic is beginning to change can be seen in the region’s expanding arsenals.

During a three-day state visit last month, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi sealed a deal for Jakarta to buy BrahMos supersonic cruise missiles – jointly developed by India and Russia – making Indonesia the third Southeast Asian buyer after Vietnam and the Philippines.

A separate deal for Jakarta to acquire India’s Astra air-to-air missiles was also signed.

Pooja Bhatt, an associate professor of international relations at India’s O.P. Jindal Global University, calls such defence cooperation “not only part of increasing trade with Asean but also a form of strategic signalling” – proof that Delhi can deliver hardware, not just handshakes.

India wanted to become Southeast Asia’s “resident partner”, Tapan said, offering “capability without a formal alliance demand attached” and without asking the region to choose sides.

Pairing defence exports with renewed free-trade negotiations showed that Delhi wanted to be seen as “a dependable partner offering security cooperation, technology-sharing and balanced regional influence”, said Shristi Pukhrem, a visiting fellow at the India Foundation think tank and director of its Act East Centre.

Foreign policy researcher Joanne Lin concurred that weapons sales alone would not be enough to anchor the relationship.

India’s relevance depended on it delivering across “trade, maritime security, connectivity, tech and supply chains”, said Lin, a senior fellow at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute and visiting scholar at the MIT Centre for International Studies.

“This is why India is trying to address concerns over trade imbalance, rules of origin and possible re-routing of Chinese goods through Asean, while Asean looks forward to market access with fewer barriers.”

Beyond US-China?

Ultimately, India’s pitch boils down to optionality.

Delhi is not seeking “supremacy in Asean”, according to Abhishek Sharma of the Observer Research Foundation think tank in the Indian capital, but rather is trying to advance its own trade interests while pushing for a stronger, more secure – and more multipolar – Indo-Pacific region.

This framing allowed the South Asian nation to cast itself as an independent pole, distinct from both Beijing and Washington and without the associated baggage, said Sharma, a junior fellow with the foundation’s strategic studies programme.

Lin agreed that India functioned as an additional option for Asean rather than a direct replacement for either the US or China.

India’s appeal is more as a balancing and diversification partner

Joanne Lin, foreign policy researcher

“They are looking for partners that can widen their strategic space without forcing them into rigid alignments,” she said of Southeast Asian nations. “India’s strategic autonomy, multi-alignment and Global South positioning resonate with Asean’s own instinct to diversify partnerships and preserve room for manoeuvre.”

In Tapan’s telling, India “lowers the cost of hedging” for the region, due to it being “aligned enough with the West to be useful, [but] non-aligned enough that buying Indian missiles doesn’t read in Beijing as joining a containment bloc”.

Still, Lin was careful not to overstate Delhi’s diplomatic standing within the region.

India “is not yet in the same league as China or the US” in terms of Southeast Asia’s “perceptions of influence”, she said.

“China remains deeply embedded economically, while the US remains central to security calculations. India’s appeal is more as a balancing and diversification partner, useful, non-coercive and increasingly visible, but still needing stronger economic delivery.”

‘Some way to go’

India still had “some way to go” to match the scale of Chinese capital, trade volume and state-driven speed, said Bhatt, the international-relations professor.

China’s trade with Asean was about eight times higher than India’s last year – a gulf that does not look likely to close any time soon.

But Delhi’s diplomacy need not be based on countering China alone.

India and Asean spoke “a common language of non-alignment” and shared “a common belief in the Global South”, Bhatt said.

Soft-power advantages bolster India’s appeal, according to Pukhrem, pointing to Delhi-funded restoration work at heritage sites such as Cambodia’s Angkor Wat and Vietnam’s My Son temples as evidence of outreach that “builds soft power rooted in shared civilisational ties rather than transactional influence”.

Tapan agreed that it was not a case of “India vs China’s clout, but India raising the price of Chinese dominance”.

The recent BrahMos sales had demonstrated regional appetite for Indian weapons systems, she said, further pointing to demand for naval hardware, generic pharmaceuticals and digital public infrastructure “that no Chinese product can substitute”.

Tapan also identified India’s growing appeal as a “China plus one” destination for companies looking to diversify supply chains.

“None of this beats a trillion dollars of trade. But Asean’s operating logic is hedging,” she said. “The realistic question is whether India can be indispensable in the places where China is either unwelcome or absent.”

Lin cautioned against India defining its Asean engagement purely in oppositional terms.

“Asean does not want to be treated as a theatre for India-China rivalry,” she said, adding that Delhi could make the most impact by helping the bloc diversify supply chains, build maritime capacity and strengthen digital and health cooperation.

“India’s broader influence will depend on whether it can also deliver in areas that matter to Asean’s economic and development priorities,” Lin added.

item.title: [SCMP] Investment with Chinese characteristics: how Beijing’s money is reshaping tech ventures
item.description:
On the surface, China’s cutting-edge tech sector – from the algorithmic breakthroughs of DeepSeek and Zhipu AI to the hardware of Unitree Robotics and ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) – mirrors Silicon Valley’s venture capital-backed ecosystem.

But a closer look at their financing histories reveals a common investor: the Chinese state.

Beijing’s strong presence underscores a more profound structural shift in how China’s frontier technology is being funded. As Western venture capital and domestic private wealth retreat, the government has been steadily expanding its role in the market, constructing a state-capitalist apparatus which blurs the line between public policy and private equity.
item.content:encoded:
On the surface, China’s cutting-edge tech sector – from the algorithmic breakthroughs of DeepSeek and Zhipu AI to the hardware of Unitree Robotics and ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) – mirrors Silicon Valley’s venture capital-backed ecosystem.
