Maybe several months ago, there were some people in Washington who thought that it might be possible to detach Russia from China in a “reverse Nixon”, or “reverse Kissinger” play, but that is not a very widely held idea any more, for two reasons.

First, people realise that there is a very close relationship between Russia and China. This was made clear by Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi when meeting his European Union counterparts. For the first time, it was much more explicit that China would not wish to see Russia lose.

The other factor is the American idea that they could detach Russia from China and bring it close to the US has fallen away. People have seen that Putin has not changed his policy towards Ukraine at all and is bombing it more fiercely than before.

We’re likely to see a scenario in which the US tries to neutralise Russia as much as possible while still looking for a negotiation on Ukraine, but essentially there probably will be more concentration on pushing back against China alone.

What conditions could bring about the end of the war?

We don’t know what conditions it will take to come to an end, but we do know that, at least in the past few weeks, President Trump has reauthorised the supply of weaponry to Ukraine to fight back against Russia, which at one point he was holding back on.

Now it’s clear that weaponry is going to Ukraine and the war may last longer than would have seemed the case just a few weeks ago, when it seemed Ukraine might run out of ammunition.

The question becomes whether Russia can maintain its all-out war-based economy and conscription of soldiers, while keeping inflation – which is very, very high – under control.

The longer the Ukraine war continues, the less likely it is that Russia can do that, and the more weapons that are supplied by the Americans, along with the Europeans, the longer the Ukrainians can keep fighting.

Under former president Joe Biden, Washington and other Western capitals formed a united stance on a wide range of China-related issues. How will Trump’s presidency change that alliance on China?

Europeans are looking to negotiate on their own issues with the US, such as tariffs. The question of China has been put a bit on the back shelf but essentially, the issue is that China provides useful supply chains.

There is also a problem, in particular for Europe, of whether it can draw on China’s markets but not be overwhelmed by Chinese exports, particularly in areas like autos and electric batteries. Those problems are not really changed by the relationship with the US.

The EU has a whole variety of fundamental issues it needs to solve – about how it creates a new industrial model, where it cooperates with China and where it needs to restrict its market.

And in some ways, it’s learning from China, because China has heavily restricted its own market in some areas, such as online service provision. So the Europeans will also pick and choose where they feel vulnerable, opening up in certain areas and closing in others.

The Trump administration is still figuring out its policy on China. There are different strands of thinking that you can see from the outside, but how important they are in relation to each other, and how they will balance out in the end, is still unclear.

For instance, there are some traditional hawks, such as Secretary of State Marco Rubio and others, who take a view on China that in some ways would not have been that different from Republicans seven or 10 years ago.

But you also have the whole technology world – Silicon Valley and beyond. A lot of them are still very interested in making sure that the relationship with China is smooth.

Apple is one of the most profitable and innovative companies in the United States, but huge amounts of its production and connection still take place in China. Of course, some production has moved to India, but China is still really important to a company like Apple.

There has been a growing interest in moving more production and intellectual property back to the US but there’s no sense yet that this is a complete disconnection from China, and that points in a different direction from the hawks.

Then there is the question of what Trump himself thinks. It’s interesting to look at the tariff policy, because tariffs have been put on China but also on other countries, including traditional US allies.

Also, when Trump says “I like to talk to my good friend Xi Jinping. We can talk about things” – what does he want to talk about? Not clear.

Compared with other presidents, Trump seems to really like personal diplomacy. In other words, he believes that his personal relationships with leaders are the important thing.

Speaking of leadership diplomacy, what conditions do you think will be needed for Trump and Xi to meet?

I think a meeting between the two leaders is quite likely. Trump is announcing that the deal has been done with China. He would only want to go to China if the deal is kind of there, so he can mark it in a big ceremony and have a prominent meeting with Xi.

I don’t think he would want to go to China to negotiate. We’re moving into a phase where the US wants to get most of its tariff deals done within the next couple of months.

During his first term, Trump had a very grand welcoming ceremony provided by Xi in Beijing. I think he would like to do that again – a big, grand meeting that Trump will think of as a historic event, that showcases he’s able to do negotiations and deals with China in a way that other presidents haven’t been able to do. I think he would want to push quite hard in that direction. That’s my guess.

Are the two presidents likely to get along?

I think that’s perfectly possible. You might remember that when Trump invited Xi to Mar-a-Lago, he said that he gave Xi a big piece of chocolate cake. He never talked about giving chocolate cake to German chancellor Angela Merkel.

That’s a sign that he feels there’s some sort of ability to speak leader to leader in that sense. Xi has said less about Trump, but he hasn’t said any very publicly hostile things personally about him.

Will it stop competition? No. Will it stop conflict? Maybe. In some areas – I would single out technology – I think the US and China are going to be increasingly in competition and there will be less sharing of intellectual property or scientific development.

That would mean other countries could benefit from both, or they may have to choose a side. This will not change because of a meeting.

But can the two leaders talk about lowering the temperature and avoiding misunderstandings that could lead to military confrontation? That might be more possible.

Turning to China’s security environment, how might Beijing’s relations with its neighbours change, given the uncertainties of Washington’s policies during the Trump administration?

My guess is that China will be assessing how solid and secure American security guarantees are in Asia. There’s some evidence that the United States might want to maintain and maybe deepen its relationship with standing allies Japan, Australia and South Korea.

We know that Trump is interested in the Korean peninsula. In his first term, he wanted to do personal diplomacy with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un. But even when South Korea is going through political change and a lot of turmoil, there’s no sense that I’ve seen that the United States is stepping back from its relationship.

I would say that if you are looking from Beijing, the conclusion to draw at the moment is that things will change much less in Asia than in Europe.

Supposing American security guarantees, naval presence and alliances were withdrawn from Asia – the first thing that would be likely to happen is that Japan and South Korea would think hard about getting their own nuclear weapons. They have the capacity, science and the technology. They could do it, but they won’t do it at the moment.

in a strange way, Beijing’s best bet for keeping the region relatively nuclear-free is to encourage the Americans to stay. And most of its neighbours would share that analysis.

They want the Chinese market, but they also want American security. They don’t want either one to disappear. I think that’s what makes the calculation different in Asia and that will affect the way that China and the US deal with other countries in the region.

What about the South China Sea?

The South China Sea is probably one of the most potentially dangerous flashpoints, along with Taiwan.

The South China Sea has more of a chance of running out of control because it’s not just between two or three entities – seven or eight are involved. The US is not so directly involved in that.

But I would say that China is missing a big soft power opportunity, which it could take up at a time of uncertainty about American security intentions, of being able to provide reassurance to regional neighbours like the Philippines.

If China is not looking to increase its maritime and territorial claims, it could create a much better basis of trust in the region. But right now there’s much more military activity from China, not just near the Philippines but also off the coast of Australia, and that’s heightening tensions in the region.

How is the importance of Taiwan to Beijing shaping the security environment?

One of the most interesting things is that after repeatedly trying to take the island, Mao Zedong basically said to then-US president Richard Nixon, when they met in Beijing in 1972, that the Taiwan problem could be left to the side for 100 years.

That’s a reminder that actually the Taiwan question has not been a constant one at the forefront of China’s relationship with the world.

Right now, there are a whole variety of reasons that China needs to think about its changing place in the world. It has an opportunity to influence the world order at a time when the United States is changing its role.

It also has significant economic problems at home, in terms of creating new forms of employment, dealing with the way technology has changed labour markets, and stimulating domestic consumption, which the party has repeatedly said is a really important domestic priority.

In that context, you could say that with all those important problems, Taiwan doesn’t appear as a major solution or issue that will help to resolve any of them.

If you look at Chinese policy priorities, it’s very clear that the single most important task for the government is the economy.

China needs the Asia-Pacific region to be economically productive to get its economy going again. That means the attention has to be on the domestic economy and how it relates to a peaceful, calm Asia that does not have any sort of confrontation.

In five to 10 years, if current trends continue, the Asia-Pacific region could be even more of a driver of the global economy than it is now. It can become the most economically dynamic region in the world, with lots of foreign direct investment and expansion.

However, for that vision of Asia to emerge, the region needs to stay peaceful and stable and absolutely avoid wars. Any regional confrontations could put that economic future in danger and that would be very bad for China and its neighbours.

Alongside the nationalism that comes with the promise of building a powerful China, there is also a revival of traditional Chinese culture in both society and the official narrative. How do you think this will shape China’s governance and foreign policy?

This is one of the most interesting and important elements of what’s going on in thought and ideology in China today.

First of all, there is a real interest in what some people call traditional thought, or pre-modern thought, which includes the Confucian tradition but also lots of other areas, such as Taoism.

The Chinese government has been sponsoring publication of China’s canon of official writings, with the parts that suit contemporary politics tending to be stressed.

For instance, Confucian thinking does have an interest in proper hierarchy and this is something that is obviously very attractive to the Communist Party, because it wants people, essentially, to be stable and ordered.

But there are other ideas – such as individual self-development or self-cultivation, which could lead more to the idea that people should have individual rights – that are less popular with the party.

China’s political culture since 1949 has been heavily shaped by the Marxism and Leninism that underpins the Chinese Communist Party.

Many of the ideas are still there and you can hear them in the language of Xi and other top leaders. Even while they are praising traditional Chinese culture and wisdom, they are also pointing out that Marxism and Leninism still have significance.

How are these two things compatible? Actually, it’s not easy.

There was a TV show broadcast in Hunan province that got a lot of criticism on Chinese social media. It was called When Marx Met Confucius and was a way of trying to talk about the difficulties in combining these ideas.

There is actually quite an interesting and difficult tension in the way that these two thought systems operate in China today, but I think that they are both very much part of the debate.

How has the Chinese intellectual landscape changed in the past 10 years? Do you share the view that it can be summarised as a rise in nationalism, Sinification of ideas and declining critical voices? What other trends are you seeing and what are their effects?

In some ways, China’s intellectual sphere has narrowed, at least in public, but in other important ways, it has expanded.

The narrowing is real, and probably the biggest obstacle that China places in its own path to developing new ideas at home and being able to exert influence abroad. It’s difficult to persuade the wider world that you’re a force for new thinking if new thinking at home is heavily restricted.

In terms of subjects, including history, most people would say that the room for publication and discussion is much more limited than it was 10, 15 or 20 years ago. Many aspects of modern history are harder to research and write about in China today than in the past.

The most productive recent time intellectually in China was the late 1990s and early 2000s, when there was the most capacity to be able to speak more freely. That time will need to come again as China comes to grips with its new role in the world. It’s not possible to have a very narrowed intellectual sphere and a very wide influence.

But there are some areas where I think things are broader, and I’m particularly thinking about social media and the way it has expanded and grown so significantly in China in the past decade.

Lots of ideas actually are discussed at a popular level, even when there’s censorship a lot of ideas still get out there – not about top-level politics as that’s too sensitive to permit – but if you think about things like concerns about economic change, people’s concerns about their own financial situation, ideas about the position of women, society, feminism, those are quite visible in Chinese social media.

That is not the same thing as two or three scholars sitting in a think tank writing some big paper, but in terms of understanding social trends and how they are shaping China today, social media has been very valuable to reflect those changes.

How has the China studies community been affected by the changes of recent years? What will the subject look like, with a growing percentage of scholars outside the country unable to conduct interviews and on-the-ground research in China?

You have put your finger on one of the most problematic issues – the number of students studying Chinese languages and doing higher-level research in the West on China is going down significantly. It was never very high, but it was going up, and now the numbers are shrinking.

One reason is the sense that doing serious research in China – particularly for social scientists but also for researchers who need to use archives and libraries – is much more difficult than it used to be.

What real China researchers need is to be able to travel and set up their own agendas, to be able to do interviews at the local level that enable them to understand how local government works, or to collect large amounts of data that enables them to see how effective or ineffective particular policies are.

This is the work of real social science, and it involves transparency and openness on data and a willingness to welcome the gathering of data, rather than assuming that it has to be banned for security reasons.

So, although more scholars are coming back to China, opening up more capacity to be able to do real research in China is the next barrier that needs to be overcome.

There are a lot of brilliant Chinese students in many countries in the West who are doing significant social science and humanities research. But their Western equivalents who study China can’t do that kind of work in China, so it becomes very unbalanced.

What about your own experience with the Asia studies and Chinese history students you taught at Oxford and now Harvard?

When it comes to postgraduate students doing PhDs, a significant number are Chinese. We do still have some Westerners, but the problem is that they have to be enthusiastic about China, willing to learn its language and culture, and then be able to find a meaningful project to research.

It’s harder now to assure students that they can find a pathway to doing really good social science research inside China, so a lot of students just leave China out. If people say China is a very difficult place to do research and South Korea is easy, maybe people just decide they want to learn Korean instead.

The sense among Western researchers that it’s hard to do serious research in China has transmitted to students finding it difficult to find a career path if they do study China. I think that’s a great shame.

item.title: [SCMP] Singapore jails and canes man for abusing boy, 6
item.description:
A man was sentenced to nine years and 10 months’ jail, and eight strokes of the cane on Friday for abusing multiple young boys who were under his care.

The man beat his youngest victim – a six-year-old boy – with a hanger more than 600 times, forced him to hold a push-up position for hours, and made him sleep in the toilet and drink his own urine.

The boy suffered severe injuries as a result, including to his ribs, lungs and kidneys, and was hospitalised for 46 days.
item.content:encoded:
A man was sentenced to nine years and 10 months’ jail, and eight strokes of the cane on Friday for abusing multiple young boys who were under his care.

The man beat his youngest victim – a six-year-old boy – with a hanger more than 600 times, forced him to hold a push-up position for hours, and made him sleep in the toilet and drink his own urine.

The boy suffered severe injuries as a result, including to his ribs, lungs and kidneys, and was hospitalised for 46 days.

The 31-year-old Singaporean man took care of young foreign students who lived in accommodation provided by the company where he worked, which his aunt owned. The man, who cannot be named to protect the identities of his victims, also abused two other boys, aged 10 and 11.

He had also pleaded guilty in July to making a false declaration related to hiring a foreign domestic worker to perform housekeeping duties for the accommodation.

District Judge John Ng said the sentence sent out the community’s collective message – that the ill treatment and abuse of young vulnerable victims cannot be tolerated and that any cruelty against them is “wholly to be condemned”.

He noted that the most serious of the man’s offences were committed against his youngest victim.

The facts “speak for themselves” on the brutality the man inflicted, said the judge, reiterating in detail what happened to the boy.

The judge noted that the man’s mitigation plea referenced the physical abuse he allegedly suffered at the hands of his alcoholic father and gangster older brother.

Judge Ng said he trusted that the man’s personal background was cited not to excuse his cruel acts on his victims, especially the six-year-old boy.

“But I have to say, on the other hand, being a young boy who had suffered at the hand of abusers, the offender should have been in a better position not to repeat such terrible treatment of vulnerable victims who had trusted him to care for them and even to protect them,” he added, as the man bowed his head in the dock.

“It was noted specifically by the psychiatrist that even if these allegations were true … it did not exculpate his physical abuse of the children under his care,” said the judge, citing a report by a doctor with the Institute of Mental Health.

When the man pleaded guilty in July, Deputy Public Prosecutors Timotheus Koh and Cheronne Lim asked for between nine years and six weeks to 10 years and eight weeks’ jail for the man, on top of six strokes of the cane.

Most of the man’s actions were captured on CCTV, and the videos “really show the extent of the depravity” of his actions and the cruelty he inflicted on his young victims, Koh said at the time, adding that the videos are very difficult to watch.

Defence lawyer Sarbrinder Singh of Sanders Law, had argued for seven years and two weeks’ prison and caning for his client instead.

In mitigation, the defence claimed that the man suffers from sleepless nights and that he was very remorseful for his actions.

The man requested to delay his sentence by one week to carry out prayers next week. The judge denied his request.

The man was responsible for managing the accommodation and teaching the primary school students mathematics and English, despite having no teaching or childcare qualifications.

In one incident, after noticing that the 10-year-old boy did not do his homework, the man demanded an explanation. Upon failing to get one, he punched and slapped the boy in the face at least five times.

He punched the boy in the face multiple times again when he could not answer one of the questions while doing his homework.

The next day, the boy’s teachers observed the bruise on his cheek and the school counsellor lodged a police report.

The man also made the two older boys hold a push-up position and hit them with a hanger multiple times.

His youngest victim – the six-year-old boy – moved into the accommodation under the man’s care in January 2023. The 31-year-old would punish the boy frequently, the court heard.

Other than forcing the boy to hold a push-up position, he also made him sleep in the toilet and fed him bread and water instead of proper meals.

In the incident that led to the 46-day hospitalisation period, the man abused the boy for about 18 hours – hitting him with a hanger at least 620 times, stomping on him at least 45 times and kicking him in the ribs at least once.

When his aunt, who was also his employer, arrived at the unit, she saw the state the boy was in and told the man to stop physically punishing the boy, but the man continued to hit and kick him.

He only stopped after his aunt carried the boy out of the toilet and away from him.

His aunt wanted to send the boy to the hospital immediately, but the man dissuaded her because he was scared and worried that he would be arrested, the court heard.

Days later, the woman called the boy’s parents. She brought him to the hospital early the next day, when the boy complained of breathing difficulties and was coughing badly.

Upon arriving at the hospital, he was immediately transferred to the resuscitation room and then the children’s intensive care unit, where he stayed for 15 days.

He suffered from lung injuries caused by blunt force and kidney failure, requiring kidney dialysis for nine days. The kidney failure also resulted in severe hypertension, or high blood pressure, the court heard.

The six-year-old boy also suffered from rhabdomyolysis – a muscle injury where muscles break down – and multiple rib fractures.

An individual who is convicted of voluntarily causing grievous hurt to a person may be punished with a jail term of up to 10 years, a fine and caning. If the victim is below 14 years old, they could face up to twice the maximum punishment.

For ill-treating a child or young person, the man could have been sentenced to up to eight years’ jail, a fine of up to S$8,000 (US$6,200), or both.

For making a false statement in a work pass application, he could have faced up to 12 months’ jail, a fine of S$15,000, or both.

This story was first published by CNA

item.title: [SCMP] Beijing calls US tariff report ‘false narrative’ as named hub Mexico plans new China curbs
item.description:
China rejected a White House report on Thursday that accused its exporters of routing goods through Mexico and other countries to avoid US tariffs, hours after word emerged that Mexico was preparing to restrict Chinese products further.

He Yadong, a spokesman for China’s Ministry of Commerce, told a regular press briefing in Beijing that the report “ignored facts and distorted reality by treating normal international trade and investment as fraud”.

He called it a “typical exercise in unilateralism and protectionism” intended to “suppress and block Chinese products”, and accused Washington of “blaming external factors for its own economic problems”.
item.content:encoded:
China rejected a White House report on Thursday that accused its exporters of routing goods through Mexico and other countries to avoid US tariffs, hours after word emerged that Mexico was preparing to restrict Chinese products further.

He Yadong, a spokesman for China’s Ministry of Commerce, told a regular press briefing in Beijing that the report “ignored facts and distorted reality by treating normal international trade and investment as fraud”.

He called it a “typical exercise in unilateralism and protectionism” intended to “suppress and block Chinese products”, and accused Washington of “blaming external factors for its own economic problems”.

“The high differentiated tariffs imposed by the United States are the real cause threatening the security of global supply chains,” He said.

The spokesman demanded an immediate end to what he called irresponsible accusations and said China would keep developing commercial cooperation with all parties on the basis of equality and mutual benefit.

The report puts the annual value of the trade anywhere between US$40 billion and US$303 billion.

Its estimates of 450,000 American jobs and up to US$150 billion in lost output are presented as model-based illustrations, although the text concedes that the shift in US import sourcing after 2018 does not prove all displaced Chinese trade was illegally diverted.

Beijing’s protest comes as the country the report names as the biggest conduit has said nothing in its own defence, while the largest foreign investors in Mexico press the government to act on the accusation rather than dispute it.

The Office of Trade and Manufacturing Policy, the White House unit run by trade adviser Peter Navarro, released the 25-page document a week ago under the title “The Great Transshipment Scam”.

It named more than 40 countries it said carried elevated risk of illegal transshipment, the practice of moving goods through an intermediate country so they enter the US under a different origin and a lower duty.

Mexico sits in the top tier of risk, alongside Canada, the European Union, India, Israel, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, a group where the report says the risk is embedded within broad and otherwise legitimate trade flows.

Chinese exporters conceal the true origin of their goods by carrying out sewing, labelling, packaging or inspection work in third countries, the document alleges, naming Mexico, Canada and several in Southeast Asia among the places used to benefit from more favourable terms with the US.

Mexico is ranked among three leading hubs worldwide, along with India and Vietnam, through which the US Commerce Department traced a combined US$67 billion in Chinese goods into the American market last year.

The publication added to friction over semiconductors, artificial intelligence and rare earths ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s planned state visit to Washington on September 24.

The trip will be the first meeting between Xi and US President Donald Trump on American soil since Trump returned to office.

Mexico under pressure to widen tariffs on Chinese goods

Meanwhile, Mexico plans to restrict selected Chinese goods and raise duties already in place, Bloomberg reported on Thursday.

Mexican officials have discussed the idea with Washington and have yet to settle on how far to go, two people familiar with the talks told the South China Morning Post, speaking on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to discuss the matter publicly.

Neither knew whether the measure would come by decree or through Congress.

Steelmakers, textile and apparel producers and heavy vehicle manufacturers have pushed for the measures, arguing that dumping is damaging domestic output and employment.

Washington has asked Mexico City to adopt tariffs mirroring those it applies to Chinese steel and aluminium under Section 232, with the aim of building a common tariff policy for North America.

The request comes as the review of the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) is under way, after Washington declined an automatic extension.

Mexico already taxes many of those goods under a package Congress approved in December.

The measure took effect on January 1 and applies duties of between 5 and 50 per cent to 1,463 products from countries without trade agreements with Mexico, among them China, India, South Korea, Indonesia, Brazil and Turkey.

Seventeen sectors are covered, including textiles, footwear, steel, aluminium, plastics, cars, auto parts and household appliances.

Economy Secretary Marcelo Ebrard said at the time that the package was designed to protect 350,000 Mexican jobs and would add about 0.2 per cent to inflation.

President Claudia Sheinbaum framed the measure as country-neutral when it was approved. The duties applied to states with which Mexico had no trade agreement and are not aimed at restricting trade between nations, she said. Ebrard said Mexico was not taxing goods because of where they were made.

A Section 232 mirror would name China in the text of the measure and set the US rate as its reference point, ending that neutrality.

Beijing responded to the December package by urging Mexico to correct what it called “erroneous practices of unilateralism and protectionism” as soon as possible, and said an investigation it opened in September 2025 into trade and investment barriers in Mexico remained under way with no conclusion announced.

American businesses operating in Mexico have urged the government to move first rather than contest the accusation.

The American Society of Mexico, a group representing US companies and citizens in the country whose honorary president is the US ambassador, said on Wednesday that Mexico should raise traceability and demonstrate with data where value is actually created.

Larry Rubin, who leads the organisation, said the main risk was not individual cases of triangulation but the absence of verification mechanisms robust enough to stop suspicion spreading to entire manufacturing sectors.

“Mexico has to reach the USMCA review with clean hands and open data,” Rubin said.

Traceability, information-sharing and origin verification mechanisms for sensitive sectors should be built with the US and Canada, the group said, without turning them into obstacles for legitimate supply chains.

It also argued that Mexican export growth could not be explained by an equivalent rise in goods arriving from China.

Mexico’s Economy Ministry and the Chinese embassy in Mexico City did not respond to requests for comment.

item.title: [SCMP] Live-streamed Philippine school shooting raises alarm over ‘memetic violence’
item.description:
A deadly school attack in the southern Philippines is drawing scrutiny as part of an apparent regional pattern of youth violence that echoes the staging, symbolism and online spectacle of mass shootings overseas.

Authorities are investigating whether the incident in Zamboanga, in which a student reportedly broadcast parts of the attack online, was influenced by exposure to digital media, while analysts said the case underscored the risk of “memetic violence” – in which past atrocities are glorified online and recast as scripts for imitation.

The attack took place on Tuesday morning at the junior high school campus of the privately run Ateneo de Zamboanga University in Zamboanga City, where police said a student brought weapons onto campus, opened fire inside a classroom and killed a fellow student. Investigators are still examining the sequence of events and the student’s motive.
item.content:encoded:
A deadly school attack in the southern Philippines is drawing scrutiny as part of an apparent regional pattern of youth violence that echoes the staging, symbolism and online spectacle of mass shootings overseas.

Authorities are investigating whether the incident in Zamboanga, in which a student reportedly broadcast parts of the attack online, was influenced by exposure to digital media, while analysts said the case underscored the risk of “memetic violence” – in which past atrocities are glorified online and recast as scripts for imitation.

The attack took place on Tuesday morning at the junior high school campus of the privately run Ateneo de Zamboanga University in Zamboanga City, where police said a student brought weapons onto campus, opened fire inside a classroom and killed a fellow student. Investigators are still examining the sequence of events and the student’s motive.

Zamboanga Mayor Khymer Adan Olaso said in a radio interview on DZBB that the student had live-streamed the attack through a body-worn camera. Olaso also said that the gunman shot at a teacher and a Grade 10 student before taking his own life.

The shooter’s father, a customs police officer, was relieved of his duties after the attack as investigators looked into reports that the firearms used belonged to him.

The attack occurred a little over a week after a 14-year-old in Thailand killed seven people in a rampage that began at home and continued at a public school on the outskirts of Bangkok.

It also came less than two months after two students opened fire at a public high school in Tacloban City in the central Philippines in June, killing at least three students and injuring 20 others.

School shootings remain rare in the Philippines, where gun ownership is regulated, although illegal firearms remain in wide circulation.

For analysts, the recent attacks are troubling less because they point to a single ideology than because they suggest a shared grammar of violence in which young perpetrators appear conscious of how their actions will be seen, shared and remembered.

These incidents shared characteristics such as “meticulous premeditation, a deliberate attention to aesthetics and presentation and a drive for notoriety through mass violence,” said Saddiq Basha, a senior analyst at the International Centre for Political Violence and Terrorism Research at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies.

The pattern had been emerging “since at least last year, probably earlier,” said Munira Mustaffa, a Kuala Lumpur-based security analyst who heads Chasseur Group and previously worked in counterterrorism roles in Malaysia’s government and military sectors.

Mustaffa said what had changed was that the last three attacks in the Philippines and Thailand were completed instead of being disrupted, “which is what has finally made it visible”.

“Authorities and observers have been slow to connect them because the modality differs each time, and that is complicated by the perpetrators’ very young age,” she added.

Beyond blaming games

The Zamboanga attack has brought renewed focus to whether children in the Philippines are being drawn into harmful online subcultures through gaming platforms or adjacent chat spaces after similar concerns were raised following the Tacloban school shooting.

Officials have been examining whether such cases bear the imprint of nihilistic violent extremism (NVE) – a loose term for online subcultures that glorify destruction, cruelty, mass violence or self-harm – but experts said the label should not be applied to the Zamboanga case without stronger evidence.

In a television interview with ANC, Olaso characterised the shooter as a “very bright student” but noted that he was a “Roblox fanatic”, referring to the popular online gaming platform that has faced scrutiny over concerns involving child safety, grooming and extremist content in connected online spaces.

Interior and Local Government Secretary Jonvic Remulla said that although authorities had yet to conduct a forensic examination on the shooter’s electronic devices, they had a “great degree of confidence” that Roblox had influenced the shooter’s actions.

“Roblox in itself is not a dangerous game. It is the chat group that is beside it, that is where the coaxing happens, where the radicalisation takes place,” he said at a briefing on Wednesday.

Authorities had previously looked into online games as a potential pathway for radicalisation during the Tacloban attack in June, while officials also examined suspicions that the Tacloban shooters were influenced by 764, a nihilistic violent extremist network accused of targeting vulnerable children online.

At a congressional hearing, Senator Risa Hontiveros also cited a photo of one Tacloban suspect wearing a KMFDM shirt – a reference associated with the 1999 Columbine High School shooting in the US – as among the signs investigators were examining.

“It is very difficult to accept that our country must face another school shooting,” Hontiveros said in a statement on Tuesday.

“For now, we cannot say whether this incident is connected to nihilistic violent extremism or other similar online communities that we have started to investigate following the Tacloban shooting,” she added.

Observers said social media could play a role in shaping such incidents but could not by itself explain why a young person would choose to attack a school.

“Social media does play a role, in the sense that it can expose individuals to the aesthetics and call-to-action of Western perpetrators of mass violence, especially amplified within the online echo-chambers of like-minded individuals,” Basha said.

“Yet, online exposure alone is insufficient to account for such acts, and we have to consider factors such as the grievances formed offline.”

The fact that the Zamboanga incident was live-streamed has drawn comparisons with earlier attacks designed to reach an online audience, such as the 2019 Christchurch mosque attack, though experts said the available evidence did not establish a direct ideological or subcultural link.

“Until we know what exactly he was exposed to online, consumed or inspired by, it is difficult to make conclusive statements,” Mustaffa said, adding that the shooter’s body camera indicated “the attack was built to be watched and the attacker intended to have an audience.”

“Aside from the premeditated act of live-streaming … there are currently no concrete indications that the perpetrator of the Zamboanga mass shooting was influenced by any specific violent online subculture, though I would not be surprised if he was,” Basha said, adding that any attempt to tie him to one at this point would be speculative.

Mustaffa said gaming platforms such as Roblox were more accurately understood as possible venues for radicalisation, not causes.

“The games aren’t what radicalising them, it’s the socialising or bonding that took place during the co-op, and there’s always a risk of grooming during those interactive sessions. The Zamboanga attack was likely animated by the attacker’s own grievance, and personal grievance is the one persistent element across the attacks in the region so far,” she said.

Basha said that while authorities might look for adult groomers influencing young perpetrators, as in the Tacloban case, they should not overlook the possibility of “peer-to-peer, horizontal grooming between youths within these online communities”.

As authorities in the Philippines, Thailand and across the region adapt to the recent cluster of attacks, Mustaffa warned against reaching for “simple explanations like blaming games, or building a narrative around the perpetrator’s bullying or personal struggles. Those things may well be part of the picture, but they don’t explain the decision to attack, and treating them as an explanation makes the next case more likely.”

“Turning schools into fortresses won’t help, and it isn’t practical … What’s needed is a networked effort across parents, schools, law enforcement, and platforms, and the first task is working out what that looks like in practice,” she said.

item.title: [SCMP] Malaysia fears military ‘miscalculation’ near Sabah amid US-China rivalry
item.description:
Malaysia faces a growing risk of miscalculation near its state of Sabah as US-China rivalry drives more military activities into the waters around Borneo, its defence minister has warned, bolstering the government’s push for higher spending on its armed forces.

The concern is particularly acute for Malaysia, a South China Sea claimant that has long sought to keep close economic ties with China while avoiding alignment with either Beijing or Washington and is feeling further unease over the expanding US-Philippine military presence just north of Sabah.

Malaysian Defence Minister Mohamed Khaled Nordin told This Week in Asia that Putrajaya did not regard the Philippines, the United States, China or any other country as a specific threat, but said the increase in military activities across the region had created a more complex and potentially combustible security environment.
item.content:encoded:
Malaysia faces a growing risk of miscalculation near its state of Sabah as US-China rivalry drives more military activities into the waters around Borneo, its defence minister has warned, bolstering the government’s push for higher spending on its armed forces.

The concern is particularly acute for Malaysia, a South China Sea claimant that has long sought to keep close economic ties with China while avoiding alignment with either Beijing or Washington and is feeling further unease over the expanding US-Philippine military presence just north of Sabah.

Malaysian Defence Minister Mohamed Khaled Nordin told This Week in Asia that Putrajaya did not regard the Philippines, the United States, China or any other country as a specific threat, but said the increase in military activities across the region had created a more complex and potentially combustible security environment.

“When you have more military assets operating within a relatively confined geographical space, the possibility of miscalculation, misunderstanding or even a small incident escalating into something more serious naturally increases,” he said.

“Geographic proximity is therefore an important consideration for us,” Khaled added. “Even if an incident does not directly involve Malaysia, any escalation in areas close to us could have wider implications for our security and for stability in the South China Sea.”

His remarks provide the clearest explanation yet from Malaysia’s defence establishment of the thinking behind Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s push for higher military spending, after Anwar publicly singled out the expanding US-Philippine military presence on Balabac Island, just north of Sabah.

Anwar said on Tuesday during an engagement session at the Finance Ministry for the 2027 budget that Malaysia might need to spend “hundreds of millions, or even a billion ringgit” to strengthen Sabah’s defences, arguing that the country needed adequate capabilities as the strategic environment around the state changed.

“This is no longer an ordinary region. It is increasingly becoming a focal point of tensions between two major powers, the United States and China,” state news agency Bernama quoted him as saying.

Balabac, at the southern tip of the Philippine province of Palawan, lies 50km (31 miles) from the Malaysian islands of Banggi and Balambangan. The latter hosts a maritime radar installation covering much of northern Sabah.

Crowded waters

In 2023, Balabac was one of four Philippine military sites added to the Enhanced Defence Cooperation Agreement (EDCA) between Manila and Washington, bringing the total to nine.

The US Defence Department said in April that year the expanded network would strengthen interoperability between the two allies and allow them to respond more readily to shared challenges across the Indo-Pacific, including humanitarian disasters.

Balabac sits between the South China Sea and the Sulu Sea, close to Malaysian territory, where US forces have shown their prowess with their military hardware in recent months.

During the annual Balikatan exercises in May involving troops from the Philippines, the US and other countries, US soldiers fired a rocket from an M142 High Mobility Artillery Rocket System (HIMARS) on the island. The US Army said HIMARS deployed there could be used to protect shipping entering the Sulu and Celebes seas.

Although Anwar stressed that relations with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr’s government were “very good”, he said Malaysia was “naturally somewhat concerned”, citing both Balabac’s proximity and Manila’s long-standing territorial claim over Sabah, according to the Bernama report.

The Philippines reaffirmed its sovereignty claim over Sabah in February, saying existing legislation continued to preserve Manila’s claim to parts of North Borneo.

Georgi Engelbrecht, senior analyst for the Philippines at the International Crisis Group, said Balabac was becoming an increasingly important part of Manila’s defence planning because of the Balabac Strait, a critical passage between the Sulu Sea and South China Sea.

But he said Malaysia had little reason to regard the Philippine infrastructure itself on the island as a direct threat.

“It is the cooperation with the US [and the Philippines] that makes Malaysia reflect,” Engelbrecht told This Week in Asia.

“For now, both forces are conducting exercises and strengthening alliances. But it is not impossible [that] US forces near Malaysia make some politicians and thought leaders in Kuala Lumpur uncomfortable.”

He said the unease stemmed partly from the proximity of US forces and fears of conflict, particularly as Chinese vessels, including People’s Liberation Army ships, also operated around Palawan.

The Sabah dispute itself was unlikely to disappear, Engelbrecht said, noting that Philippine politicians periodically revived the issue and that it remained embedded in domestic politics.

“The concern is no longer the legacy of Lahad Datu, but how this dormant dispute might be resurfacing amid growing great power competition,” he said.

In 2013, followers of the self-proclaimed Sultanate of Sulu landed in the coastal town of Lahad Datu in eastern Sabah to press their territorial claim, triggering weeks of fighting that killed over 50 militants and 10 Malaysian security personnel.

Florence Principe Gamboa, a Philippine-based analyst and fellow at research firm Verve Research, said Balabac had been part of Philippine defence modernisation even before it was designated an EDCA site.

Its location close to the West Philippine Sea, Manila’s term for parts of the South China Sea within its maritime jurisdiction, and the Philippine-held Kalayaan Island Group had long made it strategically important, she said.

US support was increasingly vital to Manila’s maritime security, Gamboa said, while also providing “a counterweight to maritime coercion” for other regional states confronted by China’s growing assertiveness.

“It also complicates navigating great power competition, especially for states like Malaysia that prioritise non-alignment and neutrality, given their strong economic ties with China,” she said.

Bigger arsenal

Malaysia was already planning to increase defence spending before the latest concern over Balabac.

Khaled said the country intended gradually to raise defence expenditure towards 1.5 per cent of gross domestic product by 2030, describing the increase as part of its long-term defence modernisation plans. In comparison, Malaysia allocated about one per cent of its GDP on defence spending in 2025.

Malaysia allocated 21.74 billion ringgit (US$5.4 billion) to the Defence Ministry under its 2026 budget, including 6 billion ringgit for the acquisition of strategic assets.

Khaled cautioned, however, against interpreting the planned increase purely as a response to the US-Philippine build-up.

Cyber and electromagnetic threats, along with mass misinformation campaigns, had also transformed Malaysia’s security requirements, demanding investment in capabilities beyond conventional weapons platforms, he said.

When asked about the higher defence spending, Malaysia-based defence analyst Zaki Salleh argued that Sabah urgently needed stronger maritime surveillance, including radar, drones and patrol aircraft, as well as better air defences and rapid-response capabilities.

He said Malaysia should acquire another three Anka-S medium-altitude long-endurance drones, continue procuring its next batch of littoral mission ships and establish an army aviation helicopter squadron in Sabah.

Military bases, maintenance facilities and resilient communications infrastructure in the state also required improvement, Zaki said.

Ian Storey, a principal fellow at Singapore’s ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute, said Malaysia faced three pressures: intensifying great-power rivalry, recurring South China Sea tensions and Malaysia falling behind some of its neighbours in military capabilities.

He said Kuala Lumpur should invest in longer-range, longer-endurance surveillance drones and eventually heavier fighter aircraft, while noting that Malaysia’s traditional reluctance to confront China meant its surveillance drones would probably remain unarmed.

We do not want developments in the region to be framed as Malaysia choosing one side against another

Mohamed Khaled Nordin, Malaysian defence minister

China asserts sweeping sovereignty across much of the South China Sea, overlapping with the maritime claims of the Philippines, Malaysia, Vietnam and Brunei.

Malaysia has generally adopted a less confrontational posture towards China than the Philippines over territorial disputes, even while rejecting Chinese claims that overlap its exclusive economic zone and continuing oil and gas operations in disputed waters, according to analysts.

Khaled said Malaysia’s move towards enhancing its defence would not change that approach.

“We do not want developments in the region to be framed as Malaysia choosing one side against another,” he said. “Our concern is about maintaining regional stability and ensuring that strategic competition between major powers does not create unintended consequences for Asean countries.”

item.title: [SCMP] Why China will need a ‘more persuasive security offer’ to win over middle powers
item.description:
Just weeks before Chinese leader Xi Jinping is due to visit the White House, tensions have flared between Washington and its allies after one of the administration’s sharpest rebukes yet.

Speaking in Manila on August 10, Elbridge Colby, undersecretary of defence for policy, pressed regional partners to increase defence spending and align more closely with American priorities.

He said Washington sought “partners, not protectorates” and cautioned against “the delusion of fashionable but superficial ideas like middle-power alliances designed to exclude America”.
item.content:encoded:
Just weeks before Chinese leader Xi Jinping is due to visit the White House, tensions have flared between Washington and its allies after one of the administration’s sharpest rebukes yet.

Speaking in Manila on August 10, Elbridge Colby, undersecretary of defence for policy, pressed regional partners to increase defence spending and align more closely with American priorities.

He said Washington sought “partners, not protectorates” and cautioned against “the delusion of fashionable but superficial ideas like middle-power alliances designed to exclude America”.

The remarks reinforced the message Colby laid out in mid-July that there was “a great deal of hubbub about a collective ‘middle powers’ strategy these days”.

On social media and in a subsequent New York Times interview, he said the strategy was based on a “faulty understanding” of international relations and that allies risked “wasting valuable time, money and political capital on a distraction”. He said access to the US defence industrial base was “a privilege, not a right”.

The remarks have intensified a debate among US allies over how to reduce dependence on Washington in the transactional Donald Trump era without drifting into Beijing’s orbit.

Shi Yinhong, a professor of international affairs at Renmin University of China, said it reflected Trump’s “flexible realist” strategy and efforts to get more from partners while discouraging coordination that did not involve Washington.

“It is easy to see Colby’s position as both doctrine and negotiating tactic, though in practice neither is simple,” he said.

“The Trump administration has for months criticised nearly all of its advanced allies, often using this as a form of extortion, yet none have significantly or lastingly improved relations with Beijing. This has been both revealing and instructive.”

Analysts also said Colby’s remarks gave Beijing an opportunity to promote its vision of a multipolar world not dominated by Washington, presenting itself as a more respectful and steadier alternative in unstable and uncertain times.

Jagannath Panda, head of the Stockholm Centre for South Asian and Indo-Pacific Affairs at the Institute for Security and Development Policy in Sweden, said Colby was signalling that Washington now saw defence cooperation as being conditional on political conformity.

“His dismissal of middle-power coordination further implies that Washington prefers capable partners individually dependent on the United States rather than collectively autonomous,” he said.

Such pressure might see short-term compliance but it could push US allies to hedge and diversify, according to analysts.

“Over time, coercive dependence generates incentives to diversify procurement, establish minilateral defence arrangements and reopen economic channels with Beijing,” Panda said.

Over the past year, the term “middle powers” has gained new currency as governments try to find room to manoeuvre between Washington and Beijing, at a time when the US and China have become more transactional and assertive.

At the June Group of Seven summit in France, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney urged middle powers to form flexible, issue‑based coalitions to preserve sovereignty and resilience in a harsher world order.

In another move by middle powers to deepen coordination and move beyond the US security umbrella, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement on August 7, declaring that an armed attack on one would be treated as an attack on all three.

Against that backdrop, Beijing has been pushing for alternatives to an increasingly unpredictable Washington. But experts said most middle powers were sceptical about China being a substitute on security matters, even as they grew wary of US volatility.

At the heart of the dilemma is how countries caught in the US-China rivalry can balance three competing goals: preserving the American security umbrella; preventing overexposure to Beijing; and building enough domestic and minilateral capacity to avoid being trapped by either superpower.

“China offers markets, infrastructure and diplomatic attention, but its partnerships are selective, transactional and rarely supported by dependable security guarantees,” Panda said.

“Beijing’s limited willingness to assume responsibility during major international crises also weakens its claim to be a comprehensive alternative.”

Ahead of another highly anticipated Xi-Trump summit, Panda said Beijing would likely use targeted incentives to show that strategic flexibility produces benefits.

“But its objective is not an autonomous third pole. Beijing prefers middle powers sufficiently independent of Washington to weaken American primacy, yet insufficiently united to constrain China collectively,” he said.

The differing calculations are already visible across Asia and beyond.

Japan has expanded cooperation with like-minded states while keeping the US-Japan alliance as the foundation of its security policy, especially given its deteriorating ties with Beijing.

South Korea remains one of the few US allies that has sought closer ties with Beijing, reflecting its deep economic dependence on China, even as it remains anchored to Washington.

Australia has moved to harden its defences and supply chains and deepen military cooperation with the US, while India has advanced its doctrine of “multi‑alignment” – seeking to preserve strategic autonomy through selective engagement with Washington, Beijing, Moscow and others simultaneously.

Shi said China’s own foreign-policy focus remained fixed on the US, and middle powers were still more likely to deepen alignment with Washington while hedging harder with Beijing.

“In essence, they remain US allies, and China is the major rival of both Washington and nearly all of them, geopolitically, militarily and across numerous trade fields,” he said.

The broader problem is structural: the US may be unwilling or unable to underwrite every alliance burden, but middle powers cannot replace that role either, according to Chong Ja Ian, an associate professor of political science at the National University of Singapore and a non-resident scholar at Carnegie China.

He said that by hedging their bets, countries might create distrust on both sides.

“A middle or smaller power trying to hedge may find that it creates suspicion and abandonment by both major powers or, worse, punishment from both,” he said.

Rana Mitter, professor and S.T. Lee Chair in US-Asia relations at the Harvard Kennedy School, said it was unlikely that most powers would seek to hedge with Beijing.

“Beijing has little tradition of providing security and has relatively limited experience of working with partner governments on these issues, though there are exceptions such as Pakistan,” he said.

Mitter argued that for those less certain about US commitments, China’s pitch could have appeal – but not enough substance where it mattered most.

“Regardless of American language around security, very few middle powers are likely to seek out China as a security alternative, as most of the issues that concern them are not ones where China is likely to provide significant additional capacity,” he said. “Beijing will need a more persuasive security offer than simply not being the US.”

There have been growing concerns among middle powers about China’s assertiveness, according to Takashi Hosoda, an assistant professor at the University of West Bohemia in the Czech Republic, who called it a form of “great-power exceptionalism”.

Beijing has drawn backlash in recent years over its close ties with Russia, growing diplomatic assertiveness, attempts to challenge the US-led post-war order, and selective invocation of the United Nations and international norms.

Meantime, Hosoda said Washington would inevitably recognise that effective cooperation with middle powers remained indispensable in areas like industrial policy, defence and economic security.

He likened the US-led alliance network to the companions in Journey to the West, a 16th‑century Chinese classic that tells the story of a monk and his unruly disciples travelling to India in search of sacred scriptures.

“Throughout their journey, they frequently quarrel over direction, priorities and individual responsibilities. Yet whenever confronted by a common adversary, they reunite and continue towards their shared destination,” he said.

Sourabh Gupta, a senior policy specialist with the Institute for China-America Studies, said Colby was articulating a coherent “flexible realist” strategy.

“It is a somewhat narrower, unenlightened and self-interested one, but it is not a mere negotiating tactic,” he said. “The United States is in relative decline, which in the national security arena means it is unable and perhaps unwilling to fully underwrite all its alliance burdens.

“The middle powers – individually or collectively – are unable to make up for this slack.”

Gupta said the practical result was that many allies would continue to align more closely with Washington while also building domestic capabilities in case US support weakened.

“Because of the great asymmetry between what the US and what its allies and partners in the Indo-Pacific bring to the table, the latter can build out their capabilities collaboratively with Washington today and yet repurpose these platforms and capabilities to comport with a more strategically autonomist policy outlook tomorrow,” he said.

Still, Gupta said Colby’s rhetoric could further undermine Washington’s credibility, even as it underscored US military and industrial strength.

“That Washington is calling upon allies and partners to furnish what it used to furnish by itself suggests in the first place that it is incapable of doing so today – a sign of its relative decline. Colby’s rhetoric betrays weakness and decline, not strength and command.”

He said middle-power activism was an “unambiguous plus” for Beijing.

“The dilution or softening of bloc-like formations has always been a cardinal priority of Chinese post-Cold War international relations,” Gupta said. “The more distributed the global power structure, the more amenable it is to Chinese diplomatic management.”

item.title: [SCMP] Will Putin’s Kuril Islands visit push Japan closer to Ukraine?
item.description:
Japan is weighing how far to push back after Russian President Vladimir Putin visited a disputed island last week, as analysts debate whether tougher measures would have much impact on Moscow.

Some observers urged Japan to recall its ambassador, impose additional sanctions and deepen cooperation with Ukraine to show it would not be “bullied”, while others said Tokyo had little economic leverage left given already weak bilateral ties and its reliance on Russian natural gas.

Putin made his first-ever visit to one of four disputed islands, collectively called the Northern Territories by Japan and the Southern Kurils by Russia, last Thursday.
item.content:encoded:
Japan is weighing how far to push back after Russian President Vladimir Putin visited a disputed island last week, as analysts debate whether tougher measures would have much impact on Moscow.

Some observers urged Japan to recall its ambassador, impose additional sanctions and deepen cooperation with Ukraine to show it would not be “bullied”, while others said Tokyo had little economic leverage left given already weak bilateral ties and its reliance on Russian natural gas.

Putin made his first-ever visit to one of four disputed islands, collectively called the Northern Territories by Japan and the Southern Kurils by Russia, last Thursday.

Japanese media reported that senior foreign ministry officials discussed possible responses on Friday, including tougher sanctions and the temporary recall of Japan’s ambassador.

On Tuesday, Japan’s envoy to Moscow Akira Muto was summoned to the Russian foreign ministry after Tokyo protested against Putin’s visit.

During the meeting, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin warned that his country reserved the “right to take appropriate countermeasures” against Japan, given Tokyo’s continued policy of sanctioning Moscow and its support for Kyiv, according to the Russian foreign ministry.

The Japanese embassy in Moscow said Muto “appropriately explained” Tokyo’s stance in the 20-minute session with Galuzin.

Putin travelled to Iturup Island – known as Etorofu in Japan – where he visited a fish-processing plant and met local residents.

Japan claims the Soviet Union illegally seized the islands – Etorofu, Kunashiri, Shikotan and the Habomai islet group – soon after Japan’s surrender at the end of the second world war in 1945. Russia maintains that the action was legitimate, however.

Describing Putin’s visit as “grave” and “absolutely unacceptable”, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi warned last Thursday that the visit would harden anti-Russian sentiment in Japan and make restoring relations more difficult in the medium to long term.

That same day, her Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi summoned Russian ambassador Nikolay Nozdrev to lodge a formal protest, making it clear that Tokyo considers the island an inherent part of Japanese territory both historically and under international law.

On Tuesday, the Russian ministry said in a statement that Galuzin had “conveyed a strong protest” to Muto over Takaichi’s and Motegi’s “anti-Russia” remarks.

Adding that the Southern Kurils were “transferred to our country following World War II”, the statement said that “any attempts by the Japanese side to directly or indirectly call this obvious reality into question are categorically unacceptable and illegitimate”.

Closer to Kyiv?

In addition to recalling its ambassador to Russia and imposing additional sanctions, Japan could respond by deepening cooperation with Ukraine, said James Brown, a professor of international relations specialising in Russian affairs at Temple University’s Tokyo campus.

Takaichi has yet to have a face-to-face meeting with President Volodymyr Zelensky, even though both leaders attended the Group of Seven summit in France in June.

“A face-to-face meeting, especially if it entailed a visit to Kyiv by Takaichi, would send a strong message that Japan will not be bullied by Russia into changing its foreign policy,” Brown said, adding that Putin’s visit came as Japan had been exploring tentative re-engagement with Russia.

This included sending a delegation from the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry to Moscow in May, and restarting foreign ministry-backed student visits in July.

“This tentative re-engagement, which was always controversial, is now likely to be curtailed,” Brown added.

A face-to-face meeting [with Ukraine’s president] … would send a strong message that Japan will not be bullied by Russia

James Brown, international-relations professor

Michito Tsuruoka, a professor of policy management at Keio University, said Tokyo’s priority should be showing Russia that it could not pressure Japan into changing its policies.

“Strengthening support to Ukraine would be a possible response, though whether the prime minister is interested in this remains unclear,” he said.

There does not appear to be a consensus within the Japanese government on how to handle relations with Russia, according to Tsuruoka.

“Different actors have different views on what Russia is and they see different aspects of [the country] and their meaning to Japan,” he added.

While the economy ministry saw Japan’s northern neighbour as an important energy source – more so given recent developments in the Strait of Hormuz – Tsuruoka said the defence ministry was increasingly concerned about deepening Russia-China and Russia-North Korea ties and the Russian military’s increasing activities near Japan.

“A new consensus needs to be built,” Tsuruoka said.

The Strait of Hormuz has been all but closed since the United States and Israel launched their war against Iran in late February. Before the conflict, Japan was importing over 90 per cent of its crude oil, and a portion of its liquefied natural gas (LNG), through the strait.

Last month, Japan’s defence ministry said that a Russian military IL-20 reconnaissance aircraft had intruded into its territorial airspace over disputed islands, with Russia conducting large-scale live-fire naval drills involving 60 warships and 13,000 troops nearby less than two weeks later.

‘No economic leverage’

Artyom Lukin, a professor at the Far Eastern Federal University in Vladivostok, questioned Japan’s ability to impose any significant economic penalties on Moscow over Putin’s visit.

“Russia-Japan economic ties have already been reduced to a bare minimum because of the Ukraine conflict,” he said, noting that bilateral trade was now largely limited to Russia supplying LNG and seafood while importing Japanese vehicles.

“Japan cannot halt LNG imports from Russia’s Sakhalin Island because it is difficult to find viable alternatives, especially amid the continuing crisis in the Middle East,” Lukin said.

There were also no alternatives to some Russian seafood delicacies, he added, saying: “For the Japanese, seafood specialities are far more important than Ukraine and the Kuril Islands combined.”

Should Japan ban car exports to Russia, Russians was likely to respond by buying from China and South Korea instead, according to Lukin.

“In a nutshell, Japan has no economic leverage over Russia,” he said, adding that Tokyo’s main response would be “rhetorical”.

Japan’s bilateral trade with Russia hit roughly US$8 billion last year, dwarfed by its trade with China at about US$300 billion. Over the same period, Japan’s Russian LNG supplies ticked up 2 per cent from 2024 levels to about 5.8 million tonnes, making up about 9 per cent of Japan’s total annual LNG imports.

By comparison, Japan imports roughly 11 per cent of its LNG from the Middle East, according to Reuters.

While Japan could “theoretically” step up military activities near Russia, Lukin said Tokyo was unlikely to do so as it needed those resources to deal with the challenge posed by China.

In its latest Defence White Paper issued earlier this month, Tokyo repeated and reinforced its stance that China’s rapid and opaque military expansion was its “greatest strategic challenge”.

Takaichi took advantage of Putin’s trip to score an easy win “with her hardcore nationalistic audience”, according to Lukin, who said Moscow had always maintained that its sovereignty over Iturup and Kunashir – the larger of the disputed islands – was non-negotiable.

“Russia was only ready to negotiate the two smaller islands, Shikotan and Habomai,” he said. “Takaichi is not naive. I guess she fully realises that Russia is never going to return Iturup to Japan.”

Bilateral relations were already in the doldrums but could worsen, Brown said, citing Japanese concerns over Russia’s possible provision of military technology to North Korea in exchange for Pyongyang’s assistance in the Ukraine war.

“If Russia [strengthens] this support by meaningfully enhancing the North’s ballistic missile and nuclear capabilities, it would lead to even greater tensions between Tokyo and Moscow,” Brown said.

Analysts say Tokyo is concerned that Russian technology transfers will accelerate North Korea’s nuclear, ballistic missile and hypersonic weapons programmes, threatening the regional security balance.

item.title: [SCMP] China becomes first nation to recover orbital launch rockets with 2 distinct paths
item.description:
In a global first, leading Chinese commercial rocket company LandSpace has recovered a stainless-steel booster after an orbital launch, marking a major step in the country’s efforts to develop lower-cost, reusable rockets.

Previous reusable boosters deployed in such launches have been made from aluminium alloys, which can be more expensive to develop due to higher design and raw material costs.

China is also the first country to succeed in orbital launch recovery down distinct technological pathways, pulling off a dual-track strategy that even the United States – which pioneered reusable rocket technology – has yet to execute.
item.content:encoded:
In a global first, leading Chinese commercial rocket company LandSpace has recovered a stainless-steel booster after an orbital launch, marking a major step in the country’s efforts to develop lower-cost, reusable rockets.

Previous reusable boosters deployed in such launches have been made from aluminium alloys, which can be more expensive to develop due to higher design and raw material costs.

China is also the first country to succeed in orbital launch recovery down distinct technological pathways, pulling off a dual-track strategy that even the United States – which pioneered reusable rocket technology – has yet to execute.

The Zhuque-3 is China’s first commercial rocket to both reach orbit and have its first stage recovered.

LandSpace also became the fourth entity – after US companies SpaceX and Blue Origin, and state-owned China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation (CASC) – to achieve controlled recovery of a reusable vehicle from an orbital launch.

Like SpaceX’s Falcon 9 and Blue Origin’s New Glenn, the Zhuque-3 uses landing legs to recover its rockets.

But last month, China was the first to recover a booster on an orbital launch with a different technique, after the first stage of CASC’s Long March 10B was recovered using a unique sea-based net capture system.

SpaceX’s Super Heavy booster, which is also made of stainless steel, is awaiting US Federal Aviation Administration approval for its first recovery flight to send the Starship into orbit.

The Super Heavy will also attempt a non-leg-based orbital recovery, using mechanical “chopstick” arms mounted on a tower to catch the booster.

Wednesday’s milestone is just the start of China’s reusable rocket recovery efforts, while the US already has hundreds of successful booster recoveries and reuses under its belt.

The 66-metre (217-foot) Zhuque-3 rocket, powered by liquid methane and oxygen, lifted off from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Centre in the Gobi Desert at 7.35am on Wednesday, according to state news agency Xinhua.

The rocket delivered a Honghu-3 internet satellite into its designated orbit, while its first stage returned to Earth and touched down vertically at a recovery site in Minqin county, Gansu province, about 390km (242 miles) southeast of the launch pad.

“This mission marks China’s first successful recovery of a first-stage reusable launch vehicle using landing legs, and also China’s first successful land-based recovery of a first-stage orbital-deployed launch vehicle,” LandSpace said.

“LandSpace will continue to advance the iteration and engineering verification of reusable technology, helping my country further improve its low-cost, high-frequency and highly reliable space transport capabilities,” the company added in a social media post.

Dong Kai, the rocket’s deputy chief designer, told the LatePost news outlet on Wednesday that LandSpace aimed to reuse the recovered rockets as soon as possible, adding that he hoped to launch the Zhuque-3 10 times a year.

Wednesday’s launch was LandSpace’s second attempt to put the Zhuque-3 into orbit and recover its first stage.

During the rocket’s maiden flight in December, the second stage reached orbit but the first stage erupted in a dramatic fireball during its final powered descent towards the landing pad.

After that mission, Zhuque-3 project chief Dai Zheng told state broadcaster CCTV that the recovery had failed because the first stage’s engine had not reignited when it was about 3km above the ground as required.

LandSpace said on Wednesday that, following the first attempt, the rocket was optimised for reusable flight by reducing the number of landing ignition engines, improving the on-board autonomous safety control system, and enhancing thermal protection for re-entry.

Now, the Zhuque-3 is China’s second orbital rocket to demonstrate first-stage recovery. The first was the state-developed Long March-10B, whose first stage was captured by a huge net on an offshore platform after launching from Hainan province in July.

The two rockets have broadly similar payload capacities and are in about the same class as SpaceX’s workhorse, Falcon 9. In expendable configuration, the Long March-10B and Zhuque-3 can carry about 22 and 21 tonnes to low Earth orbit, respectively. With their first stages recovered, the figures fall to about 16 and 18 tonnes.

Unlike the stainless steel design of the Zhuque-3, the Falcon 9 is made using an aluminium-lithium alloy. Dong said that the welding process for stainless steel was easier than for aluminium alloy, adding that the material was also cheap and had good heat resistance.

Recovering the two rockets could prove crucial to the construction of China’s broadband internet megaconstellations. Like SpaceX’s Starlink, Chinese projects such as Guowang and Qianfan envisage eventually placing more than 10,000 satellites in orbit to provide global broadband coverage, creating both a potential global market and infrastructure of strategic military importance.

So far, Starlink has deployed more than 10,000 operational satellites and attracted over 12 million customers worldwide. Its extensive use by Ukrainian forces for battlefield communications has shown the military value of such a network.

By comparison, Beijing’s Guowang constellation and the Shanghai-backed Qianfan network have each deployed only around 200 satellites. Their expansion has been constrained partly by China’s lack of a reusable workhorse comparable to the Falcon 9.

Wednesday’s feat suggests China could translate its engineering talent and manufacturing abilities into cheaper, faster launches, positioning it to compete with the US as both nations accelerate the roll-out of internet satellites.

While US space agency Nasa has left reusable rocket development to commercial partners like SpaceX, China is playing on both fronts, with its state-run space programme building reusable boosters alongside the commercial sector.

The China National Space Administration said on Wednesday that it helped coordinate the Zhuque-3 launch team, adding that it would continue to support the country’s reusable rocket technology.

The next test for China’s reusable rockets will be whether the recovered boosters can be refurbished and flown again, which is necessary to reduce launch costs and support more frequent launches.

LandSpace said the recovery of the Zhuque-3 laid a foundation for subsequent maintenance and reuse flights, and would help China improve launch capabilities to support commercial missions and the deployment of satellite constellations.

item.title: [SCMP] Foreign capital is dipping its toes into China’s property sector. Is a rebound in store?
item.description:
From shopping malls to warehousing and logistics companies, a wave of deals by foreign funds in China is injecting liquidity into a property sector scarred by years of struggle.

Several Wanda Plazas – the sprawling mixed-use developments that were once the flagship assets of tycoon Wang Jianlin’s Dalian Wanda Group – received fresh capital injections from global asset manager PAG in June and July.

The cash-strapped developer has been forced to offload properties to repay debt. Such deals, alongside a pickup in property transactions in mainland China’s top cities this year, have drawn growing market attention.
item.content:encoded:
From shopping malls to warehousing and logistics companies, a wave of deals by foreign funds in China is injecting liquidity into a property sector scarred by years of struggle.
