Several Wanda Plazas – the sprawling mixed-use developments that were once the flagship assets of tycoon Wang Jianlin’s Dalian Wanda Group – received fresh capital injections from global asset manager PAG in June and July.

The cash-strapped developer has been forced to offload properties to repay debt. Such deals, alongside a pickup in property transactions in mainland China’s top cities this year, have drawn growing market attention.

Five years after the Evergrande crisis triggered a prolonged slump in the property market, renewed activity by international investors – often thought of as “smart money” – has raised hopes over whether the sector has passed an inflection point.

“For global funds with a strategic allocation to China, the current market opens up opportunities to acquire high-quality assets at significantly more attractive pricing than in recent years,” said James Macdonald, head of research for China at property consultancy Savills.

“Investors are not necessarily calling the bottom. Rather, many believe valuations have adjusted sufficiently to offer a more favourable risk-adjusted return profile.”

The ‘bottom fishers’

Foreign commercial property investment in China peaked between 2018 and 2021.

In addition to foreign developers that benefited from the country’s decades-long residential property boom, global asset managers – including US private equity groups Blackstone and KKR, Singapore’s property group CapitaLand, and US real estate investment manager AEW – poured money into commercial property.

Sustained participation from foreign capital … has injected much-needed liquidity into the market … helping accelerate the bottom-finding process and supporting stabilisation and recovery

Yan Yuejin, E‑house China Research and Development Institute

This included grade A office buildings, urban renewal projects and long-term rental flats in first- and second-tier cities. These investors remained active even during the worst of the Evergrande crisis.

New York-headquartered Blackstone, co-founded by US billionaire Stephen Schwarzman, made headlines in June 2021 with its HK$23.66 billion (US$3 billion) offer for Hong Kong-listed Soho China, the largest office developer in Beijing and Shanghai. The deal collapsed three months later after parties failed to surmount regulatory hurdles.

In 2024, four Hong Kong-registered units under Blackstone spent 279 million yuan (US$41.3 million) to buy out the remaining 20 per cent stake in four mainland China-based warehousing and logistics companies, consolidating full ownership. The portfolio remains with Blackstone.

When meeting Vice-Premier He Lifeng in Beijing in March 2025, Schwarzman said Blackstone had full confidence in China’s economy and was willing to expand its investments in the country.

In its purchases over the summer, PAG acquired three Wanda Plaza properties: one in Shanghai; another in Quanzhou, southeastern China’s Fujian province; and another in Zhanjiang, Guangdong province. The deal, which expanded its footprint in the mainland’s commercial property sector, was closed by the PAG-led Suzhou Anyi Equity Investment Fund.

Unlike last year’s landmark transaction – in which 48 Wanda Plaza assets were sold to a consortium made up of PAG, Sunshine Insurance Group, JD.com and Tencent Holdings – the latest agreement stemmed from independent negotiations between PAG entities and Wanda Group.

Correction creates opportunity

China remains the world’s second-largest economy and one of the largest institutional real estate markets. Despite weaker household holdings, property – along with stocks, gold and other alternative investments – continues to be a key asset class for institutional investors.

National industrial and logistics transactions reached 58.5 billion yuan in the 12 months to March 15, up 19.3 per cent year on year, according to Savills.

Domestic buyer activity remained broadly stable, while foreign investment rose noticeably, with more capital deployed by overseas fund managers in the sector, the consultancy said.

“Established regional and community shopping centres with a strong mix of retail, food and beverage, and leisure tenants have generally proven more resilient, supported by stable consumer demand and uses that are less easily replicated online,” Savills’ Macdonald said.

“Combined with an experienced operating platform, this provides scope to enhance asset performance through active asset management while benefiting from long-term income generation.”

Yan Yuejin, vice-president of Shanghai‑based property consultancy E‑house China Research and Development Institute, said global capital had helped steady market expectations, particularly after years of adjustment drove a roughly 30 per cent correction in valuations across the country’s commercial property market.

“They are bullish on core cities with deep housing price corrections and robust consumer markets, with relevant policy support expected to gain further traction,” Yan said.

PAG, he added, was not just buying the assets but overseeing operations and value‑add improvements, laying the groundwork for future exit options, including through real estate investment trusts.

Asset price corrections have unlocked opportunities attracting interest from global long-term investors, who nonetheless remain selective.

“Sustained participation from foreign capital, especially inflows from opportunistic funds, has injected much-needed liquidity into the market and brought professional asset revitalisation expertise, helping accelerate the bottom-finding process and supporting stabilisation and recovery,” Yan said.

Domestic players step in

Chinese companies are also revitalising distressed assets. One Sunac Opus, a top luxury residential project near Beijing’s central business district, was scheduled to be delivered by the end of this year, China Citic Financial Asset Management said on July 30.

The state-owned asset management company (AMC) helped to complete the debt restructuring of Hong Kong-listed Sunac, founded by property magnate Sun Hongbin and once among China’s largest private developers.

A major project in downtown Beijing, the development faced numerous challenges, including construction delays and sluggish sales.

Through a full-cycle solution by the AMC – including debt acquisition, restructuring, closed-end fund management and supervision of project operations – the project’s legacy risks have been resolved, allowing the development to resume regular operations.

Hints at housing recovery

While global investors are showing interest in China’s commercial property assets, the residential housing market remains in a separate phase of the adjustment cycle, largely driven by domestic policy support and supply-demand rebalancing.

Foreign investments reflected confidence in the long-term fundamentals of specific assets rather than a broad-based recovery across China’s real estate market, Savills’ Macdonald said.

Over recent months, local governments have continued to roll out optimised home-purchase policies and inventory-destocking measures, supporting gradual stabilisation in the property market.

New home prices in China’s four first-tier cities – Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou and Shenzhen – rose by an average of 0.1 per cent in June, extending a four-month rebound and signalling a gradual recovery in sentiment, according to the National Bureau of Statistics.

Beijing’s local housing authorities jointly announced on August 7 that for households without the capital’s hukou – China’s residency registration system – the mandatory social security or personal income tax payment requirement for buying commercial housing inside the city’s Fifth Ring Road was lowered from two years to one year.

Beijing recorded 93,583 online-signed transactions for second-hand homes in the first six months, up 5.7 per cent year on year and hitting a new high since the same period in 2021, according to a report by China Index Academy this month.

While transaction volumes had rebounded notably, the sustainability of the recovery depended on whether trading momentum could hold and how price trends evolved, the report said.

Our positive sector view is backed by likely stabilising sales growth in July to September … and a stronger new launch pipeline from September

Griffin Chan, Citi Research

Signs of improving home sales have also emerged in other cities. A Citi Research report in late July forecast sales growth and a recovery in new housing launches starting in September.

July already saw improvements in transaction volumes for both new and pre-owned homes. Among 18 monitored cities, second-hand home sales rose 7 per cent year on year, with first-tier cities leading the recovery at a 14 per cent annual increase, the report said.

“Our positive sector view is backed by likely stabilising sales growth in July to September on resilient transaction volumes in core cities and a favourable low base, and a stronger new launch pipeline from September,” said Griffin Chan, an analyst at Citi Research.

Foreign capital helps steady the market

Beijing’s policymakers, who have mobilised a variety of measures to ensure home delivery in recent years, have continued rolling out supportive policies for the housing sector.

Largely driven by residential development, the property sector was once estimated by market players to contribute roughly a quarter of the country’s economy, but has turned into a drag over the past five years.

At a July 30 meeting, the Politburo – a major decision-making body of the ruling Communist Party – made fresh vows to stabilise the property market, part of its efforts to establish safeguards within broader economic risk-prevention measures.

Meanwhile, authorities have optimised institutional conditions for foreign individual investment in domestic property. Since 2025, China has refined its policy framework for stabilising foreign capital inflows, gradually rolling out a raft of supporting measures.

In September 2025, the State Administration of Foreign Exchange issued a guideline: non-resident individuals meeting home purchase conditions may settle foreign exchange funds for property purchases at banks upon presenting a sales contract, and then submit the filing documents to the bank.

The measure streamlined review procedures and expanded nationwide a scheme that was previously piloted with Hong Kong and Macau residents, allowing them to purchase homes in mainland cities that were part of the Greater Bay Area.

item.title: [SCMP] What comes next for Hong Kong as a global financial hub?
item.description:
What will a stronger international financial centre look like for Hong Kong? Doubling down on yuan internationalisation is a key focus, experts say in this second of our five-part series on the city’s first five-year blueprint. Read part one here.

With a symbolic press of a button, top officials and securities regulators from Hong Kong and mainland China earlier this month marked a historic moment for the city’s financial markets.

The August 3 launch of the first offshore Chinese government yuan-denominated bond futures contract, along with related cross-border policies, underscored what Beijing called a critical upgrade of Hong Kong’s status as the country’s largest offshore yuan trade-settlement market.
item.content:encoded:
What will a stronger international financial centre look like for Hong Kong? Doubling down on yuan internationalisation is a key focus, experts say in this second of our five-part series on the city’s first five-year blueprint. Read part one here.

With a symbolic press of a button, top officials and securities regulators from Hong Kong and mainland China earlier this month marked a historic moment for the city’s financial markets.

The August 3 launch of the first offshore Chinese government yuan-denominated bond futures contract, along with related cross-border policies, underscored what Beijing called a critical upgrade of Hong Kong’s status as the country’s largest offshore yuan trade-settlement market.

The milestone comes as Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu prepares to deliver the city’s first five-year plan aimed at aligning with national development.

A key theme is on reimagining the economy, finance and trade and in this, analysts say, Hong Kong will have to do much more to raise its status as an international financial centre.

This is why the August 3 launch was momentous. It will give a longed-for shot in the arm to Hong Kong’s mandate from Beijing to help globalise the yuan and strengthen the city’s position as an international financial centre, according to business leaders.

Market participants and policy experts, meanwhile, have called for expanded yuan products, commodity trading infrastructure, a diversified talent pool and fintech innovation to reinforce Hong Kong’s capacity to channel global capital into the country while mitigating geopolitical and currency risks.

“Yuan globalisation is a very important part of Beijing’s mandate for Hong Kong to service the country as stated in the country’s 15th five-year plan,” said Kenny Shui Chi-wai, vice-president of Our Hong Kong Foundation think tank.

“Hong Kong connects China with the world – the city’s international financial centre status means a lot to the country.”

He said Hong Kong’s financial services sector would give much-needed support not just to mainland Chinese companies, but also to local firms to raise funds via initial public offerings (IPOs).

“This directly contributes to the city’s real economy,” he noted.

Hong Kong was the world’s top IPO destination until June, when billionaire Elon Musk’s commercial aerospace company SpaceX listed in New York for US$75 billion. Hong Kong remains a prime international choice for IPOs by mainland firms largely due to political barriers in the United States. At least 500 candidates are in the pipeline for the rest of the year.

Business magnate Allan Zeman, chairman of the Lan Kwai Fong Group and a member of the Chief Executive’s Council of Advisers, noted that the Middle East war was accelerating the pivot of the region’s wealth to Hong Kong, alongside the trend of so-called de-dollarisation.

“Hong Kong’s importance ... becomes not just a support for China; we now become a bridgehead. It really elevates Hong Kong’s standing to another level,” Zeman said.

Hedging interest rate risks

While the mainland maintains a largely closed capital account, more than 70 per cent of global payments in the offshore yuan market pass through Hong Kong, with the city’s renminbi deposits exceeding 1 trillion yuan, making it the biggest pool outside the mainland, official data shows.

The latest launch – the Chinese government’s first onshore sovereign bond futures contract available in an offshore market – is designed to provide global investors with a crucial tool to manage renminbi interest rate exposure as they increase their allocations to mainland fixed-income assets.

Bond futures are derivative products with government bonds as their underlying asset, allowing traders to buy or sell the bonds at a fixed price on a specific future date.

Traders use them to protect their investments against changing interest rates or to speculate on which way bond prices will move. They allow them to trade the value of bonds without having to own the actual bonds upfront.

The five-year Chinese government bond futures contract is traded on the Hong Kong stock exchange.

“International investors’ holdings of Chinese bonds have already reached 3.2 trillion yuan, and the need to hedge interest rate risk is inevitably growing,” said Mofiz Chan, chairman of the Hong Kong Securities and Futures Professionals Association.

“Now, the government bond futures allow investors to hedge interest rate risk more efficiently without changing the structure of their underlying asset holdings. This enables more investors to hold renminbi-denominated government bonds.”

Chan said the city should offer more renminbi-denominated products, including derivatives, to boost the yuan’s pricing power among international assets.

“We need to push for more yuan-denominated futures, options and over-the-counter derivatives to go online,” he said.

To draw larger pools of capital, Chan called for the launch of an “IPO Connect” cross-border scheme to integrate primary markets and to include real estate investment trusts (Reits) in the existing southbound Stock Connect share-trading programme to satisfy mainland investors’ thirst for yield.

“If implemented, mainland investors can directly trade Hong Kong stocks using yuan, elevating the proportion of the currency used in cross-border securities investments,” Chan added.

He further urged regulators to introduce block-trading mechanisms and resolve discrepancies in trading days between the mainland and Hong Kong.

Crucially, Chan said Hong Kong had to act as a true booster for China’s new productive forces by developing intellectual property-backed bonds and tech enterprise bonds.

He also urged the city to tap into the US$6 trillion Islamic finance market by issuing sukuk, or Islamic bonds, to fund domestic megaprojects such as the Northern Metropolis.

To unleash market vitality, Chan argued that regulators must “tear down walls” by slashing prohibitive anti-money-laundering compliance costs that burden smaller brokerages.

He said another priority for Hong Kong was to expedite the adoption of the digital yuan in cross-border payments, in line with the recent commercial expansion of China’s Project mBridge platform, to mitigate geopolitical risks tied to the US-dominated Swift interbank network.

A creator or a follower?

Dan Ronald Leung Wai-tsun, CEO of Esperanza Fintech Group, a Hong Kong-based financial technology firm whose licensed businesses include gold trading and tokenised gold services, called on the government to clearly spell out its position in the five-year plan and to adopt a new mentality towards fintech development.

He said the city widely followed US-driven trends in technological adoption such as generative artificial intelligence (AI) integration and blockchain architecture.

“Does it want to be a creator or a follower?” Leung said. “Hong Kong needs to focus on helping China go global, especially during the time of deglobalisation of the US dollar.”

Leung, a lawyer by profession, said he believed Hong Kong’s niche was in having an established common law regime, which could serve as a gatekeeper for mainland companies expanding abroad.

“The Hong Kong government also needs younger leaders to bring in a new mentality and ideas,” he said, noting that Singapore was also chasing fast on fintech development.

In addition, a key pillar of the nation’s 15th five-year plan is the establishment of a physical commodities trading and storage ecosystem, including one for gold.

“Hong Kong should leverage the strengths of its internationalised financial market to address its shortcomings in physical delivery infrastructure,” Chan of the association said.

“The goal is to establish Hong Kong as the pricing centre for gold in the Asian time zone.”

The urgency of building that physical infrastructure was echoed by Wilson Chan Fung-cheung, a veteran banker and adjunct professor at City University’s College of Business.

“If there is only an exchange without a storage location … settlement can only rely on net settlement,” Chan said.

“But if we can have exchange settlement alongside physical warehousing in Hong Kong, it will increasingly encompass copper, aluminium, zinc and lead. If Hong Kong can play this role, it can help with pricing.”

Shui of the think tank said developing a commodity trading ecosystem in Hong Kong would also benefit the city’s global financial centre status and the real economy because it involved trading, warehousing, processing and refining, logistics, insurance and professional services, and more.

“It will also play a role in strengthening China’s financial security and risk management,” he said.

Wilson Chan said that the 15th five-year plan’s focus on helping enterprises “go global” was not about the US market, but mainly about emerging markets, or the Global South.

“If you are helping enterprises go abroad, you should go to the fastest-growing markets today – Southeast Asia, the Middle East and Central Asia,” he said.

“Because these are the truly growing markets that will consider using the renminbi. The US market is an environment where we have no pricing power.”

‘Find your own path’

Shui called on the government to add currencies from Asean countries and the Middle East to the city’s real-time gross settlement system, a secure electronic money transfer system where funds move from one bank to another in real time.

At present, the system includes the Hong Kong dollar, US dollar, euro and yuan.

“This will minimise currency exchange costs and will boost mainland trade with these markets,” he said.

Shui said Hong Kong required a more diversified talent pool for its ambitions to tap into new markets including countries in the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations trading bloc, the Middle East and Africa.

“Hong Kong needs to bring in a more diversified profile of talents, in addition to talents who know China or come from there,” he said.

“Anyone who was educated in or has worked in these new markets before will be helpful not just to Hong Kong, but China, as many mainland firms want to expand over there.”

Some human resource groups earlier this year argued that the city’s heavy reliance on mainland talent could downgrade Hong Kong’s status as an international hub, as 94.5 per cent of successful applicants in a top talent scheme came from across the border.

To leverage the city’s financial strength, Shui said the insurance sector could provide services to mainland companies to mitigate geopolitical risks.

Beyond product offerings, some experts argued Hong Kong had to fundamentally alter how it deployed its own reserves to chart its own path rather than chasing established Western templates.

Jun Yu Chan, a partner at Wings Capital Ventures, questioned why most of the city’s Exchange Fund – the war chest used to defend the local currency – was invested in US dollar-denominated assets through global asset managers.

“Why don’t you allocate a little bit more to the local managers, which you have more control over?” he said.

“You can give them a mandate to do a certain percentage of trading in the Hong Kong stock market or bond market. All this trading will create the liquidity to build up the depth of the Hong Kong markets.”

He suggested that the city take the regulatory lead in nascent sectors such as AI and cryptocurrencies by actively building functional use cases.

“You are not a follower of any international standard. You have to find your own path. You are making the rules for yourself, not for other people,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] In Singapore’s battle of casinos, Marina Bay Sands holds winning hand against Sentosa
item.description:
At Singapore casino Resorts World Sentosa’s Lunar New Year lucky draw for high rollers earlier this year, the biggest prize was a bottle of Martell Cognac. Across the harbour at rival Marina Bay Sands, the top sweepstakes winner walked away with a new Mercedes-Benz CLA 200 worth much more.

It is one of the incidents that has made the casino duopoly in one of the world’s top gambling venues more lopsided in the past few years. That is putting pressure on the Sentosa Island resort, whose gaming licence is due for renewal in the coming months.

The Southeast Asian financial hub has seen a strong post-Covid rebound in tourist arrivals and an increase in wealthy gamblers from neighbouring countries and China. It has also taken some business from Macau, which has been affected by Chinese government crackdowns on casino junkets and illegal money-exchange activities.
item.content:encoded:
At Singapore casino Resorts World Sentosa’s Lunar New Year lucky draw for high rollers earlier this year, the biggest prize was a bottle of Martell Cognac. Across the harbour at rival Marina Bay Sands, the top sweepstakes winner walked away with a new Mercedes-Benz CLA 200 worth much more.

It is one of the incidents that has made the casino duopoly in one of the world’s top gambling venues more lopsided in the past few years. That is putting pressure on the Sentosa Island resort, whose gaming licence is due for renewal in the coming months.

The Southeast Asian financial hub has seen a strong post-Covid rebound in tourist arrivals and an increase in wealthy gamblers from neighbouring countries and China. It has also taken some business from Macau, which has been affected by Chinese government crackdowns on casino junkets and illegal money-exchange activities.

The gains in Singapore have been heavily skewed towards Las Vegas Sands’ Marina Bay Sands. Its casino revenues for the first half of 2026 topped US$2.1 billion, while Resorts World Sentosa’s comparable numbers were less than a third of that.

The struggle to attract more high rollers even in Singapore’s growing wealth hub underscores the challenges facing Resorts World Sentosa’s operator, Genting Singapore.

Back in November 2024, Singapore’s Gambling Regulatory Authority called the Sentosa resort’s tourism performance “unsatisfactory”, and granted it a two-year casino licence that took effect in February 2025 instead of the usual three years.

“This is a soft threat” to pressure Resorts World Sentosa to improve its performance, said Zheng Feng Chee, a consumer analyst at DBS Group. “In reality, there are very few casinos that have the financial muscle to buy them out.”

The agency says it is assessing Resorts World Sentosa’s renewal application, and will announce its decision before the licence expires in February 2027.

The regulator’s evaluation takes into account the entire integrated resort’s performance. Last year, it renewed Marina Bay Sands’ casino licence for another three years.

Genting Singapore said in April that it had “maintained close engagement” with authorities and believed the group was “well positioned for the next assessment cycle.”

A Resorts World Sentosa representative said the integrated resort had over the past 18 months added new attractions and experiences, and had been “enhancing” its hospitality and gaming offerings.

Its goal was to position itself “for sustainable growth over the next decade”, the representative said, adding that “the early signs of progress are encouraging”. Marina Bay Sands declined to comment for this article.

No match for Sands

The competition between the two casinos is likely to remain intense.

“I see them losing the battle, and even more market share,” said Ben Lee, managing partner at IGamiX, a Macau-based consulting firm, of Resorts World Sentosa.

Lee said it simply had not been able to match the “luxuriate experience” of Marina Bay Sands, which has been a big draw for so-called VIPs – the biggest spenders and most highly coveted casino customers.

Singapore’s casino industry has been heavily reliant on foreigners ever since Resorts World Sentosa first opened its doors in early 2010, with Marina Bay Sands launching shortly after.

Singapore citizens and permanent residents have to pay S$150 (US$120) per day to enter either casino, while tourists can go in for free after showing their passports.

Gamblers from China have been flocking to Singapore, which offers visa-free entry to tourists from the mainland. Concerns that their personal data could be shared with Chinese authorities have also made some high rollers wary of gambling in Macau, and they see Singapore as a more discreet alternative to protect their privacy.

These days, the crowd at Resorts World Sentosa’s VIP club is far smaller than that at Marina Bay Sands, according to people familiar with both casinos. In 2023, the Sentosa casino had a larger share of the VIP market, but that tumbled to around 20 per cent in the first quarter of this year before rebounding recently to 36 per cent, according to DBS research.

While there are fewer high rollers compared to so-called mass gamers, the former make outsize contributions to casino revenues and profits.

To become a VIP, gamblers typically have to deposit or spend at least S$100,000 for starters, then accumulate more spending by making bets and playing games over a fixed period to secure a club membership. Benefits include access to private gaming suites, complimentary hotel stays, dining privileges and invitations to exclusive events.

Some members of Resorts World Sentosa’s casino club for VIPs have complained to the integrated resort’s management about what they consider as the Sentosa property’s dated infrastructure, its unresponsiveness to feedback, and even the process of exchanging cash and chips, according to people familiar with the matter.

Rolling out revamps

In addition to more generous lucky draw prizes, the VIP club at Marina Bay Sands offers perks and freebies that include suite stays with a butler service, tickets to musicals and dining credit at restaurants. Its integrated resort – which is one of the world’s most profitable – includes three 57-storey hotel towers with a large boat-shaped rooftop, an art museum and shopping centre.

Resorts World Sentosa clawed back some high rollers’ market share in the recent second quarter, after Marina Bay Sands posted weaker VIP revenue. The latter said that was partly because some of its high-value customers went to the World Cup, which drew spending away from casinos.

Genting Singapore is majority-owned by Malaysian leisure, real estate and hospitality group Genting, which is controlled by 75-year-old billionaire Lim Kok Thay. Last year, he became the Singapore unit’s acting chief executive officer following a series of leadership reshuffles.

In addition to its casino and multiple hotels, Resorts World Singapore operates Universal Studios Singapore, a large water park and other Sentosa attractions. The casino generates most of the integrated resort’s revenue and profits.

The Sentosa venue is in the midst of a S$6.8 billion revamp that includes building an all-suite luxury hotel, expanding its oceanarium and adding Super Nintendo World to Universal Studios Singapore. The improved version of the resort is to be completed by 2030.

Marina Bay Sands, meanwhile, has kicked off its own US$8 billion makeover and expansion that will add another 55-storey hotel tower and a live entertainment arena.

Marina Bay Sands had “made the property more premium, more appealing to higher-value customers,” said Vitaly Umansky, Hong Kong-based senior analyst of global gaming at Seaport Research Partners. “Resorts World has a lot of wood to chop in order to try to gain back some of that market share.”

item.title: [SCMP] Southeast Asia’s landmine clearers face closure as global aid shifts to new wars
item.description:
En Poy was minding cattle in a former Khmer Rouge stronghold in Cambodia when he set off his first landmine.

The blast from the rusty relic he picked up cost him an arm and an eye. It also inspired his career with non-profit organisation Cambodian Self Help Demining, which clears landmines and unexploded ordnance across the country, deadly remnants of wars from the last century.

Groups like Poy’s that rely on foreign aid are struggling as donors shift funding for humanitarian demining towards active conflicts in Ukraine, Gaza and Sudan, and to more recent wars, like in Syria and Afghanistan. Today’s conflicts are also driving higher defence spending, leaving less money for aid.
item.content:encoded:
En Poy was minding cattle in a former Khmer Rouge stronghold in Cambodia when he set off his first landmine.

The blast from the rusty relic he picked up cost him an arm and an eye. It also inspired his career with non-profit organisation Cambodian Self Help Demining, which clears landmines and unexploded ordnance across the country, deadly remnants of wars from the last century.

Groups like Poy’s that rely on foreign aid are struggling as donors shift funding for humanitarian demining towards active conflicts in Ukraine, Gaza and Sudan, and to more recent wars, like in Syria and Afghanistan. Today’s conflicts are also driving higher defence spending, leaving less money for aid.

President Donald Trump’s dismantling of the US Agency for International Development and a 90-day freeze on foreign aid last year worsened the problems, though American demining support to Cambodia has restarted.

Cambodia’s predicament shows that dangers remain even when fighting ends.

Demining groups say that without international support, Southeast Asia’s unfinished work clearing landmines and unexploded bombs will continue to endanger communities, maiming and killing people and slowing development for years to come.

Poy was wounded in a second landmine explosion that pierced his face and body with shrapnel and killed three of his colleagues. He now educates fellow Cambodians in high-risk areas on how to avoid such dangers.

But he is not sure how long that will last.

“If one day donors stop funding my organisation, I would definitely be sad because we haven’t finished our job,” he said. “There are still a lot of landmines left over.”

Deadly legacy

The Vietnam war bled into neighbouring Cambodia and Laos, triggering strife that lasted long after the Americans fled the fall of Saigon, including the Khmer Rouge’s reign of terror, which killed about 1.7 million Cambodians.

Cambodia is one of the world’s most land-mined countries. Laos is the most heavily bombed country per capita in history and Vietnam still battles the fallout of chemical weapons.

Since the wars ended, landmines and unexploded ordnance have killed about 90,000 people and wounded almost twice as many across the three countries.

Leftover weapons lie beneath fields and forests, blocking construction of roads and schools. They are deadly discoveries, mistaken for toys by children who account for more than 40 per cent of the civilian casualties recorded globally since 1999 by the Landmine and Cluster Munition Monitor, formed by non-profit organisations to track such issues.

Demining is slow and painstaking work. Teams first survey and map contaminated areas. Then step-by-step they clear vegetation, using metal detectors and specialised equipment to locate explosives and destroy them. Progress is measured in metres a day and work often stops in wet weather.

“These things don’t really become less dangerous with time. They become more dangerous as they deteriorate,” said Charles Ray, a Vietnam war veteran who became the first post-war US consul general in Ho Chi Minh City and later ambassador to Cambodia.

By funding demining, the US proved it cared, Ray said. “We’re not just this behemoth that comes in with our military machine and breaks things, we can also help nations rebuild,” he said.

Funding for humanitarian demining amounted to US$4.3 billion from 2020 to 2024, according to the landmine monitor.

National contributions from affected countries made up about a fifth and foreign aid provided the rest, with most of the funds from the US, Germany, the European Union, Norway, and Switzerland, the landmine monitor said.

Recent conflicts have created unprecedented demand for demining as contaminated areas expand, Maria Vardis of the UN Mine Action Service said.

Ukraine received a third of all humanitarian demining funding in 2024, more than any other country, the landmine monitor found. Other active conflict zones, like Yemen and Gaza, received increased funding, while demining efforts in Syria, Sudan and Afghanistan have also ramped up, while some Asian nations are getting less funding.

Germany is considering reducing foreign aid in favour of defence spending and military support to Ukraine.

At the same time, more landmines are being planted and bombs dropped in other conflicts such as the civil war in Myanmar and border conflicts between Cambodia and Thailand.

“Funding does fluctuate year to year, but in the big picture, even in the face of cuts by many governments, the big crises continue to be funded, but smaller and older mine action projects are struggling,” Vardis said.

Yo-yo aid

Under Trump, US demining aid to Southeast Asia has yo-yoed. That has “set a really dangerous precedent for what can be done,” Danae Hendrickson of the US-based advocacy group Legacies of War said.

Last year, the US approved US$56.5 million for war-legacy programmes in Vietnam, according to congressional documents, compared with US$197 million allocated in 2024. In July, Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced US$130 million in demining help for Southeast Asia, without giving details.

Last year’s freeze briefly halted war-legacy projects in Vietnam and weakened Hanoi’s confidence in US commitments, said Nguyen Khac Giang, a visiting fellow at Singapore’s ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute.

“The lasting damage is to the hard-earned trust between the two former enemies,” he said.

A US State Department representative said American help was “not charity” and that humanitarian demining aid would continue to serve US interests around the world.

Between 1992 and 2025, about 1.2 million mines and 3.2 million other explosive remnants of war were found in Cambodia, according to the Cambodian Mine Action and Victim Assistance Authority.

The country still had 1,749 sq km (675 square miles) of uncleared land as of last year.

Thousands or even millions more weapons might still be out there, said Bill Morse, president of the Landmine Relief Fund, which supports Cambodian Self Help Demining.

Barely an hour from the famed Angkor Wat temple complex in Siem Reap, deminers with South Korean, Swiss and American flags on their uniforms and helmets recently inched through a minefield, clearing the land one painstaking step at a time.

They found a Soviet-designed anti-personnel landmine. Another unit nearby was dispatched to destroy a mortar round and a rocket-propelled grenade at a cassava farm just off a highway leading to a new Chinese-funded airport.

The group may have to stop their work by September due to sharp cutbacks in donations. “We have simply run out of donors,” Morse said.

“If people want to pull their money away, that’s a decision that they have to make,” he said. “But when they do, people will die here.”

item.title: [SCMP] South Korea accelerates military self-reliance over Trump’s ‘unpredictability’
item.description:
US President Donald Trump’s abrupt move to scale back annual military drills with South Korea has handed President Lee Jae Myung a fresh impetus for greater defence self-reliance even as he seeks to maintain the long-standing alliance.

Lee on Tuesday called for accelerated efforts to regain wartime operational control (OPCON) of South Korean forces from the United States and build nuclear-powered submarines, casting both as part of a broader push to boost South Korea’s ability to defend itself.

His comments reflect Seoul’s growing concern over uncertainty in its alliance with the US under an “unpredictable” president, according to analysts.
item.content:encoded:
US President Donald Trump’s abrupt move to scale back annual military drills with South Korea has handed President Lee Jae Myung a fresh impetus for greater defence self-reliance even as he seeks to maintain the long-standing alliance.

Lee on Tuesday called for accelerated efforts to regain wartime operational control (OPCON) of South Korean forces from the United States and build nuclear-powered submarines, casting both as part of a broader push to boost South Korea’s ability to defend itself.

His comments reflect Seoul’s growing concern over uncertainty in its alliance with the US under an “unpredictable” president, according to analysts.

“Ironically, President Trump’s unpredictability allows President Lee to move with greater strategic flexibility,” said Chang Yong-seok, a senior researcher at the Institute for Peace and Unification Studies at Seoul National University.

“South Korea, like many other friends, has been whipsawed by President Trump, and this is another example of his capriciousness. But this gives President Lee all the more justification to push a greater self-reliance agenda,” Chang said.

At a government cabinet meeting on Tuesday, Lee highlighted South Korea’s growing defence capabilities.

“South Korea is ranked among the world’s top five military powers and is considered one of the world’s top four defence industry powers,” Lee said.

South Korea’s defence spending was equivalent to 1.4 times North Korea’s gross domestic product, he noted.

“Considering our weapons systems and the scale of our military capabilities, our ability to defend ourselves ranks among the world’s leading countries,” Lee said. “It would not be an exaggeration to say that our capabilities are more than sufficient.”

He added that “comprehensively upgrading our operational capabilities is essential to further strengthen our defence capabilities”.

Lee urged officials to step up efforts to regain wartime OPCON within his five-year term, which ends in June 2030, in line with the government’s initial plan.

At the same time, he stressed the importance of maintaining the alliance with the US while strengthening South Korea’s defence capabilities.

“A strong alliance will further solidify the foundation of our security, while strengthening our own capabilities will increase our value and necessity as an ally,” he said.

Lee also called for accelerated progress on a nuclear-powered submarine project, describing it as a symbol of a “more constructive and stronger future for the South Korea-US alliance”.

Washington has agreed to cooperate with Seoul on acquiring the necessary reactor fuel and addressing civil-military nuclear coordination to enable South Korea to build its first nuclear-powered attack submarines in the mid-2030s.

Lee’s remarks came after Trump ordered a major reduction in the scale of the Ulchi Freedom Shield (UFS), the annual South Korea-US military exercise that kicked off on Monday.

Trump said in a social media post on Sunday that the exercises were not only “costly” but also sent a “totally inappropriate and hostile” signal to North Korea. He also emphasised his “very good relationship” with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un.

At a press briefing on Monday, Trump claimed that Kim had responded to his requests for talks. Trump met Kim three times during his first term: in Singapore in June 2018, in Hanoi in February 2019 and at the inter-Korean border village of Panmunjom in June 2019.

Asked whether he was prioritising North Korea’s interests over those of long-time US ally South Korea by scaling back the joint drills, Trump argued that he was making the security situation “much safer”.

Noting that he had recently spoken by phone with Lee, Trump said the South Korean president had declined his request for Seoul’s help regarding the war in Iran. Trump nevertheless described Lee as “very nice actually”.

Chang said he was concerned that the inconsistencies in US policy could undermine South Korea’s key projects, including the OPCON transfer, nuclear-powered submarines and the reprocessing of spent nuclear fuel, all of which required US cooperation.

“President Trump is apparently dissatisfied with Seoul’s unresponsiveness to his request for help in his war against Iran and the slow implementation of its commitment to invest US$350 billion in the United States,” he said.

“Trump has some strong cards in his hand to put pressure on South Korea,” Chang said, citing Trump’s demand for greater burden-sharing by Seoul regarding the presence of 28,000 US troops and joint military exercises in South Korea.

Yang Moo-jin, a professor at the University of North Korean Studies, said Trump’s remarks were aimed not only at luring North Korea back to dialogue but also at pressuring South Korea to contribute more to US efforts to address global security challenges.

Trump’s comments came ahead of Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi’s visit to Seoul from Wednesday to Thursday. Wang is scheduled to meet Lee on Thursday.

A South Korean Foreign Ministry spokesman said Wang and his South Korean counterpart Cho Hyun would discuss “bilateral ties, the situation on the Korean peninsula, and regional and international matters”.

Wang’s visit will be his first to South Korea since 2021. His previous meeting with Cho took place in Beijing in September last year.

“Ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Shenzhen, China, in November, this will serve as an opportunity to review the results of the full restoration of Korea-China relations and to begin in earnest preparations for the next phase and high-level exchanges,” the spokesman said.

South Korea is expected to brief Wang on Lee’s latest proposal to formally end the Korean war, which ended with an armistice rather than a peace treaty.

Lee on Saturday proposed that the two Koreas begin talks on formally ending the war and discuss ways to halt the advancement of Pyongyang’s nuclear programme, pledging to seek a peace regime on the Korean peninsula.

Pyongyang, however, has yet to respond.

“Trump appears to be emphasising that any political gains achieved through a direct deal with Kim Jong-un should belong to him. The United States is likely to object if Seoul discusses an end-of-war declaration with Wang Yi,” Yang said.

He suggested that the US should hold talks with North Korea first, followed by inter-Korean talks and eventually four-party talks involving the two Koreas, the US and China.

“With Wang Yi’s visit and China’s growing interest in Korean peninsula affairs, Seoul should also make clear to Beijing that it intends to play a role as a facilitator of US-North Korea and inter-Korean dialogue,” he said.

“It is important to establish this position clearly so that China does not seek to constrain or undermine Seoul’s diplomatic efforts.”

Doo Jin-ho, director of the Eurasia Research Centre at the Korea Research Institute for National Strategy, said given Trump’s criticism of South Korea’s insufficient contributions to the alliance as well as his tendency to link trade and security, Seoul should accede to US demands to some degree.

“President Lee wants to complete key projects such as the OPCON transfer, nuclear-powered submarines and the reprocessing of spent nuclear fuel within his official term,” Doo said.

“However, South Korea can’t proceed with these agendas without consent from Washington. That’s the stark reality.”

item.title: [SCMP] Philippines’ Marcos slammed over US$3b family estate tax, says ‘very busy’ with government
item.description:
Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr has put his anti-corruption drive at the centre of his presidency, but questions over his late father’s estate taxes and the family’s past ill-gotten wealth have prompted critics to question his commitment.

Last month, Marcos pledged in his address to Congress to continue fighting alleged irregularities in flood-control projects, stressing that the campaign would be a test of whether his administration could hold even powerful allies to account.

The Presidential Commission on Good Government (PCGG) told This Week in Asia on Tuesday that it had recovered 309.84 billion pesos (US$5.05 billion) as of June 30, describing it as ill-gotten wealth linked to the Marcos family.
item.content:encoded:
Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr has put his anti-corruption drive at the centre of his presidency, but questions over his late father’s estate taxes and the family’s past ill-gotten wealth have prompted critics to question his commitment.

Last month, Marcos pledged in his address to Congress to continue fighting alleged irregularities in flood-control projects, stressing that the campaign would be a test of whether his administration could hold even powerful allies to account.

The Presidential Commission on Good Government (PCGG) told This Week in Asia on Tuesday that it had recovered 309.84 billion pesos (US$5.05 billion) as of June 30, describing it as ill-gotten wealth linked to the Marcos family.

The PCGG was created in 1986 as a special agency under the Office of the President and tasked by different administrations over the decades with recovering assets that it said were stolen by the late president Ferdinand Marcos Snr, his wife Imelda Marcos and their associates.

Asked by This Week in Asia on Friday whether he had paid more than 203 billion pesos (US$3.28 billion) in estate taxes on the estate his father left after the latter died in 1989, Marcos pushed back against any suggestion that the family assets should be treated as ill-gotten.

Speaking at a forum with the Foreign Correspondents Association of the Philippines (FOCAP), Marcos said: “To characterise them as ill-gotten wealth immediately, I have to respond and say, the reason why we won [those civil forfeiture cases] we were able to prove that these were not ill-gotten.”

The estate tax issue stems from assessments made after Marcos Snr’s death, which the Supreme Court later held had become final and enforceable, leaving the estate’s executors responsible for settling them.

“I have to admit that I have neglected some of my duties as co-executor because I’ve been very busy with all the things that a president is busy with,” Marcos said. Calling it “a family matter”, he said that “matters of state and governance are a thousand times more important than any family matter”.

He added: “And that is why I leave it, I’ve left it to the lawyers.”

Marcos promised to provide his lawyers’ contact numbers, but This Week in Asia has not received a response as of Tuesday.

The Bureau of Internal Revenue, which was also contacted for comment, sent an automated reply promising to respond “as soon as possible” but has not done so to date.

Jean Franco, a political science professor at the University of the Philippines, said Marcos’ replies “are consistent with his administration’s intention to revise history and change the narrative surrounding his father’s regime”.

“Talking about the [estate tax] issue is not a ‘family’ matter. It is something that is of great public interest. Not to talk about it is to depoliticise an important issue that has haunted the country for decades.”

She said Marcos’ anti-corruption drive “would be difficult to carry out” because “the flood control scandal has not been thoroughly resolved, aside of course from the Marcoses’ historical connection to corruption”.

The August 21 Movement (Atom), a pro-democracy group formed after the 1983 assassination of opposition leader Benigno “Ninoy” Aquino Jnr, has also accused Marcos of trying to distort history.

“Getting to Malacanang does not entitle him to distort Philippine history. Getting to Malacanang should not give anyone, for that matter, the audacity to violate the truth,” it said in a statement.

Atom’s vice-president Bien Gonzales told This Week in Asia that the group decided to speak out because it noticed the president’s “moves to change the narrative … [and] it’s the responsibility of Atom to become the vanguards of the true essence of history”.

Marcos’ long-pending estate tax case

Ruben Carranza, a former PCGG commissioner, said that as co-executor of his father’s estate, Marcos was duty-bound to pay the more than 203 billion pesos because the Supreme Court’s decision on the matter was final and binding in 1997.

Carranza called Marcos’ assertion that none of the wealth his father left behind was ill-gotten “a lie”.

“As you reminded him, the 2003 Philippine Supreme Court decision unequivocally said that any assets of Ferdinand and Imelda Marcos beyond the US$304,000 they earned as public officials is [in the Supreme Court’s words] ‘money stolen by the Marcos spouses from the Republic of the Philippines’.”

Carranza characterised Marcos’ remarks as an admission that he had failed to meet his tax obligations while in office.

Marcos’ explanation that he had not paid because “he has been busy” with matters of state as president was also “a lie” because the tax liability had existed for decades before he took office.

“If Marcos Jnr is aware of other civil cases he claimed they ‘won,’ then he can’t claim he doesn’t know that they lost that case in 2003 and that they then lost a cascade of cases based on that 2003 decision,” Carranza said.

Another unresolved case involves Arelma, an offshore entity tied to a US case to recover the Marcos assets, which the Philippine Supreme Court also awarded to the government.

US court records describe Arelma as a Panamanian entity linked to a New York Merrill Lynch account into which Marcos deposited about US$2 million in 1972.

Carranza said Marcos was wrong to suggest the issue was long dormant, saying “he lied about [Arelma] at the forum when he said he had not heard the word ‘Arelma’ in decades”.

In a separate interview with This Week in Asia, lawyer Robert Swift, who represents victims of human rights abuses during the late dictator’s rule, said that while the Arelma case remained pending, the current president’s lawyers were no longer involved in it.

The battle over the assets is now between about 10,000 human rights victims who are seeking to enforce a US$2 billion damage suit they won in 1995 against the Marcos estate before a federal court in Hawaii, and the Philippine government, which is also seeking to enforce the 2003 Philippine Supreme Court decision forfeiting the assets in favour of the state.

Swift said the victims’ motion against Manila’s claim remained pending before a federal court in New York.

In an August 2025 ruling, John M Walker Jnr, a judge of the US Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit, described Marcos Snr as “a dictator and kleptocrat...[who] stole billions of dollars from the republic and its people and used networks of foreign financial accounts and shell corporations to hide stolen funds.”

item.title: [SCMP] US transshipment ‘scam’ claims put Asean exporters in a bind
item.description:
Southeast Asian exporters may soon face a heavier burden of proof to show they are not helping Chinese goods dodge US tariffs after the White House named nine countries in the region as part of what it called a global “Shadow Transshipment Network”.

The warning came in a White House report titled “The Great Transshipment Scam”, which alleged that Chinese-origin goods were being routed through lower-tariff jurisdictions and re-entering the US market under new national identities.

Analysts said the report could create fresh uncertainty for Southeast Asian economies that had benefited from “China plus one” manufacturing, in which companies shift parts of their supply chains from China to countries such as Vietnam, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia.
item.content:encoded:
Southeast Asian exporters may soon face a heavier burden of proof to show they are not helping Chinese goods dodge US tariffs after the White House named nine countries in the region as part of what it called a global “Shadow Transshipment Network”.

The warning came in a White House report titled “The Great Transshipment Scam”, which alleged that Chinese-origin goods were being routed through lower-tariff jurisdictions and re-entering the US market under new national identities.

Analysts said the report could create fresh uncertainty for Southeast Asian economies that had benefited from “China plus one” manufacturing, in which companies shift parts of their supply chains from China to countries such as Vietnam, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia.

But they also warned that Washington risked blurring the line between deliberate tariff evasion and legitimate supply-chain diversification.

A supply chain touching China is different from illegal transshipment

Barrett Bingley, trade specialist

“A supply chain touching China is different from illegal transshipment, and we cannot let [Peter] Navarro gaslight the region on this,” said international trade specialist Barrett Bingley, Asia regional director at the Asia-Pacific Foundation of Canada, referring to the White House trade adviser who led the report.

“A multinational corporation moving production to Vietnam, Malaysia, Thailand or Indonesia can be doing real diversification, not just slapping a new label on Chinese goods.”

The 25-page report claims the United States loses “tens of billions of dollars” a year to the illegal transshipment of goods from higher-tariff countries routed through more than 40 lower-tariff jurisdictions, with much of this activity involving “Chinese-origin goods”.

It said Chinese exporters increasingly routed goods through third countries, where limited assembly, finishing, repackaging, relabelling or documentation changes “could create the appearance of a different national origin”.

Among the countries named were many of Washington’s major allies and trade partners, including nine Southeast Asian economies.

Vietnam, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia were flagged as among the countries with the industrial scale, logistics capacity and integration into China-linked supply chains to move large amounts of China-linked goods into US-bound trade flows.

Other regional nations – namely Singapore, Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar and the Philippines – were grouped in a lower category of risk due to lower absolute transshipment volumes, but the report identified them as “attractive opportunistic targets”, citing factors such as free zones, preferential US access and limited customs enforcement capacity.

Several members of this latter group – alongside Bangladesh and Sri Lanka – were labelled “micro-hubs” for allegedly facilitating the relabelling and re-export of China-linked goods, as well as providing light assembly and export-processing services.

Singapore was separately described as a “developed logistics platform” offering advanced customs, ports, trading houses, bonded warehouses and global re-export systems to the “network”.

Burden of proof

Illegal transshipment refers to the re-routing of goods through third countries with little or no processing, typically to hide their true origin and gain better market access.

This differs from legal transshipment, which allows for the necessary loading, unloading and transfer of cargo within custom-controlled zones, as well as activities to preserve the goods’ condition.

But there is “insufficient appreciation” of a third category, according to trade specialist Julia Tijaja, a non-resident fellow at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies in Indonesia: goods that had gone through “substantial transformation to claim a new country of origin”.

International trade law provided little clarity on this distinction, she said, currently offering “only a general rule of thumb with no agreed non-preferential rules of origin in detail”.

For countries that had “attracted substantial Chinese investment in recent years and rely heavily on imported industrial input”, the new US report created “significant uncertainty”, said economist Ahmed Albayrak, a research associate at the Lowy Institute’s Indo-Pacific Development Centre.

Nor is Washington’s proposed roll-out of AI-powered enforcement likely to resolve the ambiguity, according to Tijaja.

“The administrative burden of meeting the origin verification requirements will likely be high, both for the US and the exporting countries, and especially so for small and medium enterprises,” she said.

“While the potential of technology significantly reducing the verification cost is high, the core issue remains unaddressed, which is [defining] what the US means by transshipment.”

Bingley said Washington needed to be “much more responsible” in making a clearer distinction between deliberate attempts to flout the rules and “companies genuinely restructuring supply chains because of tariffs, costs or geopolitical risk”.

“If Washington treats every diversified supply chain as circumvention by default, it ends up penalising the economies it wants as alternatives to China,” he added.

Forced to choose?

Observers said the report represented another effort by the Trump administration to justify steep tariffs against members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and other trade partners while attempting to reduce dependence on China – though they pushed back against the idea of a full decoupling.

Kevin Chen, an associate research fellow at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies who tracks US-Asean trade relations, pointed to reports of a draft US State Department letter demanding that countries choose between membership in the US-led Pax Silica coalition and the Chinese-led World AI Cooperation Organisation.

“This is part of a broader push by Washington to force Asean governments to choose between them and Beijing,” he said, referring to the recent White House report.

Given China’s cost-competitiveness and the entrenched nature of its investments in regional supply chains, Chen said serious doubts remained about the feasibility of this drive – though he predicted it “will not stop Washington from trying, and it also gives US trade officials issues to pressure their trade partners on”.

Bingley called the report “less a serious decoupling effort” than an attempt by Washington to rebuild its “tariff revenue wall against the whole world and checking harder for holes in it, albeit with a special focus on China”.

It also appeared designed to build leverage ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s planned visit to Washington in September, he added.

Albayrak said trade diversion had enabled some decoupling, as reflected in rising investment in Asean, but “full separation remains extremely difficult”.

“China’s earlier rare earth export restrictions underscored how deeply the two economies remain connected,” he said. “Supply chains take years to build and any meaningful decoupling will take just as long.”

For Southeast Asian governments, Bingley said the best response to the US report would be to close “genuine customs and logistics enforcement” gaps by introducing stronger customs systems, credible rules of origin and the ability to show where value was actually being added.

Tijaja urged Asean member states to speak with one voice in the face of US pressure, despite Washington’s preference for bilateral deals rather than negotiating with the bloc as a collective.

“This is a shared concern for the region that is not going away any time soon,” she said. “But it should not stop Asean countries from coordinating with each other to arrive at a consistent shared position, including also with other partners many of whom are also implicated by the report.”

She said Asean needed to demonstrate its commitment to policing illegal transshipment while at the same time clearly communicating “that just because the exports contained China-linked goods, it does not automatically mean there are illegal transshipments”.

“It is important for Asean to work together on this so as not to end up with fragmented or variable rules of origin that would defeat Asean’s own regional economic integration agenda,” Tijaja said.

item.title: [SCMP] Zhu Rongji’s death a reminder of what US-China relations have lost
item.description:
With the death of former Chinese premier Zhu Rongji, both China and the wider world have lost a great leader.

Zhu took personal risks for better US-China ties. He believed that productive Sino-American relations were good for China and for the world.

He was a global leader before China had achieved its current great power status. In mid-1990, when I was president of the National Committee on United States-China Relations, our organisation invited Zhu, then Shanghai mayor, to the United States. Several colleagues and I spent nearly three weeks travelling to several US cities with him.
item.content:encoded:
With the death of former Chinese premier Zhu Rongji, both China and the wider world have lost a great leader.

Zhu took personal risks for better US-China ties. He believed that productive Sino-American relations were good for China and for the world.

He was a global leader before China had achieved its current great power status. In mid-1990, when I was president of the National Committee on United States-China Relations, our organisation invited Zhu, then Shanghai mayor, to the United States. Several colleagues and I spent nearly three weeks travelling to several US cities with him.

This trip occurred about a year after June 4, 1989 – the first high-level visit to the US by a Chinese leader after the trauma and bloodshed of Tiananmen Square.

Making this journey at that time was a risk for him. He could have been publicly humiliated by the withering criticisms of Americans outraged by the June 1989 tumult. If he was too strident defending his government in America, he would fail in his mission to improve ties with US citizens and leaders. On the other hand, if he was perceived back home as a weak defender of China’s dignity, he would be vulnerable to nationalistic backlash.

American praise of him could be construed by his domestic detractors as criticism of China’s central leadership. He did not want to appear to be the darling of the West when his superiors in Beijing were prohibited from contact with US officials because of Washington’s post-Tiananmen sanctions. Zhu candidly hinted at his quandary, saying: “I wish they [the US press] would quit calling me ‘China’s Gorbachev’ – it’s killing me in China. I am not China’s Gorbachev, I am China’s Zhu Rongji.”

Leadership greatness is anchored in character. Our rides together during his extended 1990 US trip, subsequent opportunities to meet him one on one and with groups over subsequent years and my conversations with other world leaders about their interactions with Zhu left me several indelible impressions about his character and qualities of leadership. The trust that Chinese citizens and foreigners alike placed in Zhu rested upon his pragmatism and cosmopolitan vision, inquisitiveness, humour, capacity to communicate across cultural divides and ability to convey reality as he saw it.

‘In the end, we are all mixed systems’

On the evening of July 7, 1990, Zhu and his delegation of five other mayors from some of China’s largest cities, plus the venerable former mayor of Shanghai Wang Daohan, landed at John F. Kennedy Airport in New York. As we rode into New York City, the illuminated bridges spanning the East River suddenly popped into view, as did the twin towers. He asked me, “Tell me. You have something here called the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey. What is it? What does it do? Why was it established?”

I inadequately explained that the Port Authority was a multi-state/municipality special-purpose jurisdiction to plan, develop and operate infrastructure and promote region-wide economic and social development. Showing his cosmopolitanism and practical nature, he said: “That is important. Though you are capitalist, you need planning. And we, though socialist, need a lot more market. In the end, we are all mixed systems.” He was right.

Congress ‘reminds me of my barber shop’

Get a person laughing or seeing things from your angle of view in the first two minutes of speaking with them, and you are 99 per cent of the way to mutual understanding. Zhu was a master at that.

In my experience, Zhu never spoke with a group before first asking who was in the audience and what they cared about. He almost never read a speech. Also, unlike most Chinese leaders, he did not live in fear that someone in the audience would ask an embarrassing question.

One day, as we headed for Capitol Hill to meet with members of Congress, he was undaunted by the prospect of meeting Nancy Pelosi, a junior House member from California. She was calling for protecting the visa status of Chinese students then studying in the US and tying most-favoured-nation status for China to its human rights behaviour. Heading towards that meeting, I cautioned the mayor that he would get what he might see as hostile, unfriendly questions, which I don’t think he needed me to tell him. I explained that he should not take personal offence at the way Congress operated. It would all be very un-Chinese. Members of Congress would convey more moderate views privately to him, then go out and lambast China.

All this he understood, and more. As we left the last meeting of that day on the Hill, he said: “Well that wasn’t as bad as you warned. Reminds me of my barber shop. People come in, people go out, everyone talks over everyone else. Yeah, like my barber shop.”

The world’s Zhu Rongji

My experience seeing many members of Congress interact with Chinese leaders is that they generally identify a legitimate concern, then come up with a proposed remedy or to-do list for their Chinese interlocutor. Such was the case in April 2002 – about a year before the US invasion of Iraq – when he was urged to support the US invasion of Iraq to forestall what the George W. Bush administration argued was Baghdad’s drive to acquire nuclear and other weapons of mass destruction.

Zhu replied: “I cannot agree with you on the Iraq issue. You can’t produce solid evidence that Iraq has nuclear weapons. To destroy a country at will is very dangerous. The whole Arab world will fall out with you. We don’t hope to see this.” Nearly two decades later, the US still lives with the consequences of not heeding this advice, as well as repeating the error with respect to Iran today.

While Zhu Rongji was China’s Zhu Rongji, he also was the world’s Zhu Rongji. Reflecting on him and the current US-China relationship shows how much the world has lost in terms of a leader and a constructive global approach.

item.title: [SCMP] How Asia’s 50 Best Bars expanded to 25 cities, from Kathmandu to Hangzhou
item.description:
Since Asia’s 50 Best Bars extended its rankings up to 100 in 2021, the number of countries and cities represented has expanded from an inaugural nine cities across eight countries in 2016 to 25 cities in 11 countries this year.

The effects have been largely twofold. First, no single city dominates as Singapore did in 2017, with its record-high 13 entries. Recognition is much more diffused now. Bangkok, the most represented location this year, fields a dominant but comparatively modest eight entries in the main list, including the year’s highest new entry – Lennon’s from Rosewood Bangkok, which landed at seventh place. A secondary effect has been that the 51-100 list serves as a hotbed for younger cocktail cities. Barc entered the list in 2023, putting Kathmandu on the map, while cities like Hangzhou and Galle made the rankings for the first time this year.

More cities on the list means more competition for stalwart venues like Singapore’s Nutmeg & Clove, debuting at 30th place in 2017, but it also means that cocktail lovers are expanding their palates rapidly. “Our guests are more well-travelled now,” says Nutmeg & Clove founder Colin Chia, “Cocktail tourism is a real thing. Consumers these days, they will travel to Sri Lanka, or go to Semarang in Indonesia for cocktails.”
item.content:encoded:
Since Asia’s 50 Best Bars extended its rankings up to 100 in 2021, the number of countries and cities represented has expanded from an inaugural nine cities across eight countries in 2016 to 25 cities in 11 countries this year.

The effects have been largely twofold. First, no single city dominates as Singapore did in 2017, with its record-high 13 entries. Recognition is much more diffused now. Bangkok, the most represented location this year, fields a dominant but comparatively modest eight entries in the main list, including the year’s highest new entry – Lennon’s from Rosewood Bangkok, which landed at seventh place. A secondary effect has been that the 51-100 list serves as a hotbed for younger cocktail cities. Barc entered the list in 2023, putting Kathmandu on the map, while cities like Hangzhou and Galle made the rankings for the first time this year.

More cities on the list means more competition for stalwart venues like Singapore’s Nutmeg & Clove, debuting at 30th place in 2017, but it also means that cocktail lovers are expanding their palates rapidly. “Our guests are more well-travelled now,” says Nutmeg & Clove founder Colin Chia, “Cocktail tourism is a real thing. Consumers these days, they will travel to Sri Lanka, or go to Semarang in Indonesia for cocktails.”

Chia, who also started the popular bars #FindThePhotobooth and #FindTheLockerRoom in Bangkok, notes that increased recognition of bars from further afield has led to a cross-pollination of sorts, even in an established cocktail scene like Singapore’s. “When connecting with these overseas guest shifts, we learn the culture and the taste profile,” he says. “We’re not just making drinks for Singaporeans; we try to be as inclusive as possible.”

Even if countries with less of a cocktail tradition are starting to make their mark, that doesn’t mean the news is resonating everywhere. In Kuala Lumpur, represented by four bars across both the main and extended lists, Angeline Tan of Three X Co claims, “A lot of Malaysians don’t even know about the 50 Best [Bars] list,” and says the KL scene is still young and dominated by beer drinkers.

Tan has not been deterred, though, in her efforts to build Malaysia’s cocktail scene, and is leading the charge. She is affectionately known as the “mama” of Kuala Lumpur’s bar scene, which includes Bar Trigona at the Four Seasons Kuala Lumpur, the fermentation-focused Reka:bar, and the more classically-oriented Penrose at 64th on this year’s extended list. Together, the bars annually host KL Cocktail Week, while Three X Co focuses on cocktail-pairing menus and approaches Gen Z in addition to their regular service. Tan finds it crucial to bring in regional influence. “Every month we bring in a guest bartender; that is our education.”

It’s not just Tan who is pushing for more cross-border collaboration. Similar attitudes exist in Nepal, home to another developing cocktail scene. “The cocktail industry in Nepal is still relatively small … and remains largely concentrated in Kathmandu,” explains Barc co-founder Adarsha Tamrakar. “Increasing engagement with bars across Asia and the rest of the world through guest shifts, masterclasses, competitions and exchange programmes will help expand our community beyond borders while exposing Nepalese bartenders to new ideas and perspectives.”

Barc is Kathmandu’s most outstanding bar, and Tamrakar observes that the city lacks diversity of concepts more than it does quality – but says new concepts are on their way. “Before a city gets to multiple internationally recognised bars, you typically see a healthy ecosystem emerge: classic bars, neighbourhood bars, hotel bars, industry bars and experimental bars,” Tamrakar says. “Kathmandu is developing several of these simultaneously, which is unusual for a young scene … driven by bartenders adapting international techniques to local ingredients and traditions.”

This is a progression that all mature bar cities go through, Tamrakar says, adding that the future looks extremely promising. “We are not yet at the level of more mature cocktail destinations like Singapore, Hong Kong or Bangkok in terms of scale and volume. But the opening of new bars, the return of Nepalese bartenders who have gained experience in world-class bars abroad, and the rise of bartending schools in the city are all contributing to a more skilled and knowledgeable workforce,” he says.

A common problem cocktail bars in Asia face is reconciling a baseline of quality with a community capable of properly expressing local cocktail culture. Even bars in Bangkok find it a challenge to thread the needle between supporting local culture and ensuring their drinks appeal to those indulging in “cocktail tourism”. Lennon’s, this year’s highest new entry on the 50 Best list, focuses on signatures with regional ingredients like pandan or calamansi, but their advocacy for Thai spirits is enthusiastic but cautious.

In January, Lennon’s Spirits of Thailand guest shift featured 12 bars and nine spirit makers in the same night. “It’s a very young industry, [starting] three to four years after Covid-19,” says KT Lam, director of bar at Lennon’s. “They’re still finding ways to make their products better, so most of them are still very raw – it’s not stable yet.”

However, bars in Singapore are an example that struggling to overcome these difficulties is a worthwhile endeavour. According to Chia, Nutmeg & Clove opened as a “very interesting, casual neighbourhood street bar” at a time when the local scene was more about speakeasies and serious cocktail bars like Jigger & Pony. Though Chia lost a small fortune in the first 18 months, as Singapore “was not ready for an Asian, Singaporean-inspired cocktail bar yet”, Nutmeg & Clove survived and is now the flagship of a bar group that includes the Japanese-inspired Last Word and Draftland Singapore.

As cities follow these road maps and build their own robust cocktail culture, seeing more locales join Asia’s 50 Best Bars seems almost an inevitability, which means visitors get more destinations with quality bars they can depend on. “[The list is] inclusive, but we can do better,” Chia remarks. “We need to travel to places and search for the next best thing. When you travel, you need to eat, you need to drink. It’s really good that bars from different cities all over Asia highlight that it’s no longer just Singapore, Japan or Hong Kong.”

item.title: [SCMP] Why does Hong Kong need a 5-year plan – and will it crimp its free-market economy?
item.description:
As the government completes a public consultation exercise to craft the city’s own five-year plan to align with national development, the first of this five-part series looks at key questions, starting with the need for such a blueprint.

Economist Heiwai Tang has a line he likes to use on free-market purists: “The market is almost always right, but it’s not always right.”

While Hong Kong has long been ranked the world’s freest economy, Tang, an associate dean at the University of Hong Kong’s (HKU) Business School, said the government’s lack of overarching, long-term planning had contributed to a housing shortage, widening inequality and limited upward mobility, among other social problems.
item.content:encoded:
As the government completes a public consultation exercise to craft the city’s own five-year plan to align with national development, the first of this five-part series looks at key questions, starting with the need for such a blueprint.

Economist Heiwai Tang has a line he likes to use on free-market purists: “The market is almost always right, but it’s not always right.”

While Hong Kong has long been ranked the world’s freest economy, Tang, an associate dean at the University of Hong Kong’s (HKU) Business School, said the government’s lack of overarching, long-term planning had contributed to a housing shortage, widening inequality and limited upward mobility, among other social problems.

“We should not be the last defender of laissez-faire, which has created a lot of prosperity for many people but has also created a lot of long-term structural problems that cannot easily be overcome by market forces,” he said.

All that may change soon if the government plays its hand well.

By the end of September, Hong Kong will make a pivot in governance by rolling out its first-ever five-year plan to set the direction for the city’s economic and social development that is aligned with national strategy.
