This is uncharted territory for Hong Kong. From the 1970s under British colonial rule to the post-handover period, the city government, characterised by its laissez-faire policy, relied on annual policy addresses and budgets for overall planning.

Soon, these two blueprints will effectively become progress reports to complement broader targets set by the new five-year master plan.

Proponents anticipate that the move can provide policy continuity, which the five-year-term government never enjoyed, while helping the international hub navigate persistent geopolitical tensions.

But some question whether this planning approach, modelled on that of mainland China, risks diluting Hong Kong’s identity as an open, free-market economy and squandering its established advantages.

What’s on the table?

The South China Morning Post has learned that as the consultation period ends this Friday, the government aims to publish public views online and finalise the plan in early September for “high-level internal review” before releasing it publicly by the end of the month.

“A mainstream view internally is to create momentum in society to discuss the plan by delivering the five-year plan first, followed by the annual policy address, which would serve as an implementation document,” a source familiar with the planning process said.

“We should seize the opportunity before the independent committee’s report on the Tai Po fire is made public in late October.”

The source said Macau’s third five-year plan, scheduled for release this month, would be studied meticulously as “an important reference”.

Beijing had viewed the casino hub’s previous two plans, which focused on economic diversification away from gaming, as “successful road maps” for guiding its development over the past decade.

The public consultation document for Hong Kong’s first five-year plan (2026-30) outlines strategic objectives across six core pillars: the development of the Northern Metropolis; the economy, finance and trade; innovation and technology; people’s livelihoods; regional cooperation; and the integration of culture, sports and tourism.

The pillars correspond to various themes in China’s 15th five-year plan, including Greater Bay Area integration, the internationalisation of the renminbi, technological self-reliance, common prosperity and Belt and Road Initiative cooperation.

While China’s blueprint contains 20 main quantitative indicators, including annual R&D expenditure growth of more than 7 per cent and a 17 per cent target for cutting carbon intensity, some observers have questioned whether Hong Kong’s road map will also include quantitative indicators.

At a recent consultation session with residents, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said Hong Kong’s five-year plan would set out “macro indicators”, while policy addresses contained more than 100 indicators for departments to follow up on.

Lawmaker Rock Chen Chung-nin expected the plan to be “directional” in nature, with the implementation details for each goal left to annual blueprints.

“It is like setting a destination first. But how do you reach it – by bus, MTR or ferry? That would be reflected in the details of the policy addresses and budgets,” he said, adding that such long-term planning could also ensure policy continuity when a new term of government begins next July.

“Even if there is a new chief executive, he or she will make slight adjustments to the measures in the policy address and budget each year according to the circumstances, but the general direction will not change.”

Why Hong Kong – and why now?

A question simmering amid the discussions is this: why does Hong Kong need a five-year plan now? What is wrong with the way things are currently done?

When Lee began the final year of his term in July, the government already had long-term policies in place in areas such as housing and healthcare. With China having released its 15th five-year plan and Macau already drafting its third, why does Hong Kong need to follow suit?

Shiu Sin-por, former head of the Central Policy Unit, recalled that initiating such a plan had long been regarded as a political taboo.

Before the handover, whenever suggestions emerged that Hong Kong should participate in the national five-year plan, the mainstream counterargument was that “one country, two systems” meant non-interference, he said. There was therefore no need to copy the mainland.

Political veterans said Beijing had assessed the political climate as finally ripe for “institutionalising” long-term planning in Hong Kong. The city was now more stable following the implementation of the national security law and an electoral overhaul after the 2019 anti-government protests, which were aimed at ensuring that only “patriots” govern Hong Kong.

Sonny Lo Shiu-hing, a veteran political commentator specialising in Beijing’s relations with Hong Kong and Macau, explained that the shift in political discourse had allowed Beijing to address Hong Kong’s persistent failure to align itself with national planning cycles.

Political discussions in the city had long focused primarily on maintaining “two systems”. But the paradigm had now shifted towards greater integration with the mainland while making use of the advantages offered by “two systems”, he said.

“More importantly, there’s a strong executive-led system, meaning that the political system should be aligned with the central government’s vision, both economically and politically.”

Will planning dilute the city’s free-market edge?

The impending shift towards a more planned approach has raised a soul-searching question: will Hong Kong’s reputation as a free-market economy suffer? American economist Milton Friedman once called it his “favourite economy”.

In 1978, Nobel laureate Friedman chose Hong Kong as the backdrop for his exploration of free-market economics. He praised the city’s low taxes and lack of state intervention as engines of prosperity, describing its approach as “positive non-interventionism”.

In a recent commentary, former Morgan Stanley Asia chairman Stephen Roach cautioned that “Chinese-style central planning” could often “over-promise and under-deliver”.

His remarks prompted a rebuttal from Deputy Financial Secretary Michael Wong Wai-lun, who wrote in a separate commentary that the critic, whom he did not name, appeared to be driven by anti-China bias and that his views were “neither backed by evidence nor aligned with facts”.

The conflation of planning with a command economy is an issue the government has had to address. During the launch of the consultation exercise in mid-June, Secretary for Constitutional and Mainland Affairs Janice Tse Siu-wa stressed that Hong Kong was not pivoting towards a command economy.

The government “steadfastly adheres to a free-market economy that is market-led and government-facilitated”, she said.

Economists have also pointed out that many countries with different economic models incorporate some form of long-term planning.

Moreover, the idea of a command economy could itself be a relic of the past if viewed through the lens of pre-reform mainland China or the Soviet bloc, where the state strictly controlled production quotas and prices.

This was vastly different from the indicative planning adopted by capitalist economies such as post-war Japan, South Korea and Singapore, where governments provided strategic direction while leaving the allocation of resources to market forces.

During his 1992 tour of southern China, the late paramount leader Deng Xiaoping said that both planning and the market were tools for allocating resources.

“A planned economy is not the same as socialism, as capitalism also involves planning. A market economy is not the same as capitalism, as socialism also involves a market,” Deng said in Zhuhai. His remarks helped accelerate the pace of China’s reform and opening up.

For Hong Kong, some critics have argued that the city was paying the price for its supposed laissez-faire principles. The resulting lack of a comprehensive industrial policy and the absence of strategic coordination, as demonstrated by the early efforts to develop Cyberport and the Science Park, had hobbled the city, they said.

They argued that the “small government, big market” policy that Hong Kong once treated as sacred was outdated, particularly as competing economies had already moved in this direction.

Can strategic planning and free markets coexist?

Lau Siu-kai, a consultant for semi-official think tank the Chinese Association of Hong Kong and Macau Studies, maintained that Hong Kong’s inaugural five-year plan would not alter the essence of its capitalist system.

The government was not attempting to replace private enterprise, commercial capital and professionals as the bedrock of the city’s long-term growth, he stressed.

Politically, he said, the framework would bring numerous benefits to Hong Kong.

For example, it would set a higher benchmark for the city’s leadership by requiring officials to grasp global macroeconomic shifts and national priorities, and to identify precisely where Hong Kong could leverage its unique advantages to drive growth.

“The bureaucratic culture has been focusing on short-term execution instead of visionary foresight,” he said.

“Formulating and executing this first five-year plan offers a steep learning curve, as well as a challenging test, for officials to cultivate a macro-level mindset and elevate strategic thinking, which is key to Hong Kong’s development.”

HKU economist Tang pointed to Asian powerhouses such as Singapore, South Korea and Japan as proof that strategic state guidance and free-market dynamism were not mutually exclusive.

He said these countries had flourished under “very strong governments” with top-down industrial policies while maintaining “open, free and capitalist” economies.

He said the five-year plan was also a crucial step towards helping Hong Kong diversify its economy, generate fresh growth momentum and navigate geopolitical shocks.

“Given the geopolitical turmoil … [we shouldn’t] allow just the global free market to drive us in any direction. And Hong Kong needs to be more resilient and continue to be open. And at the same time, we need to think more strategically about our position in the global economy.”

After all, he said, whether the inaugural plan could achieve its goals would hinge on the rigour of its execution.

“We need specific action plans, clear KPIs across the design, implementation and review stages, and accountability for government officials if targets are missed,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Hong Kong’s 1,000-year-old tea heritage is being rediscovered and rehabilitated
item.description:
Ask a Hongkonger where the city’s tea story begins, and they will probably point to the British – the colonial traders who funnelled Chinese leaves through Victoria Harbour to the world.

Only, they would be off by about eight centuries.

Most Hongkongers today don’t know the city ever had its own tea plantations, let alone that tea had been growing here long before the British arrived in the mid-19th century. Li In, a co-founder of the Hong Kong Tea Production Institute (HKTPI) who has practised the art of tea-making for more than a decade, found out in 2017 – in a London classroom, at the UK Tea Academy.
item.content:encoded:
Ask a Hongkonger where the city’s tea story begins, and they will probably point to the British – the colonial traders who funnelled Chinese leaves through Victoria Harbour to the world.

Only, they would be off by about eight centuries.

Most Hongkongers today don’t know the city ever had its own tea plantations, let alone that tea had been growing here long before the British arrived in the mid-19th century. Li In, a co-founder of the Hong Kong Tea Production Institute (HKTPI) who has practised the art of tea-making for more than a decade, found out in 2017 – in a London classroom, at the UK Tea Academy.

“I was born and raised in Hong Kong and it took a British instructor, Jane Pettigrew, mentioning tea gardens in Lantau for me to first hear about [Hong Kong’s tea heritage],” she says.

Ngong Ping Tea Garden, the plantation in question, on Lantau Island, was founded in 1948 by Brook Bernacchi, a British lawyer and politician who arrived in Hong Kong as a marine with the World War II liberation forces in 1945. He built a life on the plateau near the Po Lin Monastery. His Lotus Brand was marketed as “the only Hong Kong tea”.

By the early 1980s, unable to compete with mass production, the tea plantation area was downsized. After cycling through different hands and functions – a recreational space, a restaurant – the site was eventually abandoned in 2014, its remnants still sitting beneath a pine tree, on a trail south of the Big Buddha – a colonial relic.

Li went looking for it anyway. In March 2023, she and a small group of enthusiasts harvested what they could from the site’s overgrown tea bushes and processed them into a small batch of red and green teas. It didn’t amount to much, but it proved one thing: tea was still growing in Hong Kong, decades after Lotus Brand had folded and the city had moved on.

Li was determined to take local tea cultivation seriously, but she needed more than a ruin. Four months later, her search took her to the upper slopes of Tai Mo Shan, to Kadoorie Farm and Botanic Garden.

Established in 1956 by the Kadoorie brothers as an agricultural aid station for struggling farmers, the 148-hectare sanctuary is widely recognised for its “nature as a classroom” model, welcoming visitors to see its resident animals, wander the terraced gardens and breathe air that doesn’t taste like exhaust fumes. Less known is the fact that Kadoorie has been quietly growing tea on its property since the early 2000s.

Kadoorie’s plantation wasn’t always hidden in plain sight: the farm first brought tea plants over from Ngong Ping in the 70s and 80s, strictly for exhibition. In 2004, the decision to actually grow tea was made, born of a pragmatic desire to fully use the available land. At 400 metres above sea level, the mountainside terrace is a difficult site, plagued by strong winds, thin soil and no reliable water source. Vegetables would struggle in these conditions, the team at Kadoorie assessed. But the same terrain was ideal for tea.

“It was about picking the right plant for the right place,” says Yip Tsz-lam, Kadoorie’s regenerative agriculture manager, who has worked at the farm since 2003. “Of course, we also wanted to continue Hong Kong’s centuries-old tea culture.”

Single-lane and steep, the road up to the terraces is a series of hairpin turns. It takes about 10 minutes by car, before the incline levels out. On our visit, Tai Mo Shan lives up to its colloquial name – “Big Mist Mountain” – its slopes wrapped in clouds so dense the tea bushes in the distance vanish into white.

It’s the kind of climate tea plants dream about. China’s great tea-growing regions, such as Fujian and Yunnan provinces, thrive in similar environments. Mist diffuses the sunlight, slowing photosynthesis to give the leaves time to accumulate amino acids, the compounds that become sweetness and complexity in the cup.

On these terraces are three cultivars, all sourced from Fujian: Ming-fa, Wong-chi-heung and Purple Bud Buddha’s Hand. Many people assume green and red teas come from different plants, when, in fact, they all belong to the same species; the difference is in the processing. Likewise, herbal teas are not tea at all. Only leaves from Camellia sinensis qualify; the rest are tisanes (herbal infusions). What Kadoorie is growing is the real thing.

Of the 2,000 bushes planted in 2004, about half died in the first few years. “We lacked experience with the terrain,” says Yip. But the survivors spread into the gaps and the yield held steady.

Growing the tea, however, was just the start. Kadoorie’s first harvest, in 2008, caught the team off guard. “Our initial amateur attempts resulted in terrible-tasting tea,” Yip recalls.

Kadoorie needed help, and found it closer than they expected. A colleague at the farm’s apiary introduced his mentor, Wong Tung-pui. Si Gung (“Grandmaster”), as he was known, was a Hakka man from Huizhou, in Guangdong province, who came to Hong Kong in the 70s. In his youth, he managed a tea plantation on the mainland and had learned the Hakka tradition of pan-frying leaves by hand.

When Kadoorie approached him, Si Gung was no longer working in agriculture – he kept bees and grew plants for pleasure in the countryside – but he still had the knowledge. “We were lucky to find him,” Yip says. “At that time, finding anyone in Hong Kong who still knew how to manually fry and process tea was incredibly difficult; the broader tea industry, including in mainland China, had already shifted almost entirely to machine-processing.”

Si Gung passed on the pan-frying tradition of his people, a rare skill that has faded even within Hakka communities. Kadoorie adopted it by default. “It wasn’t a planned cultural preservation effort,” Yip says. “It was born out of sheer necessity.”

For the next 15 years, Kadoorie’s tea operation ticked along quietly, following the rhythm of the 24 terms in the solar calendar. Between the winter solstice and Ching Ming in early April, the plants were pruned and fertilised, then the leaves were harvested until the end of the rainy season, usually around the autumn equinox. A limited amount was sold at the farm shop. Kadoorie never thought to promote the tea; they saw no reason to draw attention to something that still felt unfinished.

Connecting with Li and her HKTPI co-founders, Chan Tsz-ting and Season Li Tin-on, gave Kadoorie the downstream partner it needed. Kadoorie would manage the tea-growing and HKTPI would take the leaves further than ever before, experimenting with oxidation levels, producing multiple styles from a single cultivar and bringing the results to the public through workshops. Without them, “a lot of the tea’s potential would be wasted”, Yip says.

Li developed a method she calls “guerrilla tea-making” to process the leaves. On harvest days, the initial withering took place on the farm, in the sunlight. By dusk, the leaves were packed and taken home. In her living room, with no climate-control equipment, she relied entirely on her senses: watching the leaves, feeling the humidity, adjusting each step. “My job is not to decide what the tea tastes like,” she says. “It’s to show what the land, the weather and the leaves are giving us.”

With just the Ming-fa cultivar, Li produced several teas with different characters, evoking Hong Kong’s history as a crossroads of tea cultures, where the toasted-rice notes of Hakka pan-fried green, the floral sweetness of British-style black tea, the intense fragrance of Chaozhou Phoenix Dancong and the roasted oolongs of Fujian had come together and been absorbed.

When Li gave a finished red-tea variant to Ip Wing-chi, founder of Lok Cha Tea House and a doyen of Hong Kong’s tea world, he likened it to Taiwan’s Oriental Beauty. Also known as Dongfang Meiren, Oriental Beauty is one of the most expensive oolong teas in the world – harvests can sell for thousands of dollars per kilogram – so this was no small compliment. But why would a red tea from Tai Mo Shan carry that same oolong note at all?

Plot 107, where the leaves were plucked, held the answer: the buds there were stunted, fibrous and difficult to process. “We investigated and found tea green leafhoppers,” says Li.

Barely visible, the leafhopper’s bite causes the plant to release a chemical defence with a honeyed fragrance: the signature of Oriental Beauty. In Taiwan’s Miaoli and Hsinchu regions, farmers deliberately cultivate these insects. A pest, under the right conditions, became a gift for the tea-makers.

Li had not expected to find leafhoppers thriving on Tai Mo Shan. Warmer temperatures, driven by climate change, scrambled harvest seasons, but it also made the insects more prolific.

“It’s a double-edged sword,” Li says. Leafhoppers trigger the sweet aroma, but they reduce yields to one-fifth of a standard harvest. For a farm already operating at micro scale, the numbers were punishing.

But the trade-off posed an important question: “Do we want volume or quality? Hong Kong has the means and should pursue quality. If we could only produce a plain, characterless tea, producing it here would be meaningless.”

Li does not claim perfection for the “Hong Kong Oriental Beauty”, but the experts have given their verdict. Dr Chen You-ren, former director of the Taiwan Tea Research and Extension Station, and Dr Kim Young-suk, a Korean tea studies professor, were satisfied with the quality. It matters to Li that the validation comes from Asia’s tea-making heartlands: “It gave us confidence that Hong Kong tea can reach the international artisan stage.”

But Li had more in mind than just making good tea – she wanted to know its origins. HKTPI co-founder Chan, a tea historian, had dug through academic papers and Qing dynasty gazetteers in an attempt to map out where Hong Kong’s earliest tea gardens used to be.

His findings rewound the clock by centuries. Hong Kong Society Before the Colonial Era, a 1990 textbook by historian Siu Kwok-kin, described tea cultivation in the New Territories during the Ming dynasty (1368-1644). By 2019, Siu had revised his position, arguing for Song dynasty origins, and Chan found further evidence: Southern Song (1127-1279) records of tea-growing clans migrating to the New Territories and Northern Song (960-1127) tea-ware excavated at Sung Wong Toi, in Kowloon. Compare that to the start of British colonial rule, in 1841 – tea was never just a footnote in Hong Kong’s history.

During the Qing dynasty (1644-1911), the written record started to catch up. An account in the 17th century Guangdong Xinyu encyclopaedia described tea-growing on the cliffs of Bui Dou Saan – present-day Castle Peak – with “the scent of orchid and jasmine, sweet and fragrant”.

By the Jiaqing period (1796-1820), the Xin’an County Gazetteer, a pre-colonial record of the region, had listed four famous teas grown locally: Phoenix Tea, from Lantau’s Phoenix Mountain, harvested by indigenous villagers and prized for its cooling properties; Mung Saan Tea, from Castle Peak, steeped in cloud mist and said to rival its famous Sichuan province namesake; Daam Gon Tea, from Tsing Yi, known for aiding digestion; and Ching Ming Tea, from Tai Lam, a fermented, medicinal tea preserved with salt.

Chan’s research included a 1986 paper by Dr Patrick Hase, a historian specialising in the New Territories. It described Hakka families in Mau Tso Ngam, a village in the foothills of Fei Ngo Shan, who still grew tea, sustaining two centuries of continuous cultivation.

In December 2024, the co-founders went on a “treasure hunt” to Mau Tso Ngam, along the MacLehose Trail, timed to the flowering season of Camellia sinensis so its white blossoms would make surviving tea trees visible. What they found was not a ruin.

A handful of elders remained in Mau Tso Ngam, along with mature tea trees planted decades and centuries ago, by mothers, grandmothers and ancestors. Cheng Kwun-ming, the village head, walked the visitors through the trees, pointing: this one, his mother planted 50 years ago; that one, a woman in her 80s told them, had been there since her father-in-law was alive. He used to carry the leaves across Fei Ngo Shan to Hong Kong Island to sell. Stories unspooled, rooted in the soil, still growing.

One of the villagers still harvesting and processing the leaves is Cheng Hung-ying. Now in her 70s, “Sister Hung” has picked and pan-fried tea since her teens. In her 30s, she cleared a patch of bamboo forest on the slope behind Mau Tso Ngam and planted tea trees. “Her mother could only drink the village’s own tea,” Li says. “So, that’s why she started. It was an act of care.”

“Cheng [the village head] always asks me the same question,” Li recalls. “‘What do you taste?’ And I tell him about the aroma, the sweetness, the body. And he says, ‘No. It’s yan ching mei [the taste of connection and community].’”

Somewhere along the way, Li’s search for Hong Kong’s forgotten tea had become a search for herself. Last year, while consulting with Lam Man-ying, director of the Hong Kong Hakka Association, to gather context on Mau Tso Ngam, the conversation turned to her family background. As they mapped out her grandfather’s village, the pieces clicked: Li is of Hakka descent. She has, unknowingly, spent years chasing her own heritage.

Li keeps returning to Mau Tso Ngam. On another visit, Sister Hung shows her the Hakka pan-frying process from start to finish.

Moving through her tea trees with ease and familiarity, Sister Hung demonstrates how to pick the bud and the two youngest leaves, pinched clean with a flick of the wrist.

Back in the village, at an outdoor wok set-up weathered by years of use, she gets the fire going in just a few minutes, using wood she chopped herself, from behind the small row of houses, most of them now uninhabited. In the three hours it takes to pan-fry the leaves, one person tends the fire, the other keeps the leaves moving to stop them from burning. She uses no thermometer, no timer – only her hands and decades of instinct.

With the wok at around 300 degrees Celsius, Sister Hung works fast to saat ching (“kill the green”), using a Y-shaped wooden tool passed down from her father. Next, she rolls the leaves back and forth on a bamboo withering tray with her gloved palms – the same motion as kneading dough – until the cell walls break down and the juices coat the surface, so the flavour can build.

Finally, the leaves return to the wok at a lower heat. With her bare hands, she turns them, lifting and dropping, pressing and spreading, for the better part of two hours. If she loses the rhythm, the batch is ruined.

Sister Hung no longer lives in Mau Tso Ngam year-round, but she comes back to pan-fry tea and make alkaline rice dumplings, another Hakka tradition recognised as part of Hong Kong’s intangible cultural heritage. She is the last person in her family who knows how to do it.

“My children didn’t want to learn; they don’t even want to try the tea I pan-fry any more,” she says. “I come back every year anyway. It has become a ritual for me.”

Li, who trained in Taiwan, Japan and Britain, understands the science of oxidation, amino acids and catechins. But what Sister Hung knows is held in the body, passed down through years of watching and copying until the skill becomes instinct.

“My job is to understand her, to turn what she knows into something we can replicate, to carry forward the culture,” says Li.

When the village head learned that Li and her team worked with Kadoorie, he welcomed them without hesitation. In the 50s and 60s, the Kadoorie Agricultural Aid Association supported Hakka farmers across the New Territories; the trust already existed.

HKTPI is reviving that decades-old partnership for a new purpose. Mau Tso Ngam’s tea trees represent a living gene bank of cultivars that have adapted to Hong Kong’s terroir. If the ageing tea-makers can’t tend to them, the genetic knowledge will be lost.

Last November, HKTPI invited the villagers to Kadoorie Farm and Botanic Garden to plant saplings from Mau Tso Ngam’s heritage trees, bringing their cultivars into Kadoorie’s conservation infrastructure.

“We’re not reviving a lost craft,” Li says. “We’re a bridge. One end connects to the tea traditions Hakka ancestors cultivated; the other end connects to the present, the land, what’s still here.”

HKTPI and Kadoorie now co-host workshops where the public can harvest leaves from the terraces and try their hand at traditional pan-frying. At the Hong Kong International Tea Fair 2024, they poured cups of Tai Mo Shan tea for visitors who did not believe the city could produce anything worth drinking.

Some visitors asked what the point was. Even if the tea were good, what did a few kilograms from a mountainside matter? It’s true that Kadoorie’s harvests are too limited to sustain widespread commercial production. But Chan has greater ambitions than just retail growth: “Our dream is that one day, when foreign dignitaries visit the city, the tea they are served is ours.”

Inspired by her findings, Li is building another stage: the Hakka Tea Theatre, a clear expression of her role as a “translator”. Here, the tea served is Hakka pan-fried green, the food is Hakka yellow-wine chicken, the stories are from Mau Tso Ngam and the crafts are local. But the format is British afternoon tea.

The project mirrors her own trajectory, from running a British-style tearoom in Mong Kok, training overseas in various tea cultures, to serving tea at a consulate in London. She understands both lexicons – the formal precision of a Western tea service and the embodied knowledge of a Hakka village. At the Tea Theatre, the two meet. “I’m not asking people to choose between Chinese and Western,” she says. “I’m showing them that the tea doesn’t belong to either. It belongs to the land it came from.”

Chan thinks about the future in two timelines. In five years, HKTPI will have the resources to sustain the partnership with Kadoorie, safeguard tea-making traditions in Mau Tso Ngam, explore other forgotten tea plantations and stage more Hakka Tea Theatre experiments. In 10 years, a younger generation will join them, “to inherit the culture, the technique and the vision of this land”.

Li had learned, through a serendipitous journey, that this land belongs to her, too. She had started in a London classroom, followed the trail through an abandoned colonial plantation, up a misty mountain and into a tiny village that had never stopped making tea, and found herself inside the story she was chasing.

“Letting the next generation know that Hong Kong has this history is not just about tea,” Li says. “It’s the confidence of knowing that we are not rootless; we carry something we can be proud of.”

[Correction: An earlier version identified Cheng Sui-wing as the village head who welcomed the visitors to Mau Tso Ngam. It has been amended to Cheng Kwun-ming, who also serves as the village head for Mau Tso Ngam, alongside Cheng Sui-wing.]

item.title: [SCMP] How China got caught in the crossfire of a US bacon fight
item.description:
Midwestern Americans watching television this summer may have been surprised to see China and bacon appearing together in political advertisements.

“The corrupt Save Our Bacon scam in the farm bill – it’s a giveaway to Chinese corporations,” one advertisement declared over images of the Chinese flag and Chinese President Xi Jinping. “Whose side is your senator on? America or China?”

Viewers might assume the advertisement was promoting yet another Republican-led effort to counter Beijing.
item.content:encoded:
Midwestern Americans watching television this summer may have been surprised to see China and bacon appearing together in political advertisements.

“The corrupt Save Our Bacon scam in the farm bill – it’s a giveaway to Chinese corporations,” one advertisement declared over images of the Chinese flag and Chinese President Xi Jinping. “Whose side is your senator on? America or China?”

Viewers might assume the advertisement was promoting yet another Republican-led effort to counter Beijing.

The reality is far more complicated.

Behind the aggressive campaign against the Save Our Bacon Act lies a fight over how pigs are housed – and perhaps the latest example of China being weaponised in US domestic politics.

The bill has created an unexpected collision of animal welfare, agricultural regulation and America’s growing political anxiety over China, with opponents accusing a Republican-backed farm measure of putting a Chinese-owned pork giant ahead of American farmers.

What is the Save Our Bacon Act?

The controversy traces back to California’s Proposition 12, which voters approved in 2018. The measure established minimum space requirements for breeding pigs and prohibited the sale of pork from animals raised below those standards, forcing producers nationwide either to modify their operations or risk losing access to one of the country’s largest markets.

The US Supreme Court upheld the measure in 2023 after legal challenges.

The economic impact of California’s law has become a key point of contention. A recent North Dakota State University study found that Proposition 12 was associated with a roughly 73-cent-per-pound increase in California’s retail pork price premium after full enforcement. Researchers estimated that consumers in California and Massachusetts, both of which have similar animal-confinement laws, spent an additional US$403 million on pork from 2024 to 2026.

Pork producers have argued that constructing Proposition 12-compliant housing could cost as much as US$4,000 per sow, a burden that could weigh particularly heavily on smaller family farms.

Enter the Save Our Bacon Act. Introduced by congresswoman Ashley Hinson of Iowa, the legislation would overturn Proposition 12’s requirements for pork sold in California.

Hinson, who is running for Senate and has secured the Republican nomination, has argued that the measure would protect interstate commerce for Iowa livestock producers by preventing one state from imposing production standards on farmers in another while preserving states’ authority to regulate their own producers.

Opponents, led by the American Meat Producers Association (AMPA), have launched a national campaign against the new bill in Congress.

“Farmers have built their lives and communities on fair, responsible farming,” AMPA said in a statement on its website. “If Congress eliminates these laws, those livelihoods will vanish, supply chains will shatter, and rural towns will lose the people who fuel their economy.”

AMPA was formed in late 2025 and led by Holly Bice, a government relations professional with experience lobbying on agriculture and animal welfare. The group has launched a US$30 million campaign targeting lawmakers in the Midwest over the Save Our Bacon Act.

Hinson has accused the group of being backed by meat companies that have already spent millions of dollars transitioning to Proposition 12-compliant facilities, giving them a financial stake in preserving and expanding such mandates across state lines and limiting competitors’ ability to operate under conventional production standards.

It is unclear who is funding the US$30 million campaign. Federal Election Commission filings show that the American Meat Producers PAC, an affiliated political committee, had raised about US$55,000 and spent about US$8,000 by the end of June. The filings list individual donors from across the country, including a US$5,000 contribution from Bice herself.

The campaign’s advertisements, targeting Midwestern states, have also attracted over a million views on YouTube.

Hinson, AMPA and Bice did not respond to requests for comment.

Why is China involved?

AMPA has transformed the debate into something much larger, arguing that the legislation would ultimately benefit Chinese corporations – an apparent reference to Smithfield Foods, America’s largest pork producer.

Smithfield, based in Virginia, was acquired in 2013 by WH Group, formerly known as Shuanghui International, a Chinese company listed in Hong Kong.

That acquisition, completed more than a decade ago, sits at the centre of the current political battle, as AMPA’s ads portray the legislation as a handout to Chinese-owned corporations rather than a measure intended to help American farmers.

Ray Atkinson, a spokesperson for Smithfield, said the company believes animal-welfare standards should be based on science and veterinary expertise, rather than voter initiatives.

“The reason we oppose Prop 12 is that it has raised pork prices for consumers and doesn’t objectively improve animal welfare,” Atkinson said. “The Save Our Bacon Act would prevent individual states from creating a patchwork of livestock production practices that make it difficult to keep food affordable for all Americans.”

Atkinson did not directly address how much of Smithfield’s production complies with Proposition 12. He said the company has established supply agreements for Proposition 12-compliant pork and is willing to work with retail and food service customers to expand the availability of compliant products.

The National Pork Producers Council (NPPC), one of the Save Our Bacon Act’s strongest supporters, told the South China Morning Post that AMPA’s campaign is an activist-driven effort, and pointed to a June statement describing the group’s claims as “baseless”.

In a video interview with Farm Journal in June, NPPC president Rob Brenneman said that AMPA’s campaign “is a lie”.

“It’s not about China. It’s not about any foreign-owned company,” Brenneman said. “It’s about livestock production in general and the consumption of meat in the United States, and they want to eliminate that, plain and simple.”

Smithfield, which raised about 550,000 sows in 2025, is a major player in the NPPC, with two company representatives currently serving on its board. NPPC says it represents more than 60,000 US pork producers. AMPA has not disclosed its membership, but its website features a handful of individual farmers supporting Proposition 12.

Hinson has similarly slammed AMPA as a radical animal rights activists, arguing that misinformation campaigns have falsely suggested the legislation would benefit foreign-owned corporations or harm American producers. Hinson’s Senate campaign is also being scrutinised over donations it received from organisations linked to Smithfield.

The Chinese embassy in Washington said that investment by Chinese companies in the United States had contributed to employment and economic growth while criticising the politicisation of mutually beneficial economic and trade relations.

“Actions and rhetoric that overstretch the concept of national security and politicise economic, trade and investment issues run counter to market economy principles and international trade rules,” the spokesperson said. “They undermine confidence in the US market environment and harm the interests of the American people themselves.”

China as an easy political target

The fight over the Save Our Bacon Act reflects a broader reality in American politics: invoking China has become one of the most effective ways to frame a political argument.

According to the Chicago Council on Global Affairs’ latest survey, 50 per cent of Americans view China’s rise as a critical threat to the United States, a figure that rises to 66 per cent among Republicans, making China a politically convenient target in domestic campaigns.

Democrats have embraced the same line of attack. The Iowa Democratic Party published a blog post titled: “Ashley Hinson Is ‘Holding Up the Farm Bill’ With Her Pro-China Save Our Bacon Act.”

The controversy also mirrors a political battle over Chinese ownership of American agricultural assets.

Filers whose primary investor was China reported owning 247,659 acres of US agricultural land as of December 31, 2024, according to the US Department of Agriculture. That represents roughly 0.5 per cent of the 46.3 million acres of farmland held by foreign investors nationwide.

Two of the five largest Chinese-linked landholders in the country are Smithfield entities, Murphy-Brown LLC and Murphy-Brown of Missouri, together accounting for roughly 40 per cent of all Chinese-held US farmland.

Congress has tried to address those concerns. The Protecting American Agriculture From Foreign Adversaries Act would expand federal oversight of farmland purchases by entities linked to countries such as China. But the legislation remains stalled in Congress.

The fate of the Save Our Bacon Act remains uncertain.

The House passed the measure as part of its farm bill in April, but the Senate version does not include it, and the Senate Agriculture Committee failed to advance its legislation before the August recess. Any final version would have to be negotiated if lawmakers eventually reconcile the two bills.

But the political lesson may already be clear: in today’s America, even a fight over how pigs are housed can quickly become a debate over China.

item.title: [SCMP] Will Washington’s tech crackdown test fragile US-China truce?
item.description:
Ahead of next month’s expected summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Washington, a low profile US regulatory agency has opened a new front in the technology battle between the world’s two superpowers, even as it attempts to avoid sabotaging the vital high-stakes meeting.

The latest action by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) in July saw it advance stringent bans on new Chinese robots and power inverters.

The move came after months of FCC measures that did not prompt a direct retaliatory response from Beijing, even as the agency continued to expand its restrictions.
item.content:encoded:
Ahead of next month’s expected summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Washington, a low profile US regulatory agency has opened a new front in the technology battle between the world’s two superpowers, even as it attempts to avoid sabotaging the vital high-stakes meeting.

The latest action by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) in July saw it advance stringent bans on new Chinese robots and power inverters.

The move came after months of FCC measures that did not prompt a direct retaliatory response from Beijing, even as the agency continued to expand its restrictions.

Although China held its fire ahead of the last Trump-Xi summit in May, that restraint appears to have ended following the FCC’s latest steps.

Beijing’s retaliation last week – imposing drone export controls and sanctioning US testing firms – signalled the expansion of an already crowded field of tit-for-tat actions involving tariffs, export controls and the blacklisting of each other’s companies.

Former senior FCC officials defended the agency’s national security mandate to protect US technology sectors and communication networks from Chinese influence.

But analysts said these aggressive regulatory moves highlighted a delicate balancing act for the Trump administration, which is seeking to curb Chinese presence without shattering the fragile trade truce brokered last October.

Experts argued the FCC offers the administration a relatively low profile tool to advance its technology agenda, targeting specific sectors, equipment categories and approval processes rather than relying on broad tariffs or export controls. Its existing regulatory authority also allows it to act through national-security and communications rules.

However, they cautioned that the approach could increase the chances of missteps.

“Securing the nation’s networks has always been a priority,” Tom Wheeler, the FCC chairman from 2013-2017, said in an email to the South China Morning Post.

“The Trump administration may be trying to restrict Chinese tech products without upsetting the Busan trade truce,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the John L. Thornton China Centre at the Brookings Institution.

“There is certainly a risk of miscalculation here,” he added.

FCC spearheads China crackdown

The FCC has quietly emerged as one of the Trump administration’s most aggressive agencies targeting Chinese technology companies on national security grounds, even as other departments, including Commerce and Treasury, have taken a back seat.

Under Chairman Brendan Carr, the agency has pursued a two-pronged strategy: combining targeted measures against individual Chinese companies with sweeping, category-wide bans and supply-chain restrictions.

In April, it advanced a proposal to ban Chinese telecoms operators – China Mobile, China Telecom and China Unicom – from operating data centres in the US.

It also moved to bar Hong Kong telecoms carrier HKT International from operating in America, with Carr asserting that “CCP-controlled entities that pose national security risks to our country cannot connect to our telecom networks.”

That salvo followed a move in December last year, when the agency implemented a series of sector-wide crackdowns, including a stringent ban on imports of new Chinese drones, followed by restrictions on new models of consumer routers in May and robotics and power inverters in July.

The products were among those targeted by the FCC’s Covered List, which identifies communications equipment and services deemed to pose an unacceptable risk to US national security.

“Advanced robotic devices collect data that could be leveraged by malign actors to surveil Americans, enhance the capabilities of foreign intelligence services, or to remotely commandeer the robots,” the FCC said after announcing the robotics ban in July.

Additionally, it advanced a proposal to ban what it calls Chinese “bad labs” from testing electronic devices headed to the US. According to the agency, around 75 per cent of all US electronics are tested in China.

“Some of those labs themselves were linked or controlled by or tied to the PLA [People’s Liberation Army], so not necessarily the most trustworthy,” Carr told TBPN, a technology-focused online network, earlier this month.

“We’re now inserting national security checks in that lab process.”

The agency has increasingly invoked national security to justify measures targeting Chinese companies and technology across the US communications and technology ecosystem.

In March last year, Carr launched the FCC’s Council on National Security to “promote America’s national security and counter foreign adversaries.”

“Today, the country faces a persistent and constant threat from foreign adversaries, particularly the CCP,” Carr said at the time.

In response to a query from the SCMP, an FCC spokesperson said that “Covered List actions are country-neutral and apply to all foreign-produced devices that meet the criteria.”

“The FCC will continue to be in lockstep with the entire administration to protect Americans from foreign threats and make sure that the United States is in the best position to deliver on President Trump’s vision to lead the world on the next generation of technologies,” the spokesperson added.

The Chinese embassy in Washington did not respond to a request for comment.

Trump has repeatedly used the national security rationale to justify policies ranging from border fencing and mass deportations to tariffs, domestic energy policy and timber harvesting on federal land.

Analysts and legal scholars argue that “crying wolf” – using “national security” as a pretext for political expediency – risks undermining faith in institutions and eroding trust if a genuine catastrophe strikes.

However, Wheeler asserted that protecting national security is a core mandate of the FCC, noting: “National security is a Section One responsibility of the FCC, meaning the first section of the Communications Act.”

The FCC was established in 1934 under the Communications Act, which states that the commission was created “for the purpose of the national defence” and “for the purpose of promoting safety of life and property through the use of wire and radio communications”.

Rachelle Chong, a former FCC commissioner, argued that the agency’s council on national security “centralises the effort across multiple bureaus” and “expressly treats strategic competition with China as an organising agency priority”.

“The FCC’s national-security role is both older and broader than many people realise,” she said.

She described the first Trump administration as an “important turning point”, pointing to the FCC’s denial of China Mobile’s application, restrictions on the use of federal universal-service funds for Chinese tech companies Huawei and ZTE equipment, and the establishment of the Covered List and removal-and-replacement programme.

“Over the last decade, the FCC’s role has evolved from reviewing individual foreign entrants to protecting the communications supply chain as a whole,” Chong said.

Chan, of the Brookings Institution, noted that the FCC has emerged “as an increasingly popular tool for restricting Chinese tech products”.

“It can act relatively swiftly compared with other government restrictions,” he said, adding that the administration “appears to be making moves designed to operate below the threshold of upsetting the Busan truce”.

“The FCC is further away from trade negotiations with China compared with Commerce and Treasury.”

After months of escalation marked by high tariffs and China’s restrictions on rare earths, the two sides reached a one-year arrangement in Busan, South Korea, last year under which Washington agreed to suspend additional export controls in exchange for continued flows of critical minerals from Beijing.

Under the arrangement, the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) suspended its Affiliates Rule, which had expanded export restrictions to companies owned 50 per cent or more by entities on the Entity List, and has not added new Chinese entities to the list since last October.

While the Busan understanding was reaffirmed during the Trump-Xi summit in May, both sides have kept the pot simmering with tit-for-tat actions without allowing tensions to spiral, particularly ahead of Xi’s expected visit to the US next month.

After more than a year of refraining from directly retaliating against FCC actions, China’s response last week went beyond the tighter drone export controls to include sanctions against seven US companies and Beijing’s first foreign trade-related national security investigation.

“I assess it as a shot across the bow, especially as the FCC actions began to add up,” said Sourabh Gupta, the head of the Trade and Technology programme at the Institute for China-America Studies.

“You could call it a case of the ‘new normal’ in ties taking shape, one uncoupling at a time.”

Chan argued that there is a “risk of miscalculation” where a “relatively minor action by Washington may be interpreted as a major escalation by Beijing”.

However, according to Gupta, the FCC’s “nicks and cuts” are just “a small sting each time”.

“The very fact that the administration took recourse to the FCC in the first place rather than have Commerce’s BIS issue the order – say, by dumping the Chinese vendor on the Entity List – itself suggests that the administration is attentive to avoiding miscalculation.”

item.title: [SCMP] Wang Yi heads to Seoul as Trump cuts South Korea drills, opening door for China
item.description:
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi is set to visit Seoul days after Donald Trump called for the US to scale back military exercises with South Korea, sending ripples of unease through American allies in Asia.

The US president posted his decision to social media on Sunday, raising questions about the durability of Washington’s security commitments in a region increasingly defined by competition with Beijing.

He offered several rationales, including cost-saving considerations, a goodwill gesture towards North Korea, and dissatisfaction with Seoul’s refusal to join the US in the war against Iran.
item.content:encoded:
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi is set to visit Seoul days after Donald Trump called for the US to scale back military exercises with South Korea, sending ripples of unease through American allies in Asia.

The US president posted his decision to social media on Sunday, raising questions about the durability of Washington’s security commitments in a region increasingly defined by competition with Beijing.

He offered several rationales, including cost-saving considerations, a goodwill gesture towards North Korea, and dissatisfaction with Seoul’s refusal to join the US in the war against Iran.

Observers said such moves threatened to damage alliance coordination, causing disquiet among regional partners and handing China a strategic opening to dilute America’s network of regional partnerships.

Trump posted on Sunday that he had instructed the Pentagon to scale back what he termed “inappropriate and hostile” military drills with South Korea – exercises traditionally aimed at deterring North Korea, a country he described as “unthreatening and respectful” during his time in office.

He added that he had ordered the US defence secretary to “substantially reduce” the drills, citing Seoul’s reluctance to support America’s efforts towards the “denuclearisation of the Islamic Republic of Iran”.

As Seoul and other US partners navigate the latest shocks, Wang will begin a two-day trip to Seoul on Wednesday, his first bilateral exchange trip in five years.

Trump’s call for reduced commitment came just hours before Washington and Seoul launched the 11-day Ulchi Freedom Shield drills, one of the two major annual exercises.

Lee Dong-gyu, a senior research fellow at The Asan Institute for Policy Studies, said Trump’s statements revealed his willingness to trade alliance security for political gains, such as re-engagement with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, a calculation Lee said would increase Seoul’s trust deficit in its alliance with Washington.

William Yang, senior analyst for Northeast Asia at the International Crisis Group, said the statement matched Trump’s usual playbook of signalling frustration towards allies he viewed as failing to respond to US demands for support.

“While the order may be a tactical move from the US, it could undermine long-standing trust between the two countries and prompt Seoul to put more resources into hedging between Beijing and Washington,” he said.

Leif-Eric Easley, professor of international studies at Ewha Womans University in Seoul, said that curtailing joint manoeuvres risked undermining operational coordination and weakening deterrence against possible conflicts in Asia.

Experts noted that the latest remarks would unnerve regional partners such as the Philippines and Japan, saying their frictions with China left them particularly exposed.

Trump has regularly criticised US allies during his second term, intensifying concerns over the reliability of Washington’s commitments and pushing partners towards self-reliance and strategic hedging.

However, in a sign of reassurance, the US undersecretary of defence for policy, Elbridge Colby, used his first Southeast Asia tour last week to stress that Washington was not disengaging from Asia but “digging in” to maintain a favourable balance of power in the Indo-Pacific.

But he added that Washington was prioritising burden-sharing as it realised its allies “can and are prepared to do more”.

According to Yang, Washington’s allies will bear in mind the more transactional foreign policy outlook that Trump subscribes to and try to respond to demands from Washington.

Meanwhile, Lee noted that Beijing was likely to exploit the scaled-back exercises as a tool, seeking to constrain Seoul’s participation in the US alliance network and diminish America’s military footprint in the region.

“At the same time, leveraging its friendly ties with Pyongyang, China is likely to intensify both its appeasement and pressure on South Korea under the pretext of fostering a favourable environment for US-North Korea dialogue,” Lee said.

Trump’s directive has sparked anticipation of his renewed engagement with Kim, although it remains uncertain whether the North Korean leader will reciprocate – particularly as Pyongyang appears to hold more cards than at the last summits with Trump in 2018 and 2019.

Following his summit with Kim in Singapore in June 2018, Trump abruptly suspended major joint military exercises with South Korea, calling them provocative, inappropriate and too expensive.

But since the collapse of high-level diplomacy in 2019, Pyongyang has aggressively expanded its missile tests and gained more battlefield experience by sending its soldiers to take part in the Russia-Ukraine war.

Lee Choong-koo, a research fellow at the Korea Institute for Defence Analyses, said Trump’s directive was part of a broader US diplomatic charm offensive towards North Korea – one that might require China’s cooperation.

Seoul has long expected Beijing to play a role in bringing Pyongyang back to the negotiation table, as Pyongyang neglects Seoul’s repeated calls to improve inter-Korean relations.

“His move may encourage greater diplomatic engagement between the US and China on North Korea,” Lee Choong-koo said, adding that Beijing might welcome Trump’s announcement.

“With Foreign Minister Wang Yi expected to visit Seoul this week, China may emphasise that its support is essential to advancing South Korea’s diplomatic initiative to launch multilateral peace talks.”

On Monday, Trump told reporters that Kim had responded to his recent overtures and described the current state of communication as “very positive”. Kim has not yet commented publicly.

Easley, however, offered a more sceptical assessment. He argued that Pyongyang was not interested in talking because it was profiting from Russia’s war on Ukraine while modernising its own military.

“The Trump administration’s ongoing difficulties negotiating with Iran do not enhance its credibility with the Kim regime.”

Meanwhile, some observers pointed out that Trump’s announcement could further weaken US-led deterrence against China – a development that might work in Beijing’s favour.

The mismatch between US strategic documents on defending the first island chain and Trump’s decision on joint drills with South Korea would strengthen regional countries’ belief that they needed to adopt risk-reduction measures against the US, Yang said.

“This trend will benefit China, as it creates an opportunity for Beijing to drive a wedge between the US and its regional allies.”

The first island chain consists of several strategic arcs – stretching from Japan and Taiwan through the Philippines to Borneo – that underpin a US-aligned security architecture to check Beijing.

Although traditionally not viewed as part of the chain, South Korea, now hosting some 28,500 US troops under a decades-old alliance, is increasingly seen as the northern anchor of the chain’s defence network.

item.title: [SCMP] Singapore’s universities race to embrace AI as job demands transform
item.description:
After years of concern over students using artificial intelligence to cut corners, Singapore’s universities are embracing the technology, driven not just by changes in the classroom but by pressure to prepare graduates for an economy that increasingly prizes AI literacy.

But analysts say educators still face the challenge of ensuring students use AI to sharpen their critical thinking rather than relying on it for quick answers and guidance.

On August 11, the National University of Singapore (NUS) announced that its students and faculty members would have access to ChatGPT Edu, an enterprise-grade platform by OpenAI, from August 31.
item.content:encoded:
After years of concern over students using artificial intelligence to cut corners, Singapore’s universities are embracing the technology, driven not just by changes in the classroom but by pressure to prepare graduates for an economy that increasingly prizes AI literacy.

But analysts say educators still face the challenge of ensuring students use AI to sharpen their critical thinking rather than relying on it for quick answers and guidance.

On August 11, the National University of Singapore (NUS) announced that its students and faculty members would have access to ChatGPT Edu, an enterprise-grade platform by OpenAI, from August 31.

The platform would be piloted in selected courses during the initial phase and be progressively made available for other courses where AI “adds educational value and augments learning objectives”, the university said in a statement.

Other universities are also expanding the use of the technology, with many mandating AI literacy courses.

Starting this month, students at the Nanyang Technological University (NTU) were given full access to a suite of Google AI tools, including Gemini Enterprise, as part of what the institution coined an “ambitious effort to transform its undergraduate education with AI”.

The university aimed to embed AI into 40 per cent of its courses by 2030, to reach its goal of producing students who could create and work with AI agents, it said.

“So much is happening so quickly with AI, and universities are playing catch up,” said Reuben Ng, an associate professor at the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy.

There was a huge skills gap in the employment market, with many job notices requiring AI skills left unfilled, he said. “One of the key purposes of Singapore’s universities is to funnel people towards the job market, so they need to create students that have these skill sets.”

Vijayakumar Tangarasan, International Workplace Group’s country head for Malaysia, Singapore and Brunei, said most local employers were willing to “pay a premium” for AI literacy, and academic qualifications alone were no longer the focus.

“Singapore’s modern workforce demands a symbiotic combination of technological literacy and irreplaceable human qualities,” he said, highlighting the importance of technological and human skills.

“As AI becomes increasingly embedded in our daily workflows, the traditional checklist for talent is being rewritten.”

AI paradox

While critics in the education field have long worried that generative technology is eroding critical thinking, Singapore’s universities seem to have a change of heart on AI.

Aaron Thean, NUS’s deputy president of academic affairs and provost, said the institution aimed to use the tools not as replacements, but as “powerful amplifiers of human intellect, creativity and judgement”.

While the goals set out are achievable, whether AI proves a boon or bane largely depends on how it is used, according to educational experts.

If a student were to accept the first output from the prompt, the tool would become a substitute for thinking, said Ina Conradi Chavez, an associate professor at NTU’s School of Art, Design and Media. But if students were to reject, re-prompt and critique, the technology would help refine thinking, she added.

Still, Conradi highlighted several risks, such as the inability to discern AI-generated content from authorship and the acceptance of visually plausible but incorrect output.

Mutlu Cukurova, the 18th CJ Koh professor at NTU’s National Institute of Education, acknowledged that current evidence showed the technology posed more harm, potentially leading to stagnant and declining competency levels. Recent research also found that it reduced persistence, with students instinctively turning to AI to solve difficult problems, he added.

But Cukurova said AI could have a positive impact if the system were built to ask, rather than answer or solve. “Intellect, creativity and critical thinking are not by-products of access to capable tools, but outcomes of deliberate design.”

Conradi urged institutions to teach students to use AI to examine bias and train data, rather than primarily for generative or interpretive purposes. “Students who only use AI generatively will be replaced by the next generation of tools and those who learn to interrogate AI critically will not.”

She highlighted that not all AI-assisted works should be put in the same box, noting the difference in user effort between continuously refining prompts and accepting the first output.

“Public conversation collapses everything into a single category called ‘AI art’ or ‘AI use’. That framing does real damage,” she said. “The paradox is real, but often framed the wrong way.”

Evolving assessments

With chatbots producing polished essays and high-definition visuals within seconds, concerns about plagiarism and integrity have also surged.

Last year, three NTU students were penalised for academic misconduct and given zero marks for an assignment after they were found to have used generative AI tools. Their assignments had contained non-existent academic references and statistics or broken web links.

Surveillance and detection were a “losing battle”, said Curukova, who is also a professor of learning and AI at University College London.

He urged institutions to design tasks that would require students to interact with and evaluate AI and its output. “A graduate who can prompt well but cannot judge when the output is wrong, or when the task should not have been delegated at all, is not AI-competent,” he said.

NTU will be moving away from automated surveillance to assessment designs that evaluate student learning, according to local media, citing an email from the institution to its faculty last Thursday.

Recognising that the detection tools used currently were “fundamentally unreliable”, the university said it would stop using them next year.

Conradi has already shifted her assessment focus. She now evaluates her students based on documentation and oral explanations, rather than the final product alone. Her students are asked to present their works on screens or at exhibitions, and she studies how they adapt conversations about their submissions to different audiences.

She also requires students to detail their use of AI, including exact prompts, rejections and reasoning behind each input.

“Assessment built around the finished artefact alone is increasingly meaningless,” she said. “The principle is now to assess the practice, not just the product.”

Ng noted that AI had sparked a return to the pen-and-paper format in physical settings, a method which he had adopted with his students.

“There needs to be a space where people do deep thinking and work, such as journaling with a pen and paper, debating or reflecting,” he said. “We need protected time for these things which cannot be replaced by technology.”

item.title: [SCMP] Trump’s decision to scale back South Korea drills unsettles Asian allies: ‘makes no sense’
item.description:
President Donald Trump’s decision to scale back joint military exercises with South Korea does not just slight a long-time ally but raises broader concerns about the security interests of the United States in Asia and elsewhere.

Trump explained his decision by citing South Korea’s refusal to join his war against Iran and pointing to what he said was his good relationship with North Korea’s reclusive dictator Kim Jong-un, a transactional and personal approach to foreign policy that has defined the Republican’s presidency.

“There is no American interest that I can see in this,” said Dan Fried, an assistant secretary of state for European affairs in the George W. Bush administration. “On all levels it makes no sense. It undermines the South Koreans, undermines the Japanese, frightens the Taiwanese, unnerves Nato and emboldens the Chinese, not to mention the North Koreans.”
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump’s decision to scale back joint military exercises with South Korea does not just slight a long-time ally but raises broader concerns about the security interests of the United States in Asia and elsewhere.

Trump explained his decision by citing South Korea’s refusal to join his war against Iran and pointing to what he said was his good relationship with North Korea’s reclusive dictator Kim Jong-un, a transactional and personal approach to foreign policy that has defined the Republican’s presidency.

“There is no American interest that I can see in this,” said Dan Fried, an assistant secretary of state for European affairs in the George W. Bush administration. “On all levels it makes no sense. It undermines the South Koreans, undermines the Japanese, frightens the Taiwanese, unnerves Nato and emboldens the Chinese, not to mention the North Koreans.”

Trump’s decision to side with North Korea, which strongly objects to the annual joint military exercises, was “firmly in the ‘hard-to see-how-it-could-be-worse’ category”, said Danny Russel, former assistant secretary of state for East Asia and the Pacific in Barack Obama’s administration.

Trump is punishing an ally while encouraging an adversary

Danny Russel, a scholar at the Asia Society Policy Institute

“It is tragically upside-down. Trump is punishing an ally while encouraging an adversary,” said Russel, now a scholar at the Asia Society Policy Institute in New York. “He is protecting Kim Jong-un’s sensitive feelings from an unfriendly signal at the expense of US-South Korean security.”

Trump on Sunday ordered the US military to downsize the 11-day Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises, which began on Monday as scheduled. It is not known which parts of the training are being scaled back.

His announcement baffled many in South Korea, which has been closely allied with the US for decades and where national security is a top priority due to threats from nuclear-armed North Korea.

It also drew instant criticism from many Democrats in Congress. “Treating one of America’s closest allies like an adversary weakens our alliances and benefits China and North Korea,” Representative Greg Meeks of New York, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said in a statement.

Japanese Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said Tuesday Tokyo strongly supported joint security cooperation with key defence backer Washington and neighbour Seoul.

“As Japan faces the most severe and complicated security environment in the post-war era, the cooperation among Japan, the United States and South Korea is critical to the peace and stability of the region,” Koizumi said during a visit to Australia.

His Australian counterpart, Richard Marles, said Canberra was “very concerned about North Korea’s nuclear programme as well as its missile programme, and we have consistently made that point”.

South Korean officials have said the exercises had begun as planned and that they hoped the personal chemistry between Trump and Kim would bring them back to talks. Seoul’s presidential office said on Tuesday the drills did not reflect “any intention to attack North Korea or escalate tensions on the Korean peninsula”.

Its unification ministry – responsible for relations with the North – said it could not confirm whether communications between Kim and Trump had taken place. “While communication channels between the two sides exist, we cannot verify the specific content of the exchanges,” it said.

‘Great respect’

Trump on Monday doubled down, posting a photo of North Korea’s leader speaking on a phone. The caption read: “Hey Donald … We cool, right?”

Asked by a reporter in the Oval Office on Monday if Kim had replied to entreaties for talks, Trump said “he has”, without elaborating. The president called the development “very positive”. The White House declined to provide further details.

“Kim Jong-un has always treated me with great respect,” Trump said. “I understand him; he understands me.”

Retired US Ambassador Robert Wood, who served under Republican and Democratic presidents, said the joint military exercises were critical to deterring North Korea, which has shunned any talks with the US over its nuclear programme and has accelerated weapons testing.

“We also don’t want South Korea to draw the conclusion that a nuclear weapons capability is the only guarantee it has to ensure its security,” Wood said.

Matthew Kroenig, who previously served in defence and intelligence positions in Republican and Democratic administrations, said polls show that South Koreans had increasingly supported the idea of pursuing their own nuclear weapons.

“The United States has been working really hard to try to persuade South Korea that they are protected,” said Kroenig, who is now with the Atlantic Council, a Washington think tank. Scaling back the exercises “potentially undermines that message”.

Trump’s turnabout came even after the South Koreans worked to flatter the American president, eager to gain favour on critical issues such as trade and defence.

As soon as he sat down for his meeting with Trump last year, new President Lee Jae Myung praised the Oval Office’s elaborate decor. Laying it on thick, Lee affirmed Trump’s assertion that Kim would not have pursued his nuclear ambitions had Trump won a second consecutive term in 2020, while dangling the prospect of an eventual Trump Tower in North Korea.

Trump just hours earlier had appeared to show sympathy for Lee’s predecessor, Yoon Suk-yeol, who had been ousted from office after imposing martial law in December 2024.

On Tuesday, Lee’s office said the Ulchi exercise was defensive and not intended to attack the North or raise tensions.

Removing umbrella

Charles Kupchan, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, said Trump’s scaling back of the exercises might prompt long-time allies to think more about their own security without US help.

“They are hoping that the American umbrella is there for the future,” said Kupchan, who worked on the National Security Council under Democratic presidents Bill Clinton and Obama, “but they have to at least contemplate the idea that Uncle Sam won’t be there for them”.

Kupchan said Trump was not mistaken in wanting to have South Korea, as well as the Europeans, contribute more to their defence. But, he said, the president’s unpredictable approach cut through the solidarity that undergirded those alliances “because he ends up insulting allies”.

Fried said Trump seemed unwilling to “take a win” after browbeating Nato members and Asian allies into increasing their defence spending.

“Nato is building up, South Korea is building up, Japan is building up. Trump has a problem with taking the win,” said Fried, who is currently at the Atlantic Council. “It’s like he wants to burn it all down.”

John Herbst, a former ambassador to Ukraine under president George W. Bush, said the Korea decision showed how inconsistent the Trump administration could be in its policy pronouncements. But in general, he said, the US had maintained long-term alliances.

“If these things grow in frequency and in importance, obviously we will be in the process of taking apart the alliance system, which has served us so well since the end of World War II,” said Herbst, who also is with the Atlantic Council. “But despite some statements which seem to head in that direction, we have not headed there in a consistent, strong way.”

Kupchan agreed. While the president’s language could be taken as “we’re done with you”, he said, “the reality is that, at least as of today, Trump has left intact America’s forward bases and its core alliance relationships”.

Whether Trump’s message to South Korea will amount to a meaningful policy change or a fleeting social media post is up in the air.

“He’s an unpredictable president,” Kroenig said. “If we move on and the exercises go as planned and we never hear anything about this again, I wouldn’t be surprised.”

Additional reporting by Bloomberg, Reuters

item.title: [SCMP] Can Indonesia build on rising EV demand to become a production powerhouse?
item.description:
Indonesia’s next electric-vehicle push will test whether President Prabowo Subianto can turn rising demand, nickel wealth and consumer subsidies into an integrated domestic industry that captures more value at home, or merely make imported and locally assembled EVs cheaper to buy.

Analysts warn that without stricter local-content rules and stronger links between nickel processing, battery production and vehicle assembly, the incentives risk reinforcing Indonesia’s role as a large EV market rather than moving it up the supply chain.

Prabowo gave the agenda a public stage on August 13, when he marked the production of the 20,000th electric motorcycle at ALVA’s factory in Cikarang, West Java, and called on the manufacturer’s parent company, Indika Energy, to raise output to 200,000 units and eventually 2 million.
item.content:encoded:
Indonesia’s next electric-vehicle push will test whether President Prabowo Subianto can turn rising demand, nickel wealth and consumer subsidies into an integrated domestic industry that captures more value at home, or merely make imported and locally assembled EVs cheaper to buy.

Analysts warn that without stricter local-content rules and stronger links between nickel processing, battery production and vehicle assembly, the incentives risk reinforcing Indonesia’s role as a large EV market rather than moving it up the supply chain.

Prabowo gave the agenda a public stage on August 13, when he marked the production of the 20,000th electric motorcycle at ALVA’s factory in Cikarang, West Java, and called on the manufacturer’s parent company, Indika Energy, to raise output to 200,000 units and eventually 2 million.

The event launched what Prabowo and the government described as a “national electric-motorcycle ecosystem”, with a government release saying the initiative would include lower instalment rates and zero down payments.

Prabowo also said Indonesia aimed to begin mass production of home-grown electric cars no later than 2028.

The bigger test will come with a separate EV stimulus package, which officials have said will be announced shortly and is expected to set the rules for which vehicles, battery types and local producers receive support.

In his 2027 budget address on Friday, Prabowo linked those consumer incentives to industrial policy, promising support for domestic electric-motorcycle production and outlining plans for a wider supply chain covering batteries, components, software and after-sales services.

“Electric motorcycle subsidies and probably later electric cars will create markets for the national industry,” Prabowo said.

The key question is how far the eligibility rules will support local factories, component suppliers, battery production, technology transfer and jobs, rather than only reducing the cost of vehicles already on the market.

Earlier this month, officials said the stimulus would cover about 500,000 electric motorbikes and focus on products creating high value in Indonesia, but domestic-content (TKDN) requirements were still being finalised.

Purchasing incentives

The incentives being considered include a full exemption from the luxury goods sales tax and a government-borne value added tax incentive of 40 per cent for eligible models.

The relief would apply strictly to battery EVs, excluding hybrids and plug-in hybrid types. Battery composition was also confirmed as a criterion, with officials weighing whether to favour nickel-based batteries over other chemistries.

The Association of Indonesia Automotive Industries (Gaikindo) recorded sales of 69,739 battery EV units in the first half of 2026, an 80.8 per cent year-on-year increase for the category.

A July 15 report by Detikoto, an Indonesian car news portal, based on Gaikindo sales data, showed the top five brands dominating the national EV market were BYD at 30.73 per cent, followed by Jaecoo at 24.36 per cent, then Geely, Wuling and GAC Aion.

These figures indicate a rapidly expanding market where consumer incentives could play a decisive role.

In May, the Indonesian Business Council said electric motorcycle sales exceeded 100,000 units in 2024 for the first time but fell to 55,059 the next year after the previous subsidy programme – at 7 million rupiah (US$393) per unit – ended.

“This shows that public interest is growing, but affordability remains a key factor in consumer decisions,” the council said.

Missing segments

For analysts, the bigger question is whether fresh incentives can draw more production into Indonesia, rather than simply accelerate sales in a market still led by foreign brands.
